S001. The Spring That Talks Back   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
(Name) has been walking in the hills all morning and is thirsty enough to drink a river. At last (he/she) finds a little spring tucked under a rock, where ferns lean over the water and a single blue dragonfly keeps guard on a reed. (Name) kneels and cups (his/her) hands. Before (he/she) can drink, the water clears its throat.
"Ask me anything," it says, in a voice like a very old aunt who has been interrupted in the middle of something. "But only one thing. I'm busy."
(Name) looks around for whoever is playing the joke. There is nobody, only the dragonfly, which looks as if it has heard all this before.

Choice A: Ask What to Be Good At
Choice B: Ask Nothing and Just Drink

CHOICE A: ASK WHAT TO BE GOOD AT
First popup: (Name) clears (his/her) own throat, feeling very silly. "What am I meant to be good at?" (he/she) asks. The spring bubbles thoughtfully for a long moment, the way a person drums their fingers on a table...

Ending A1 -- THE GREEN THUMB. Chance 50%. EFFECT: gains 20 to 30 Farming; now likes vegetables (story only: VV2-VV5 vegetables, VV1 turnips; no like word changes farming)
"Plants," says the spring. "You've always liked plants. You just never noticed. Who do you think kept that bean vine alive by your door all last summer?" (Name) opens (his/her) mouth to argue, and finds (he/she) can't. On the walk home (he/she) stops to look at every leaf, every seedling, every weed pushing through a crack in the path. By the end of the week (he/she) has dirt under every fingernail and can't stop talking about soil. The farmers, who have been asking for help for years, are delighted. Everyone else is a little tired of hearing about soil.

Ending A2 -- THE RUDE SPRING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: now dislikes swimming (VV1-VV5: swimming)
"Not swimming, that's for sure," says the spring, and gurgles with laughter. "I've seen you paddle. You swim like a coconut with ambitions." It goes on for some time about (name)'s kicking, (his/her) splashing, and one particular afternoon at the lagoon that (name) had hoped nobody remembered. (Name) gets up, red to the ears, and stomps off down the hill without drinking a drop. From that day on, (he/she) can't stand the sound of running water, and nobody can talk (him/her) into so much as wading.

CHOICE B: ASK NOTHING AND JUST DRINK
First popup: (Name) decides that talking water is none of (his/her) business. (He/She) says "No thank you," politely, and drinks. The spring goes very quiet, as if it is deciding whether to be offended...

Ending B1 -- JUST WATER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The spring seems almost insulted to be treated like a spring, and says nothing more. The water is cold, sweet and perfectly ordinary. (Name) drinks until (his/her) belly sloshes, fills (his/her) gourd, thanks the spring anyway, and walks home very refreshed. When (he/she) tells the story at supper, half the village laughs and the other half goes quiet and asks exactly which rock it was.

Ending B2 -- A TASTE OF HONEY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: one of these, 50:50: loses one dislike (at random), OR gains 10 to 20 in one random skill (never Farming)
The water tastes faintly of honey, and something else, something like the first warm day after the rains. (Name) drinks, sits back on (his/her) heels, and feels a knot (he/she) didn't know (he/she) had come undone somewhere in (his/her) chest. (He/She) comes home humming. The next morning (he/she) picks up the one job (he/she) has always grumbled about, or never had the knack for, and does it, and does it well, and doesn't grumble once. The others keep glancing at (him/her) as if (he/she) might be ill. "The spring," is all (name) will say.

  seeker: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)

[answers: Ask What to Be Good At] [mood: warm] [EFFECT: gains 20 to 30 Farming; now likes vegetables (story only: VV2-VV5 vegetables, VV1 turnips; no like word changes farming)]

  - "Patience," says the spring. "You're good at waiting for people." (Name) goes home and is suddenly wonderful with the little ones. [answers: Ask What to Be Good At, Argue with the Spring] [mood: warm] [EFFECT: gains 10 to 20 Parenting]

S002. A Face in the Tide Pool   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
At low tide the rocks are a maze of warm, still pools, and (name) has come down to look for crabs. The air smells of salt and sun-dried seaweed, and a single hermit crab is the only one watching. (Name) leans over a perfectly round pool to see what's in it. (His/her) reflection leans over too.
Then the reflection smiles, a moment too late. Then it waves.
(Name) did not wave. (Name) is not smiling. The reflection keeps waving, friendly and patient, as if it has been waiting a long time for (him/her) to come by.

Choice A: Wave Back
Choice B: Throw a Pebble In

CHOICE A: WAVE BACK
First popup: Slowly, feeling very foolish, (name) lifts a hand and waves. The reflection's smile grows wider. The water in the pool begins to tremble, though there is no wind at all...

Ending A1 -- THE ONE WHO CLIMBED OUT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: DUPLICATE of (name), named (made1); joins the village
The reflection reaches up, takes hold of the rock, and climbs out of the pool, dripping, to shake (name)'s hand. It has (name)'s face, (name)'s hair and (name)'s knobbly knees. It does not have (name)'s opinions. "Is that how you wear your hair?" it says. "On purpose?" It follows (name) home, criticising the path, the weather and (name)'s walk the whole way. The village takes a week to tell them apart, and then decides it doesn't matter. The newcomer chooses the name (made1), takes up all the jobs (name) never liked, and has never once been seen near a tide pool again.

Ending A2 -- POLITELY TURNED DOWN. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The reflection waves again, a slow, kind little wave, the way someone would wave to a child on a passing canoe. Then it sinks back into the dark of the pool and is gone, and the water shows only (name), looking very confused. (He/She) sits on the rocks until the tide comes back in, waiting for it to return. It never does. (Name) walks home with the strange feeling of having been politely turned down by (himself/herself).

CHOICE B: THROW A PEBBLE IN
First popup: (Name) picks up a pebble and, before (he/she) can think better of it, tosses it straight at the smiling face. Plop...

Ending B1 -- JUST A POOL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The ripples spread out and break the face into a hundred wobbling pieces. When the water settles, the pool is just a pool, with (name)'s ordinary, worried face in it. A small striped fish swims out from under a rock, looks at the pebble, then looks at (name) with deep reproach, and swims back under again. (Name) apologises to the fish. It does not accept.

Ending B2 -- THE POOL GOES DARK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: now dislikes swimming (VV1-VV5: swimming; crabs are story only)
The pebble hits the reflection right on the nose. The face flinches, really flinches, and the pool goes dark and cold, as if a cloud has passed over just that one small circle of water. The hermit crab that was watching from the rocks drops off its perch and hurries away. (Name) is very cross with (himself/herself) for the rest of the day, and can't shake the feeling that (he/she) hurt someone. (He/She) never swims near the tide pools again, and if anyone asks why, (he/she) changes the subject.

MIXER SEED S002
Premise: At low tide, looking for crabs among the warm pools, (name) leans over a perfectly round pool, and (his/her) reflection smiles a moment too late. Then it waves.
Roles:
  looker: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
Approaches: Wave Back | Throw a Pebble In | Call Someone Over | Walk Away Without Looking Back
Outcome pool:
  - The reflection climbs out, dripping, with (name)'s face and hair and knobbly knees, but not (name)'s opinions. "Is that how you wear your hair? On purpose?" It takes the name (made1) and all the jobs (name) never liked. [answers: Wave Back, Call Someone Over] [mood: funny] [EFFECT: DUPLICATE of (name), named (made1); joins the village]
  - The reflection gives a slow, kind little wave and sinks back into the dark of the pool. (Name) walks home feeling politely turned down by (himself/herself). [answers: Wave Back, Walk Away Without Looking Back] [mood: eerie] [EFFECT: none]
  - The ripples break the face into a hundred wobbling pieces, and a small striped fish swims out and looks at (name) with deep reproach. Just a pool after all. [answers: Throw a Pebble In] [mood: funny] [EFFECT: none]
  - The pebble hits the reflection right on the nose. It flinches, and the pool goes dark and cold. (Name) never swims near the tide pools again. [answers: Throw a Pebble In] [mood: eerie] [EFFECT: now dislikes swimming (VV1-VV5: swimming; crabs are story only)]
  - By the time a friend comes running, only one face looks up from the pool. The friend thinks (name) has had too much sun. [answers: Call Someone Over] [mood: funny] [EFFECT: none]
  - (Name) walks away fast, and that night finds wet footprints on the floor of (his/her) hut, leading in and back out. [answers: Walk Away Without Looking Back] [mood: eerie] [EFFECT: none]
Flavour lines:
  - A single hermit crab is the only one watching.
  - The tide pool is perfectly round, as if someone measured it.
  - The air smells of salt and sun-dried seaweed.
  - The reflection keeps waving, friendly and patient.

S003. The Very Long Nap   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 18 to 40 (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
It is the hottest afternoon of the year. The cicadas are whirring like a hundred tiny saws and even the chickens have given up and lain down in the dust. (Name) has been working since dawn and spots a strange tree at the edge of the clearing, with leaves the soft blue of a morning sky and a patch of shade beneath it that looks cool as a river.
"Five minutes," (he/she) tells nobody, and lies down.
When (name) wakes, (his/her) back aches. (His/her) knees creak like an old door. And there are little white flowers growing in (his/her) hair, rooted in it, as though (he/she) were part of the ground.

Choice A: Hurry Home
Choice B: Lie Back Down

CHOICE A: HURRY HOME
First popup: (Name) scrambles up, groaning, brushing at the flowers, and hobbles towards the village as fast as (his/her) complaining knees will go. Behind (him/her), the blue leaves rustle, though there is no wind...

Ending A1 -- TWENTY YEARS IN ONE NIGHT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: changes age (20 years older; never past elder)
Nobody recognises (him/her) at first. A child points and asks if a visitor has come. Only one night has passed in the village, but while (name) slept, the tree's roots drank years from (him/her) and pushed them out again as those little white flowers. The elders look at the flowers for a long time and say nothing helpful. (Name) sits down heavily on (his/her) own doorstep, looks at (his/her) wrinkled hands, and takes it surprisingly well. "At least I'm well rested," (he/she) says. "Somebody else can do the afternoon work."

Ending A2 -- A LITTLE DISTINGUISHED. Chance 50%. EFFECT: changes age (5 years older); new look (the "old" head look)
(Name) gets away before the roots can drink more than a few years. One by one the little white flowers drop out of (his/her) hair on the path home, and wither the moment they touch the ground. By the time (he/she) reaches the village, all that's left is a streak of grey at (his/her) temples and a few new lines around (his/her) eyes. "You look distinguished," everyone says, very kindly, which is what people say when they mean older. (Name) avoids the blue tree from then on, and spends the next hot afternoon resting in the most ordinary shade (he/she) can find.

CHOICE B: LIE BACK DOWN
First popup: (Name) is very comfortable, and very tired, and the shade is very cool. (He/She) remembers something the elders once said about blue trees, though not quite what. (He/She) closes (his/her) eyes to think about it...

Ending B1 -- EAT THE FLOWERS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Then (he/she) remembers. Whoever eats the blue tree's flowers gets back what the tree drank. (Name) sits up and picks every single white flower out of (his/her) hair, wincing, and eats them one by one. They are horribly bitter, like chewing a sandal. Then (he/she) lies down and naps again, just to be sure. (He/She) wakes up with (his/her) own knees, (his/her) own back, and (his/her) own luscious hair, and runs home, and is late for supper. Nobody believes a word of it, which (name) feels is very unfair.

Ending B2 -- THE LONGEST NAP. Chance 50%. EFFECT: changes age (to elder)
The second nap is even longer. The roots go deeper, and drink more, and the flowers grow thicker until (name)'s hair is a white crown of them. When (he/she) finally wakes, the sun is setting and (name) is an elder, with soft grey skin and slow, careful hands. (He/She) lies there for a while looking up through the blue leaves. "Well," (he/she) says at last. "That's that, then." (He/She) is so comfortable under the tree that (he/she) doesn't mind one bit, and the village has to send two strong young people to carry (him/her) home for dinner.

MIXER SEED S003
Premise: On the hottest afternoon of the year, (name) lies down "for five minutes" in the cool shade of a strange tree with sky-blue leaves, and wakes with an aching back, creaking knees and little white flowers rooted in (his/her) hair.
Roles:
  sleeper: one villager aged 18 to 40 (not protected)
Approaches: Hurry Home | Lie Back Down | Pull the Flowers Out | Ask the Tree to Give Them Back
Outcome pool:
  - Only one night has passed, but the tree's roots drank twenty years and pushed them out as flowers. "At least I'm well rested," says (name). "Somebody else can do the afternoon work." [answers: Hurry Home, Ask the Tree to Give Them Back] [mood: funny] [EFFECT: changes age (20 years older; never past elder)]
  - The flowers drop out on the path home and wither, leaving a streak of grey and a few new lines. "You look distinguished," everyone says, very kindly. [answers: Hurry Home, Pull the Flowers Out] [mood: warm] [EFFECT: changes age (5 years older); new look (the "old" head look)]
  - (Name) remembers: whoever eats the blue tree's flowers gets back what it drank. They taste like chewing a sandal, but (he/she) wakes with (his/her) own knees, back and luscious hair. Nobody believes a word of it. [answers: Lie Back Down, Pull the Flowers Out] [mood: funny] [EFFECT: none]
  - The second nap is longer, the roots drink more, and (name) wakes an elder with a white crown of flowers. "Well. That's that, then." Two strong young people carry (him/her) home for dinner. [answers: Lie Back Down] [mood: warm] [EFFECT: changes age (to elder)]
  - (Name) pleads with the tree. A single blue leaf drops onto (his/her) chest, and the years seep back in with the evening dew. [answers: Ask the Tree to Give Them Back] [mood: eerie] [EFFECT: none]
  - Each flower comes out with a sting like a plucked hair, and a year comes back with each one, all but a handful. [answers: Pull the Flowers Out] [mood: tense] [EFFECT: changes age (3 years older)]

S004. Two Hammocks, One Storm   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: two villagers aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
A summer storm rolls in after dark, smelling of hot stone and green rain. The palms bend and whip like dancers who have had too much to drink, and the whole village is shut up tight. Except (name1) and (name2), who both decided it was too hot to sleep inside and strung their hammocks between the same two palms on the beach. Both of them sleep through everything.
At midnight a bolt of lightning strikes the sand between the hammocks with a crack that shakes every hut on the island.
In the morning, (name1) wakes up, yawns, and finds (himself/herself) looking at (name1)'s own face, snoring in the other hammock. (Name2) wakes up a moment later and screams in (name1)'s voice.

Choice A: Try to Switch Back
Choice B: Make the Best of It

CHOICE A: TRY TO SWITCH BACK
First popup: The healers have never heard of anything like it. The elders say lightning took them, so lightning must give them back. That evening (name1) and (name2) sit back to back on the sand between the two palms, under a sky that is, very annoyingly, clear...

Ending A1 -- THE SECOND STORM. Chance 50%. EFFECT: body swap, then swapped back (no lasting change)
They sit there for three nights. On the third, the clouds come boiling back over the hills and the thunder rolls in like a wave. Both of them squeeze their eyes shut. CRACK! The lightning strikes the sand between them again, almost exactly where it struck before, and in the morning they're back in their own bodies, ears ringing and very glad of it. "Your knees are terrible," says (name1), rubbing (his/her) own. "Your stomach is worse," says (name2). "What do you even eat?" They don't speak for a day, and then they laugh about it for the rest of their lives.

Ending A2 -- THE STORM THAT NEVER CAME. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent)
They wait all through the stormy season. The rain comes, the wind comes, but the lightning never strikes the beach again. In the end (name1) and (name2) give up, and learn to live each other's lives. It is harder than either of them expected. (Name1) finds out why (name2) always walks so slowly in the mornings. (Name2) finds out why (name1) never sits on the left side of the fire. By the end of the season they know more about each other than anyone else in the village, and they argue less than they used to, which their families find very strange.

CHOICE B: MAKE THE BEST OF IT
First popup: "Well," says (name2), in (name1)'s voice. "We can't go anywhere like this. Could be worse. I've always wondered what you actually do all day." (Name1) looks down at (name2)'s hands, and has to admit (he/she) has wondered the same...

Ending B1 -- THE NEW JOBS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent); each gains 10 to 20 in the other's best skill
They each try the other's job for a day, with a great deal of shouting across the village for advice. "Which end of this do I hold?" "The END THAT ISN'T SHARP!" By evening they're both exhausted and oddly proud of themselves. It goes so well that they do it again the next day, and the next. They never do swap back, and after a while they stop trying. Both of them end up better at the other one's work than they ever were at their own.

Ending B2 -- THE HEALERS' TEA. Chance 50%. EFFECT: body swap reversed; both now dislike medicine (VV1-VV5: medicine)
By midday they can't stand it. (Name1) keeps tripping over (name2)'s feet and (name2) keeps eating (name1)'s lunch "because this stomach is always hungry." They march to the healers together and demand that something be done. The healers mix up something thick, grey and bubbling and make them drink every drop. It tastes like a swamp. It smells worse. But in the time it takes to stop gagging, each of them is back behind their own eyes. Neither of them can taste anything for a week, and from then on neither of them will go near the healers' hut unless they're carried.

S005. The Wind That Took a Name   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
A warm wind comes through the village one morning, from no direction in particular. It picks up leaves, feathers and loose bits of string, and smells faintly of cinnamon bark. All the chickens turn to face the same way as it passes, which chickens never do.
Just then, (name) steps out of (his/her) hut and calls good morning to a neighbour. The gust snatches the words right out of (his/her) mouth, name and all, and blows them into a dry seed pod rolling past. The pod rattles away down the path.
(Name) opens (his/her) mouth to say something else, and realises (he/she) can't remember what (he/she) is called. The neighbour scratches their head. Neither can they. Neither, it turns out, can anyone.

Choice A: Chase the Wind
Choice B: Pick a New One

CHOICE A: CHASE THE WIND
First popup: (Name) takes off after the seed pod, barefoot, past the huts, through the gardens, scattering chickens in every direction. The pod bounces ahead along the path towards the cliffs, never quite close enough to grab...

Ending A1 -- THE POD AT THE CLIFFS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none (the name comes back)
At the cliff edge, the wind finally runs out of island and lets go of everything it took. A feather, somebody's hat, a long tangle of string and the little seed pod come tumbling down at (name)'s feet. (He/She) snatches up the pod and cracks it open, and very faintly, in (his/her) own voice, hears (his/her) name whispered inside. It comes back at once, like remembering a word that was on the tip of (his/her) tongue. (Name) walks home saying it out loud to everyone (he/she) passes, just to be sure. (He/She) also returns the hat.

Ending A2 -- THE WIND IS FASTER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: LOSES NAME (name becomes "?")
The wind is faster. It swings the pod up over the trees and away out to sea, and that is the last anyone sees of it. (Name) comes home out of breath, with burrs in (his/her) feet and nothing to show for it. The villagers try every name they can think of, but none of them is right, and none of them sticks. In the end they call (him/her) "?" for now. (He/She) answers to it cheerfully enough. Sometimes, on windy days, (he/she) stands at the cliff edge for a while and listens.

CHOICE B: PICK A NEW ONE
First popup: "Well, there's no use running after the wind," says one of the elders. "Nobody's ever caught it yet. Somebody fetch the drum." In no time at all, half the village has gathered around (name) in a ring...

Ending B1 -- THE NAMING CEREMONY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: CHANGES NAME (to a random default name)
The village holds a little naming ceremony right there in the middle of the path. Everyone shouts suggestions at once. Some are lovely. Some are rude. One is the name of a fish. The elders bang the drum and tell everyone to shout louder, and at last one name rises above all the others, and (name) hears it and thinks, "Yes. That one." The name that sticks is (renamed). There's a small cheer, the chickens turn back to face their normal directions, and everyone goes back to work.

Ending B2 -- THE WIND COMES BACK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: LOSES NAME (name becomes "?")
Nobody can agree. Every name gets shouted down. One family insists on a name that another family thinks is unlucky. The children want something that rhymes with "pudding." And every time the village finally settles on one, the warm wind gusts back through the ring, smelling of cinnamon bark, and snatches that one away too, until nobody can remember any of the names they tried. By evening the wind has gone, and so has every name, and (name) is left with none at all: just "?". It never comes back. Years later, (name) is still "?", and quite likes it, and the argument still flares up every so often at festivals.

S007. The Granary Gets Wet   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: no one picked (the whole village)
EVENT TEXT
The roof of the food store has been leaking for weeks. It started as one drip. Then a brown stain appeared on the inside wall, and grew, slowly, day after day, until it turned into a large mushy mess. Several people pointed it out to each other. Everyone thought someone had told the builders.
Nobody did.
Last night it rained harder than it has rained all year, and the rain found every hole. This morning the store is ankle-deep in water, the baskets are sagging and dripping, and most of the food is waterlogged.

Choice A: Dry What's Left
Choice B: Blame Someone

CHOICE A: DRY WHAT'S LEFT
First popup: The whole village forms a chain, passing dripping baskets hand to hand out of the store and into the open air. Every flat rock, every roof and every mat is covered with soggy food spread out in hopes the sun will dry it out...

Ending A1 -- MOSTLY A SMELL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (normal amount)
The sun takes its time. By noon the village smells like a wet dog that has rolled in fruit. Some of the food dries well enough to keep, and is carried back in, wrinkled and sad-looking. Most of it does not, and by evening it is just a smell, and then a pile, and then the pigs' problem. The builders finally go up on the roof and find eleven holes. "Eleven," they keep saying, to anyone who'll listen. "You should have said something when there was one." Your village loses (award) food.

Ending A2 -- THE SUN SHOWS UP. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (small amount)
Just as the last basket comes out, the clouds tear open and the sun blazes down like it's trying to make up for last night. Steam rises off every rock in the village. By afternoon almost everything is dry and only a little is spoiled. The roof is mended by lunchtime the next day, mostly out of embarrassment, and somebody patches over the mushy parts. Your village loses (award) food.

CHOICE B: BLAME SOMEONE
First popup: "Who was supposed to fix it?" someone asks, and the whole village turns to look at someone else. Within moments everyone is pointing, and everyone is pointing at a different person...

Ending B1 -- THE BIRDS WIN. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (large amount)
The argument goes on for most of the day. The builders say nobody told them. The farmers say they told the builders, sort of, once, in passing. Someone brings up something that happened at a festival two years ago, and that starts a whole new argument. Nobody wins. While they argue, a great flock of birds settles on the soaked baskets left outside the door and eats until they can barely fly. Your village loses (award) food.

Ending B2 -- THE ROOF-MENDING PICNIC. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (small amount)
Everyone blames everyone. Voices are raised. Someone stomps off. And then, slowly, everyone starts to feel a bit bad, because they all knew about the mess. One by one, people start climbing onto the roof with armfuls of thatch, still muttering. By evening the roof is mended, the food is drying in the sun, and somehow it has all ended with a picnic on the grass. The villagers end up eating up the food that wouldn't keep anyway. Your village loses (award) food.

S008. The Coconut Bonanza   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: no one picked (the whole village); in ending A2 one random villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
Every palm on the island has decided, all at once, that this is the year to sprout coconuts. Nobody knows why. The elders say it happens once in a lifetime, if a village is lucky. The whole village smells of split husks and sweet milk, and ripe, tasty coconuts fall day and night, thudding into the sand, bouncing off roofs, rolling down the paths and into the cooking pots.
Everyone can hear the thuds from every hut. Babies have stopped flinching at them. Nobody walks under a palm tree any more without looking straight up first, and the chickens have learned to run in zigzags.

Choice A: Gather Them All
Choice B: Throw a Coconut Festival

CHOICE A: GATHER THEM ALL
First popup: The village puts down every other job and turns out with baskets. Children race each other to the fallen nuts, adults haul full baskets on their shoulders, and the elders sit in the open sand well away from the trees, shouting directions...

Ending A1 -- FULL TO THE RAFTERS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (large amount)
Every basket in the village is filled, then every pot, then every bowl, then every hat. When they run out of hats, they start piling coconuts in a great pyramid in the middle of the village, and the children climb it and refuse to come down. The stores have never been so full. For a whole season the village drinks coconut milk with every meal, and the coconut-shell pile grows into a little hill that the goats use as a lookout. Your villagers gain (award) food.

Ending A2 -- THE ONE THAT FOUND (NAME). Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (normal amount); (name) is INJURED (loses health)

CHOICE B: THROW A COCONUT FESTIVAL
First popup: "We'll never eat all these anyway," someone says, "so let's not try. Let's celebrate!" The idea catches like fire in dry grass. Within an hour there are cooking fires lit all over the village and the first drums are going...

Ending B1 -- THE COCONUT-SHELL BAND. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (normal amount); every villager is happier (stock island-event effect)
There is coconut milk and coconut bread and coconut stew and coconut sweets. There are coconut-rolling races and coconut-catching contests and a very serious coconut-balancing competition that one of the elders wins easily. There's even a band of coconut-shell drummers, who are terrible and loud and wonderful. Everyone eats too much and nobody regrets it. The leftovers alone fill the stores. Your villagers gain (award) food.

Ending B2 -- EATEN ON THE SPOT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (small amount)
The festival is so good that it goes on for three days, and half the coconuts on the island are eaten right there, on the spot, by people lying in the sand with their eyes closed. S019. The Glowing Berries   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]

S021. The Spring of Small Years   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one adult aged 20 to 45 (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
High in the hills there is a spring that, the elders say, "gives back what you spent." Nobody quite knows what that means, and the elders won't say any more. But the children whisper that a very old water spirit lives at the bottom and keeps the years that people spend. The water is the blue of a kingfisher's wing, and nothing grows on its banks but soft white moss.
(Name) has been cutting wood up there all morning and is hot, sticky and sore. Without thinking about any of the stories, (he/she) strips off and wades in. The water is wonderfully cool. And as (he/she) scrubs (his/her) arms, the years start to wash off (his/her) skin like grey silt, clouding the blue water around (him/her) in soft swirls.
(Name) climbs out feeling very light. Rather too light. (His/her) clothes, when (he/she) pulls them back on, are suddenly far too big. Should (he/she) run home before it gets any worse, or climb back in to see what else the spring will give back?

CHOICE A: RUN HOME

The elders say the cave is so old it has heard every voice on the island, and that once in a long while, when someone shouts with all their heart, it gives back more than the voice.

S023. Lightning on the Research Hut   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: no one picked (the whole village); in ending B2, every villager who carries a bucket
EVENT TEXT
A storm sits over the village all night, grumbling like a hungry belly and flashing white behind the hills. Nobody sleeps much. Just before dawn, a single bolt of lightning splits the sky and strikes the research hut with a crack so loud that half the village falls out of bed.
Flames lick up through the thatch. Smoke pours out of the door in a thick grey column.
And then, out of the smoke, comes a researcher, coughing, blackened from head to foot, (his/her) hair standing straight up on end, waving (his/her) arms and shouting, at the top of (his/her) lungs, that something "ABSOLUTELY FASCINATING" has happened. Choice A: Go and See
Choice B: Put Out the Fire First

CHOICE A: GO AND SEE
First popup: The researcher is so excited that a small crowd follows (him/her) right back into the smoking hut, ducking under the burning edge of the thatch and coughing, to see what all the fuss is about...

Ending A1 -- GLASS FLOWERS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (large amount)
In the middle of the floor, where the lightning came down through the roof, the sand that the researchers keep for their experiments has melted into glass. Not a lump: shapes. Long, branching, twisting shapes, like frozen flowers, like the roots of a tree made of ice. They glow faintly in the firelight. Everyone forgets about the fire for a moment and just stares. The researchers will have new questions for a year about how heat can do such a thing, and the bucket chain gets the fire out just in time. Your villagers gain (award) tech points.

Ending A2 -- THE FASCINATING THING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech loss (normal amount)
It turns out the fascinating thing is that the roof is gone. Entirely. The researcher points up at the open sky with a delighted look, and everyone looks up, and then down at the floor, where the roof has landed, still burning, on top of the shelf where the notes were kept. Nobody wants to be the one to point that out. By the time the fire is out, the notes are ash. The researcher stops being excited quite suddenly. Your villagers lose (award) tech points.

CHOICE B: PUT OUT THE FIRE FIRST
First popup: "Fascinating later! Water now!" someone bellows. In moments the whole village is lined up from the river to the hut, passing buckets, pots and bowls hand over hand, while the smoke rolls overhead...

Ending B1 -- NOTHING LOST. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The bucket chain works like a dream. The fire is out before it can reach the shelves, and nothing is lost but the roof thatch, which can be replaced. Everyone stands around steaming, soot-faced and pleased with themselves. The fascinating thing, when the researcher finally gets to show it, turns out to be a small scorch mark in the shape of a fish. Everyone agrees it does look like a fish. The researcher's hair takes a whole week to lie down.

Ending B2 -- THE BUCKET CHAIN. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech loss (small amount); every villager in the bucket chain gains 5 Building
By the time the fire is out, half the notes are ash and the hut is a black, dripping shell. But the bucket chain was so well run, so quick and clever, that the builders were watching it and learned something: where to put people, how to pass things fastest, which way the wind carries sparks. They rebuild the hut stronger and better than before, with everyone who carried a bucket helping, and every one of them comes away knowing a little more about building. Your villagers lose (award) tech points.

S024. The Sleepwalkers   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: two villagers aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
(Name1) and (name2) both sleepwalk. Everyone knows it. Usually it's harmless and very funny: once (name1) was found fast asleep in a fishing net hanging from a tree, and once (name2) woke up at dawn in the middle of the goat pen, holding a goat, which did not seem to mind.
Last night there was a full moon, huge and orange over the sea. Under it, without waking, (name1) and (name2) both got up off their mats, walked out of the village and up the hill to the old carved stones, where nobody goes. They met in the middle of the stone circle. They bowed to each other, very formally. Then they walked home, and each went into the other one's hut. The elders say the first people raised those stones so two souls could trade places for a night and learn each other's burdens, and that the swap is meant to wear off by morning.
When they wake up in the morning, they are in the wrong beds. And the wrong bodies. It hasn't worn off. Should they try to sleepwalk back to the stones, or tie themselves down so the stones can't call them again?

Choice A: Sleepwalk Back
Choice B: Tie Their Ankles to Their Beds

CHOICE A: SLEEPWALK BACK
First popup: The elders say whatever happened at the stones can only be undone at the stones. So on the next full moon, (name1) and (name2) go to bed very early, in their own huts, lie down very still, and hope with all their hearts...

Ending A1 -- THE BOW. Chance 50%. EFFECT: body swap, then swapped back (no lasting change)
In the morning, they both wake up at the stones, cold and stiff and wet with dew, lying side by side in the middle of the circle. They sit up. They look at each other. Without a word, without knowing why, they both stand up and bow. Something shifts, like stepping off a boat onto land. They walk home, the right way this time, into the right huts, and climb into the right beds, and when they wake up again at noon they are themselves. Neither of them has sleepwalked since.

Ending A2 -- BEHIND THE CLOUDS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent)
They try. They really try. But on the night of the full moon, the clouds roll in thick and grey off the sea and the moon never shows its face at all. Neither of them sleepwalks a single step. They wake up in their own huts, in each other's bodies, exactly as before. After three more cloudy full moons, they give up. "Well," says (name1), stretching (name2)'s arms. "I suppose it's an adventure." They decide to treat it as one, and it is.

CHOICE B: TIE THEIR ANKLES TO THEIR BEDS
First popup: "No more wandering," says one of the healers firmly, and ties a length of soft rope around each of their ankles, with the other end tied to the posts of their sleeping mats. "Nobody goes anywhere until we've worked this out." (Name1) and (name2) look at the knots and then at each other...

Ending B1 -- STIFF ANKLES. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent)
It works perfectly. Nobody sleepwalks. Nobody goes near the stones. Nobody swaps back either. Every morning (name1) and (name2) wake up tied to their beds, in each other's bodies, with stiff ankles, and the healers come round, untie them and shake their heads. After a month of this, everyone agrees to stop. The ropes come off. They stay swapped, and in time they get used to it.

Ending B2 -- THE SAME BIT OF ROPE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: body swap reversed; nothing else
The healers tie good knots, but not good enough. In the middle of the night the ropes slip loose, and (name1) and (name2) sleepwalk straight out of their huts and up the hill to the stones again. In the morning they wake up in the middle of the circle, back in their own bodies, both of them holding the same bit of rope, one at each end. Nobody can explain how. The healers keep the rope, and don't let anyone touch it.

S025. A Quiet Afternoon   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager of any age (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
Nothing is happening. Nothing at all. The breeze is soft and smells of warm grass, the work is done for the day, and somewhere a woodpecker is knocking, slow and lazy, as if it has nowhere in particular to be.
(Name) is sitting in the shade of a big rock, doing absolutely nothing, and watching a small crab try to climb the rock. It is a very small crab, and a very large rock. It has been trying for some time. It gets about halfway, slips, tumbles down to the bottom, rights itself, and starts again, with what (name) can only describe as determination.
This is the most interesting thing that has happened all day. Should (name) give the crab a helping hand, or just keep watching?

Choice A: Help the Crab
Choice B: Keep Watching

CHOICE A: HELP THE CRAB
First popup: (Name) watches the crab fall off for the seventh time. That's enough. (He/She) leans over and, very gently, holds out one finger behind the crab, so it has something to push against...

Ending A1 -- THE TOP OF THE ROCK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
With a little nudge, the crab scrambles up the last stretch of rock and reaches the very top. It stands there for a moment, claws raised, looking around at the view as if it has conquered a mountain. Then it immediately climbs straight down the other side and scuttles off into the grass, without so much as a backward look. (Name) sits back against the rock and decides that it was worth it anyway. It's the best thing (he/she) has done all week.

Ending A2 -- FAIR ENOUGH. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The crab does not want help. It whips round and pinches (name)'s finger, hard, for interfering. (Name) yelps and shakes it off, sucking (his/her) finger. The crab glares at (him/her) with its little stalk eyes, then turns round and starts climbing the rock again, on its own, the way it wanted to in the first place. "Fair enough," says (name). (He/She) watches it until the sun goes down, and keeps (his/her) hands to (himself/herself).

CHOICE B: KEEP WATCHING
First popup: (Name) settles back against the warm rock. This is none of (his/her) business. The crab gets halfway, slips, falls, rights itself, and starts again. And again. And again...

Ending B1 -- THE CHEER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
On the eleventh try, the crab finds a little crack in the rock that nobody noticed before, gets a claw into it, and hauls itself up and over the top. "YES!" shouts (name), leaping to (his/her) feet and punching the air. A few villagers walking past stop and stare. They look around for whatever has happened. There's nothing to see but (name), cheering at a rock. Nobody else ever understands why that was the best afternoon of (his/her) whole season.

Ending B2 -- TWO NAPS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Somewhere between the ninth try and the tenth, the sun gets very warm and the woodpecker gets very slow, and (name)'s eyes close. When (he/she) wakes, the shadows are long and gold. (He/She) looks down. The crab is asleep too, tucked right up against (his/her) foot in the warm shade, as if they'd agreed to take the afternoon off together. (Name) doesn't move until it wakes up and wanders off.

S032. The Shipwrecked Family   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: no one picked (the whole village)
EVENT TEXT
At dawn, under a sky still grey and heavy with last night's rain, the fishers spot something out past the reef: a battered outrigger canoe, low in the water, half its float torn away, drifting slowly towards the bay. There are three people clinging to it. A tired, sunburnt adult. A teenager with an arm hooked round the mast. And a small child, wrapped in a soaked cloth, tucked between them.
They are cold. They are hungry. They don't seem quite sure where they are, or which way is land.
They only know where they want to be, the adult calls hoarsely across the water: anywhere dry. The swell over the reef is rough. Should the village risk the canoes to bring them ashore, or send food out to them?

Choice A: Bring Them Ashore
Choice B: Send Food Out to Them

CHOICE A: BRING THEM ASHORE
First popup: Three canoes go out at once. The fishers paddle hard through the swell, lash the wreck to their own boats with rope, and tow it in, while the whole village gathers on the sand with blankets, shouting encouragement...

Ending A1 -- THEY STAY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: NEW VILLAGERS (one adult, one teen aged 14 to 17, one child) arrive and stay; food loss (small amount)
The three of them are carried up the beach and wrapped in every blanket the village owns. The cooks bring warm soup, and then more soup, and then mashed fruit for the little one, and the village keeps feeding them until they finally stop shivering and start to smile. They were fishing, the adult says, and the storm took them, and they've been drifting for four days. When they've rested, the elders offer them a hut. The adult looks at the teenager. The teenager looks at the child, who is already playing with the village children in the sand. They decide to stay. Your village loses (award) food.

Ending A2 -- THE TEENAGER STAYS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: NEW VILLAGER (a teen aged 14 to 17) arrives and stays
They rest for several days, eating and sleeping and slowly getting their strength back. The adult is very grateful, but restless, and spends a lot of time looking out to sea. "The rest of our people will think we're lost," (he/she) says. The builders help mend the outrigger, and the adult and the child paddle off to find home, with full bellies and a basket of food. But the teenager asks to stay. "I like it here," (he/she) says simply. "It's quiet." The adult hugs (him/her) for a long time, then lets (him/her) go.

CHOICE B: SEND FOOD OUT TO THEM
First popup: The reef is rough and the swell is high. Instead of risking more canoes, the fishers paddle out just far enough to throw a bundle of food and a gourd of water across to the wreck. The adult catches them, clumsily, and holds them up with a tired wave...

Ending B1 -- THE BOAT COMES BACK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (normal amount)
They take the food gratefully and eat it there on the drifting wreck. Then the current catches them and carries them on past the bay and round the point, and they're gone. A week later, the very same outrigger comes back into the bay, mended and fully patched, paddled by the same adult and two other strangers, and loaded to the brim with fresh fish, as thanks. "You fed us when we were starving," the adult says. "Now we feed you." Your villagers gain (award) food.

Ending B2 -- "WE COULD SMELL THE COOKING." Chance 50%. EFFECT: NEW VILLAGERS (one adult and one child) arrive and stay
They wave from the boat, and eat, and then, to everyone's surprise, they start paddling. Not out to sea: straight for the shore, as hard as they can, wrecked float and all. They wash up on the beach in a tangle of rope and wet cloth. "We could smell the cooking," the child explains, very seriously, as the villagers help them out. The teenager, it turns out, had only been helping them out at sea, and swims off round the point to (his/her) own people. The adult and the child stay.

S033. The Monkey Raid   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: no one picked (the whole village)
EVENT TEXT
The monkeys have been watching the food store for days. They do it the way only monkeys can: pretending very hard to be interested in absolutely anything else. One of them has been grooming the same patch of fur on its arm for an hour without once taking its eyes off the door. Another has been "sleeping" on the roof of the next hut since breakfast, with one eye open.
This morning, while everyone is out in the fields, they make their move.
By the time the first villager comes back, there are monkeys everywhere. On the roof, in the doorway, in the baskets, swinging from the rafters with yams in both hands and a banana in their teeth. One of them is wearing a bowl as a hat. Should the village chase them off, or try to outsmart them?

Choice A: Chase Them Off
Choice B: Leave Out a Decoy Basket

CHOICE A: CHASE THEM OFF
First popup: The alarm goes up. The whole village comes pelting back from the fields, shouting, waving their arms, banging pots and pans and digging sticks together. The monkeys look up. They do not look worried...

Ending A1 -- AS MUCH AS THEY CAN CARRY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (normal amount)
The villagers run, shout and bang, and the monkeys scatter, eventually, screeching and laughing, up into the trees with as much food as they can carry, and quite a lot that they can't. Fruit rains down on the villagers' heads as the monkeys drop it in their hurry. One of them sits on a high branch and eats a mango slowly, looking down at everyone. The one with the bowl hat keeps the bowl. Your village loses (award) food.

Ending A2 -- SECONDS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (large amount)
The chase goes on all morning. The monkeys run round the huts and the villagers run after them, then the monkeys run back the other way and the villagers turn round, again and again, round and round, until half the village is collapsed in the shade, wheezing. All the field work for the day is undone. And as soon as everyone sits down, the monkeys come straight back for seconds. Your village loses (award) food.

CHOICE B: LEAVE OUT A DECOY BASKET
First popup: The cleverest of the farmers has an idea. Quietly, while the monkeys are busy, (he/she) fills the biggest basket in the village with the rotten fruit from the compost heap, covers the top with a few good mangoes, and leaves it out in the open where the monkeys can't miss it...

Ending B1 -- BETRAYED. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (small amount)
Every monkey in the store drops what it's holding and dives on the decoy basket. They tear away the good mangoes on top, dig in deeper, and come up with handfuls of brown mush. The look on their faces is pure betrayal. They glare at the villagers. They throw some of the mush. Then they leave, deeply offended, and don't come back for a month. The real store is mostly safe. Your village loses (award) food.

Ending B2 -- BOTH BASKETS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (normal amount)
The monkeys take the decoy. They take it very carefully, two of them carrying it between them, up into the trees. Then, while everyone is watching the decoy go, the rest of the troop quietly empties the real store from the other side. By the time anyone notices, they're all gone. Everyone stands in the empty store, impressed despite themselves. "They're cleverer than us," someone says. Nobody argues. Your village loses (award) food.

S037. The Coughing Season   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: no one picked (the whole village); some endings pick random villagers or a random elder (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
A cough is going round the village. It started with one sneeze at breakfast, a week ago. Nobody thought anything of it. Then the person next to the sneezer started coughing, and then the person next to them, and now at night the village sounds as if a flock of geese has moved into every single hut.
The healers have run out of honey. The children have been sent to bed early for three nights running. And nobody, nobody at all, will admit to being the one who sneezed first. Should the healers take everyone in, or should the village let it run its course?

Choice A: Send Everyone to the Healers
Choice B: Let It Run Its Course

CHOICE A: SEND EVERYONE TO THE HEALERS
First popup: The healers set up mats all round the hospital, boil every pot of herbs they have, and line up the whole coughing, sneezing, sniffling village outside the door, one at a time...

Ending A1 -- EVERY LAST COUGH. Chance 50%. EFFECT: all sick villagers are cured (stock island-event effect); every healer gains 5 Healing
The healers work day and night. They make tea after tea, rub chests with strong-smelling ointment, hold steaming bowls under people's noses and make them breathe. They sleep in shifts and eat standing up. By the end of the week, the last cough is gone, and the village is quiet at night again. The healers are so exhausted that they sleep for two whole days, but every one of them comes out of it knowing more than before.

Ending A2 -- TWO FOR EVERY ONE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: three random villagers have an ILLNESS (need the healers)
The healers try. But crowding everyone together in one long line turns out to be the worst idea anyone has had all year. For every villager they cure, two more catch it from the people waiting in line. By the end of the week three of them are properly sick, burning with fever and too weak to get up, and the healers have to keep them in the hospital while everyone else is sent home to cough in peace.

CHOICE B: LET IT RUN ITS COURSE
First popup: "It's just a cough," say the elders. "We've all had coughs. It'll pass." So everyone keeps working, keeps sneezing, keeps coughing, and waits...

Ending B1 -- GRUMBLING BETTER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
It runs its course. Slowly, one by one, everyone gets better on their own, with a lot of grumbling and a great deal of nose-blowing into leaves. After two weeks the geese have left the huts and the village is quiet at night again. Somebody finally admits to being the first sneezer, and is made to fetch everyone's water for a week as punishment.

Ending B2 -- THE OLDEST VILLAGER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: (elder) has a PERMANENT DISABILITY (health loss 20%); now dislikes work (VV1-VV5: work); "old" head look

S038. The Prank Mirror   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]

EVENT TEXT

S039. The Sacred Pool   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: two villagers aged 18 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
Deep in the hills there is a pool inside a ring of black standing stones. The elders say that if two people bathe in it together at midnight, they "will see through each other's eyes." Most people think it's just a nice saying, the kind of thing people say at weddings. The elders say the first two people on the island bathed there so that each could see the world the way the other did, and the stones have kept the custom ever since.
(Name1) and (name2) think it's just a saying too. They've decided to go and find out anyway, mostly for the walk.
They get there just before midnight. The pool is perfectly still, and holds the stars so clearly anyone could count them. The black stones stand around it like people waiting. It is very, very quiet. Should they bathe now, at midnight, as the custom says, or come back when it's light?

Choice A: Bathe at Midnight
Choice B: Bathe at Noon Instead

CHOICE A: BATHE AT MIDNIGHT
First popup: They take a deep breath, grin at each other, and step down into the water together, right in the middle of the reflected stars. It's warmer than they expected. The moment the moon reaches the top of the sky, the stars in the water begin to swirl...

Ending A1 -- VERY ROMANTIC. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent)
They climb out of the pool, dripping, and look at each other. And see themselves. "Well," says (name1), in (name2)'s voice. "Well," says (name2), in (name1)'s. They stare. Then, slowly, they start to laugh. It's not just a nice saying after all. They walk home through the dark hand in hand, getting used to each other's legs. They decide it's very romantic, actually. Nobody else in the village agrees, and their families find the whole thing exhausting.

Ending A2 -- ONE BREATH. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
For exactly one breath, they see through each other's eyes. (Name1) sees (himself/herself), standing in the starlit pool, looking a little frightened and very hopeful. (Name2) sees the same. Then the stars in the water go still, and they're themselves again, each behind their own eyes. Neither of them says a word. They walk all the way home in silence, very close together, and very quiet, and neither of them ever tells anyone else what they saw.

CHOICE B: BATHE AT NOON INSTEAD
First popup: Standing there in the dark with the black stones all around them, they both lose their nerve at the same moment. "Maybe," whispers (name2), "we could come back tomorrow. When it's light." They sleep under a tree nearby, and come back at noon...

Ending B1 -- A SUNBURN. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
At noon the pool is just a pool. A pretty one, with little blue fish in it and a frog on a stone, and the black stones are just stones, warm in the sun. They splash about for an hour and nothing happens at all, except that they both fall asleep on the bank afterwards and wake up with terrible sunburns. They walk home red as crabs, laughing about how frightened they were the night before.

Ending B2 -- A DIFFERENT CLOCK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent)
At noon, nothing happens. They splash about, shrug, and walk home, a little disappointed. But the pool, it seems, keeps a different clock to everyone else. That night, at exactly midnight, asleep in their own beds on opposite sides of the village, they swap anyway. In the morning (name1) wakes up in (name2)'s hut, and (name2) wakes up in (name1)'s, and both of them sit bolt upright and scream.

S041. The Naming Shell   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]

S046. The Shortcut over the Ridge   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 18 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
There's a shortcut over the ridge to the far beaches. It runs along a knife-edge of crumbling red rock, no wider than a sleeping mat, with a long drop straight down to the sea on one side and a wall of thorn bushes on the other. It cuts the walk in half.
Everyone knows it's dangerous. Every parent has told every child never to take it. And every single adult in the village has taken it at least once, and quietly not mentioned it.
Today it's (name)'s turn. (He/She) is coming home late from the far beach, with a basket so heavy (his/her) shoulders are aching, and the sun is going down. The long way is very long. The ridge is right there. Should (he/she) risk the shortcut, or take the long way home?

Choice B: Take the Long Way

CHOICE A: TAKE THE SHORTCUT
First popup: (Name) shifts the basket on (his/her) back, takes a deep breath, and steps out onto the ridge. The wind comes up from the sea in gusts, tugging at (him/her). Far below, the waves boom against the rocks. (He/She) doesn't look down...

Ending A1 -- FASTER THAN EVER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (normal amount)
(Name) doesn't look down, and doesn't look back, and doesn't stop. One foot in front of the other, quick and light, the basket steady. Halfway across a gust nearly takes (him/her), and (he/she) drops to a crouch, heart hammering, and waits it out, and goes on. In no time at all (he/she) jumps down onto the soft grass on the far side, and laughs out loud. (He/She) gets home before dusk, faster than ever, with a full basket and a huge grin, and tells everyone (he/she) took the long way. Your villagers gain (award) food.

Ending A2 -- ONLY THE BASKET. Chance 50%. EFFECT: DISAPPEARS (no grave)
It rained up on the ridge in the afternoon. (Name) didn't know. The red rock is slick and wet, and halfway across, where the path is narrowest, (his/her) foot slides out from under (him/her). There's nobody there to see. (He/She) does not come home. When (he/she) still hasn't come back by morning, the searchers go out along both paths, calling, and on the ridge they find (his/her) basket lying on its side at the edge, with the fruit spilled out over the rocks. Nothing else. The sea below gives nothing back. Nobody in the village takes the shortcut again, for a while.

CHOICE B: TAKE THE LONG WAY
First popup: (Name) looks at the ridge for a long time, at the red rock and the drop and the setting sun. Then (he/she) sighs, shifts the heavy basket, and turns down the long, winding path through the jungle instead...

Ending B1 -- TIRED, GRUMPY, SAFE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: now dislikes berry and fruit picking (VV1: berries; VV2: coconuts; VV3: fruit; VV4: berries or fruit; VV5: berries)
The long way is long. It is very, very long. It goes down into a valley and back up again, through mud and mosquitoes, and the basket gets heavier with every step. (He/She) drops the basket in the store and swears, loudly, that (he/she) is never going on a long gathering trip again.

Ending B2 -- THE FORGOTTEN GROVE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (large amount)

S047. The Night of Falling Stars   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: no one picked (the whole village); in ending A2, three random villagers aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
For one whole night, the stars fall over the island like rain. Not one or two: hundreds of them, thousands, streaking down the sky in thin silver scratches, so many and so bright that the whole village is lit as if by a pale moon.
Hardly anyone sleeps. Everyone sits out on the beach and the hills with their heads tipped back and their mouths open. The babies stop crying to watch. The children make wishes until they run out of things to wish for, and then start wishing for silly things, and then fall asleep in a heap.
In the morning, when the sun comes up, there are little bright stones scattered all along the beach, glinting in the sand, still faintly warm. Should the village gather them up, or leave them where they fell?

Choice A: Collect the Star Stones
Choice B: Leave Them Where They Fell

CHOICE A: COLLECT THE STAR STONES
First popup: The whole village goes along the beach with baskets, picking up the stones one by one. They're heavy for their size, dark and pitted, with flecks of something bright inside that catches the light...

Ending A1 -- STRANGE METAL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (normal amount)
The researchers take the whole basketful to their hut and don't come out for days. They break the stones open, heat them, scratch them, weigh them. Inside, every one of them is full of strange metal, heavy and bright, that bends instead of breaking and doesn't rust in water. Nobody has ever seen anything like it on the island. The researchers study the star stones for months, and come out of it with more questions than answers, which they say is the best kind of discovery. Your villagers gain (award) tech points.

Ending A2 -- THREE NECKLACES. Chance 50%. EFFECT: NEW LOOK for three random villagers (star-stone jewellery)
When everyone tips their baskets out together, there turn out to be fewer stones than they thought, only enough for three necklaces. The village decides to give them to the three villagers who stayed up the longest, watching every last star fall: (name1), (name2) and (name3). The stones are polished, drilled and strung on plaited cord, and the three of them wear them proudly from then on. On clear nights, for anyone who looks closely, the stones still glimmer, very faintly, like they remember where they came from.

CHOICE B: LEAVE THEM WHERE THEY FELL
First popup: The elders say the stars came down on their own, and should be left where they chose to land. So nobody touches them. The children are told to walk around them. For days, the beach sparkles...

Ending B1 -- THE BEACH FEELS DIFFERENT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Over the next few days, the stones sink slowly down into the sand, a little deeper with every tide, until one morning they're all gone. Nobody digs them up. But something about the beach feels different after that. In a good way. Warmer, somehow. Calmer. People like to sit there in the evenings. Couples walk there. Old people go to think. Nobody can quite say why, and nobody wants to.

Ending B2 -- THE CRAB'S HOARD. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small amount)
A big blue crab walks out of the surf, picks up one of the star stones in its claw, and carries it off very purposefully up the beach. A couple of the researchers follow it, out of curiosity. It leads them to a hole under a fallen tree, and disappears inside. When they dig it out, they find the crab's hoard: the star stone, and dozens of old shiny shells, and a whole pile of lost tools that people have been missing for years, including a very good knife, a fishhook made of bone, and somebody's grandfather's carving chisel. Your villagers gain (award) tech points.

S051. The Parrot with Opinions   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
A big green parrot has moved onto (name)'s roof. Nobody invited it. It has a red patch over one eye like a little cap worn at an angle, and when it's bored it pulls bits out of the thatch and drops them on (name)'s head.
It knows three words. Two of them are (name)'s name, which it shouts at dawn, every dawn, very loudly. The third is "No."
It says "No" whenever (name) starts a job. Picks up a hoe: "No." Reaches for a basket: "NO." Bends to tie a sandal: "No," quietly, almost sadly, as if it's disappointed in (him/her). (Name) has started to wonder if the parrot knows something. Should (he/she) listen to it, or ignore the bossy bird?

Choice A: Listen to the Parrot
Choice B: Ignore the Parrot

CHOICE A: LISTEN TO THE PARROT
First popup: (Name) decides to try an experiment. For a whole week, (he/she) picks up each tool in turn, holds it up towards the roof, and waits to see what the parrot says. The neighbours think (he/she) has lost (his/her) mind...

Ending A1 -- "NO" TO BUILDING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: now dislikes wood (VV2-VV5: wood; story only in VV1); loses a different dislike (at random)
The parrot says "No" loudest, by far, whenever (name) picks up a building tool. It screams it. It flaps its wings and bobs its head and screams "NO NO NO" until (name) puts the hammer down. So (name) stops building, and after a while, without the parrot even saying anything, (he/she) finds (he/she) has come to dislike the feel of wood. But the parrot never once says no to the thing (name) used to hate the most. It just watches, quietly, with its head on one side. And (name) finds, to (his/her) astonishment, that (he/she) doesn't mind that thing any more.

Ending A2 -- YES TO COOKING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: now likes eating (VV2: eating; story only in VV3, VV4, VV5; no such word in VV1); gains 10 Farming
The parrot says "No" to absolutely everything. Hoe, hammer, scroll, basket, net: "No." Then one evening (name) picks up a cooking pot, and the parrot goes completely silent. It hops down from the roof onto the edge of the pot and looks inside, hopefully. (Name) takes up cooking. (He/She) spends the whole season at the fire, gathering herbs and roots and fruits, stewing and roasting and baking, and turns out to be wonderful at it. The parrot was right. It gets the first taste of everything, which may have been the point all along.

CHOICE B: IGNORE THE PARROT
First popup: (Name) refuses to be bossed about by a bird. (He/She) picks up (his/her) tools, walks right past the hut, and gets on with the day. "No," says the parrot. "No. NO." (Name) doesn't look up...

Ending B1 -- SOMEONE ELSE'S ROOF. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The parrot sulks. It sits on the roof with its feathers puffed up, saying nothing, all afternoon. The next morning, (name) wakes up to silence. No name shouted at dawn. No "No." The parrot has flown off to sit on someone else's hut on the other side of the village, and is shouting their name instead. (Name) is very relieved. And then, a few days later, rather to (his/her) own surprise, (he/she) misses it. A little.

Ending B2 -- TO PROVE IT WRONG. Chance 50%. EFFECT: gains 10 to 20 in (his/her) best skill
"No," says the parrot, as (name) heads out to work. So (name) works harder. "No," says the parrot, as (name) comes back. So (name) goes out again, and works even harder, just to show it. Every day for a month (name) works twice as hard as anyone else in the village, out of pure stubbornness, to prove that bird wrong. By the end of the month (he/she) is far better at (his/her) work than (he/she) ever was. The parrot says "No" anyway. But it sounds, perhaps, a little impressed.

Premise: A big green parrot with a red patch over one eye has moved onto (name)'s roof uninvited. It knows three words: (name)'s name, twice, shouted at every dawn, and "No," which it says whenever (name) starts a job.
Roles:
  owner: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)

Outcome pool:

(Name) finds (he/she) doesn't mind that thing any more. [answers: Listen to the Parrot] [mood: funny] [EFFECT: now dislikes wood (VV2-VV5: wood; story only in VV1); loses a different dislike (at random)]
  - It says "No" to everything, until (name) picks up a cooking pot, and the parrot goes silent and hops onto the rim, hopefully. (Name) turns out wonderful at cooking. The parrot gets the first taste of everything. [answers: Listen to the Parrot, Bribe It with Fruit] [mood: warm] [EFFECT: now likes eating (VV2: eating; story only in VV3, VV4, VV5; no such word in VV1); gains 10 Farming]
  - The parrot sulks off to shout someone else's name on {someone else's roof|the meeting hut|the chief's doorway}. (Name) is very relieved, and then, rather to (his/her) surprise, misses it. A little. [answers: Ignore the Parrot] [mood: sad] [EFFECT: none]
  - Every "No" makes (name) work harder, out of pure stubbornness. By the end of the month (he/she) is far better at (his/her) work, and the parrot's "No" sounds, perhaps, a little impressed. [answers: Ignore the Parrot] [mood: funny] [EFFECT: gains 10 to 20 in (his/her) best skill]
  - After a week of patient lessons, the parrot learns "Yes." It uses it only for naps. [answers: Teach It a New Word] [mood: funny] [EFFECT: none]
  - The parrot eats the fruit, says "No," and eats more fruit. [answers: Bribe It with Fruit] [mood: funny] [EFFECT: food loss (small amount)]

  - "No," quietly, almost sadly, as if it's disappointed.
  - The red patch sits over its eye like a little cap worn at an angle.
  - The neighbours think (name) has lost (his/her) mind.

S052. The Old Wanderer   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: no one picked (the newcomer is a new villager)
EVENT TEXT
One afternoon an old traveller comes walking slowly up the path into the village, leaning on a long stick worn smooth by years of hands. (He/She) has a bag over one shoulder that smells of every forest on the island, sandals tied together with vine, and a long white beard so full of twigs and leaves that a small bird could live in it, and possibly does.
(He/She) stops in the middle of the village, looks around at the huts and the fire and the children, and sighs a long, contented sigh.
"I've walked every path on this island," (he/she) says, to nobody in particular. "Every single one. This is the last." (He/She) lowers (himself/herself), very carefully, onto a log. "I'd like to sit down now. For a few years." Should the village give the old traveller a hut, or a good meal and a fond farewell?

Choice A: Give (Him/Her) a Hut
Choice B: Give (Him/Her) a Meal and Send (Him/Her) On

CHOICE A: GIVE (HIM/HER) A HUT
First popup: The elders look at each other, and then at the old traveller, and nod. There's an empty hut at the edge of the village, with a good view of the sea. The children carry (his/her) bag. The builders patch the roof. Someone brings a mat...

Ending A1 -- STORIES EVERY NIGHT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: NEW VILLAGER (an elder) arrives and stays
The wanderer settles in as if (he/she) has always been there. And every night, at the fire, (he/she) tells stories: about the waterfall that runs uphill on the far side of the island, about the village where everyone speaks in whispers, about the lizard (he/she) once shared a cave with for a whole rainy season. Some of the stories might even be true. The children adore (him/her). They sit at (his/her) feet every evening with their mouths open, and pick twigs out of (his/her) beard when (he/she) dozes off.

Ending A2 -- THE PLANT KNOWER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: NEW VILLAGER (an elder, with 50 Farming) arrives and stays; tech gain (small amount)
The wanderer settles in, and on the very first morning goes for a slow walk round the gardens with (his/her) stick, stopping to look at every plant. Then (he/she) starts talking. "This one wants more shade. That one is planted too deep. This weed, here, the one you keep pulling up, is good to eat if you boil it twice." It turns out the old traveller knows a great deal about plants, more than anyone on the island, gathered on every path (he/she) ever walked. The farmers follow (him/her) around with their mouths open, and the researchers write it all down. Your villagers gain (award) tech points.

CHOICE B: GIVE (HIM/HER) A MEAL AND SEND (HIM/HER) ON
First popup: The village is kind, but cautious. They bring the old traveller a big bowl of stew, a cup of water and a fresh pair of sandals, and sit with (him/her) while (he/she) eats, and wait to see what (he/she) does next...

Ending B1 -- ONE MORE PATH. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (small amount)
The wanderer eats every bit of the stew, slowly, with great enjoyment, and mops the bowl with bread. Then (he/she) ties on the new sandals, thanks everyone warmly, gets up with a great creaking of knees, and picks up the stick. "I thought this was the last one," (he/she) says, smiling. "But there's always one more path." And (he/she) walks off down the far side of the village, humming, and is never seen again. Your village loses (award) food.

Ending B2 -- "FOR A MINUTE." Chance 50%. EFFECT: NEW VILLAGER (an elder) arrives and stays
The wanderer eats, thanks everyone, and then says (he/she) will just sit by the fire "for a minute" before setting off. In the morning (he/she) is still there, asleep by the ashes with (his/her) bag for a pillow. And the morning after that. On the third morning, someone quietly builds a little roof over (his/her) spot. On the fourth, someone brings (him/her) a mat. Nobody ever actually says "you can stay." (He/She) just never leaves.

S053. The Child from the Forest   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
(Name) is gathering deep in the forest, much further out than usual, when (he/she) gets the feeling of being watched. (He/She) looks up slowly. Behind a tree, half hidden, there's a small child, watching (him/her) with enormous dark eyes.
The child is wearing a cloak made of big green leaves, stitched together with grass. (His/her) feet are bare and black with mud. A tiny brown bird is riding on one of (his/her) shoulders, perfectly calm. The child is thin, and very quiet, and looks as if (he/she) has been alone out here for a long, long time. (Name) remembers the canoe from another island that was wrecked on the far shore two seasons ago; nobody ever found who was on it.
(Name) holds out a piece of fruit, very slowly. The child looks at it. Then, one small step at a time, the child comes closer. Should (name) try to bring the child home, or leave food and walk away slowly so as not to scare (him/her)?

Choice A: Bring the Child Home
Choice B: Leave Food and Walk Away Slowly

CHOICE A: BRING THE CHILD HOME
First popup: (Name) crouches down, so (he/she) isn't so tall, and holds out (his/her) hand instead of the fruit. The child looks at it for a very long time. The little bird on (his/her) shoulder chirps, once...

Ending A1 -- NEVER LEAVES (HIS/HER) SIDE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: NEW VILLAGER (a child) arrives and stays
The child takes (name)'s hand, very tightly, and doesn't let go. Not all the way back to the village, not when everyone comes out to stare, not when the healers check (him/her) over, not when (he/she) eats. For a whole month, the child never leaves (name)'s side, sleeping curled up at the foot of (his/her) mat, following (him/her) to the fields and the river. The child never says where (he/she) came from, and nobody presses. Slowly, the village takes the child in, and slowly, the child starts letting go of (name)'s hand, just a little, to play with the others. The little brown bird stays too.

Ending A2 -- THREE BOWLS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: NEW VILLAGER (a child) arrives and stays; food loss (small amount)
The child follows (name) all the way home, a few steps behind, and stands in the doorway of the cooking hut looking at the pot. (Name) gives (him/her) a bowl of mash. The child eats it so fast that (name) gives (him/her) another. And then a third. Then the child curls up right there by the fire, cloak of leaves and all, and falls fast asleep in the middle of everyone. In the morning the child is still there, sitting up, looking around at the village, and that, everyone agrees, is a very good sign. Your village loses (award) food.

CHOICE B: LEAVE FOOD AND WALK AWAY SLOWLY
First popup: (Name) doesn't want to frighten the child. (He/She) sets the fruit down on a flat stone, and a bundle of bread beside it, and backs away one slow step at a time, smiling, and then turns and walks off through the trees...

Ending B1 -- EVERY WEEK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (small amount)
When (name) looks back from the edge of the clearing, the food is gone, and so is the child, vanished into the trees as if (he/she) was never there. (Name) comes back the next week, and leaves more food on the same flat stone. The next week, it's gone again. Every week after that, (name) leaves food on the stone, and every week, it's gone. Once, there's a feather left in its place. Once, a little carved stick. (Name) never sees the child again, but (he/she) never stops leaving food. Your village loses (award) food.

Ending B2 -- AT THE FIRE BY SUPPER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: NEW VILLAGER (a child) arrives and stays
(Name) walks away slowly, not looking back. But (he/she) can hear little footsteps behind (him/her), all the way through the forest, stopping whenever (he/she) stops, at a careful distance. By the time (he/she) reaches the village the footsteps have gone quiet, and (he/she) thinks the child has turned back. But at supper, when (name) sits down at the fire with (his/her) bowl, there's the child, sitting on the other side of the flames, cloak of leaves and all, holding out an empty bowl.

Premise: Gathering deep in the forest, (name) feels watched, and finds a thin, quiet child behind a tree, in a cloak of big green leaves stitched with grass, with a tiny brown bird on one shoulder; perhaps from the canoe wrecked on the far shore two seasons ago.
