S054. The Moon's Mirror   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
Tonight the full moon is reflected in the lagoon so perfectly that it looks like there are two of them: one in the sky, one in the water, both exactly as bright. The water is still and warm as a bath, and little silver fish keep leaping through both moons at once, sending out rings of light.
(Name) can't sleep, and has come down to look. The elders say that on the one night a year the moon sees itself perfectly in the lagoon, it gets lonely, and makes a copy of whatever it finds in the water. It's so beautiful that (he/she) wades in, up to (his/her) waist, to get closer to the moon in the water.
When (he/she) wades back out, there are two sets of footprints in the wet sand behind (him/her). And two shadows. (Name) turns round. Standing in the shallows, dripping, smiling, is (name). Should (name) welcome (his/her) double, or wait for sunrise and see if it's still there?

Choice A: Welcome the Second One
Choice B: Wait for Sunrise

CHOICE A: WELCOME THE SECOND ONE
First popup: (Name) takes a long breath. Then (he/she) holds out (his/her) hand. "Well," (he/she) says, a little shakily. "You'd better come and get dry." The second one smiles (his/her) own smile back...

Ending A1 -- STRAIGHT TO WORK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: CLONE of (name), named (made1); joins the village
The second (name) is exactly the same in every way. Same voice, same laugh, same habit of humming while (he/she) works, same favourite food, same scar, same everything. It walks back to the village beside (name), step for step, and when the village wakes up in the morning, nobody can tell them apart. The second one agrees to be called (made1), "to keep things simple," and goes straight to work without being asked, doing exactly what (name) would have done. It's very efficient. It's also slightly unsettling, and the village never quite gets used to it.

Ending A2 -- THE SECOND MOON SETS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The second one takes (name)'s hand for a moment. It's cool, like the lagoon. Then it smiles, and lets go, and shimmers, like the moon on the water when a fish jumps. It turns and walks back out into the lagoon, deeper and deeper, until the water is over its head, and when (name) looks up, the moon in the water has gone. Only the one in the sky is left. The lagoon is very dark and very quiet. (Name) walks home slowly, and doesn't tell anyone for a long time.

CHOICE B: WAIT FOR SUNRISE
First popup: (Name) doesn't trust anything that comes out of the water by moonlight. (He/She) sits down on the sand, arms round (his/her) knees, and waits. The second one sits down too, a little way off, in exactly the same position. They wait together, in silence, for the dawn...

Ending B1 -- COMPLAINING ABOUT THE COLD. Chance 50%. EFFECT: CLONE of (name), named (made1); joins the village
At sunrise, the second one is still there. Yawning. Rubbing its arms. Complaining, loudly, about how cold it is, how damp the sand is, how its back aches from sitting all night. It's a perfect copy, so it complains exactly the same way (name) does, with exactly the same words, at exactly the same moment as (name). They both stop and stare at each other. Then they both burst out laughing. The second one takes the name (made1), and the two of them walk up to the village for breakfast, still complaining.

Ending B2 -- TWICE THE WORK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
As the first light touches the water, the second one gets up, stretches, gives (name) a little wave, and simply isn't there any more. Just one set of footprints on the sand. Just one shadow. (Name) gets up, and nearly falls down again. (He/She) feels very, very tired, more tired than (he/she) has ever felt, as if (he/she) has done twice the work, or lived twice the night. (He/She) sleeps all the next day, and wakes up feeling perfectly normal, and very confused.

MIXER SEED S054
Premise: On the one night a year the full moon sees itself perfectly in the lagoon, (name) wades in up to (his/her) waist to get closer to the moon in the water. When (he/she) wades back out, there are two sets of footprints, two shadows, and a second (name) standing dripping and smiling in the shallows.
Roles:
  wader: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)

Outcome pool:

  - It takes (name)'s hand, cool like the lagoon, then walks back into the water until it's over its head. When (name) looks up, the moon in the water has gone. [answers: Welcome the Second One, Walk Back into the Water] [mood: eerie] [EFFECT: none]
  - At sunrise it's still there, complaining about the cold in exactly the same words as (name), at exactly the same moment. They both burst out laughing, and the second one takes the name (made1). S055. The Fire Spirit's Joke   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: two villagers aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
(Name1) and (name2) are arguing about whose turn it is to keep the cooking fire going overnight. They have been arguing about it since supper. "I did it yesterday." "You did it HALF of yesterday." "I did it the day before!" "That was a NAP." It has been going on so long that the fire has sunk down to a low, sulky orange glow, and everyone else has gone to bed.
The fire has been listening. Everyone knows a mischievous spirit lives in the old cooking fire, which is why nobody ever lets it go out.
Suddenly it gives an enormous crackle and a great burst of blue sparks, and somewhere in the middle of it, just for a moment, there's a small laugh. A smoky, crackly, delighted little laugh. When the smoke clears, (name1) and (name2) are looking at each other's faces. From the wrong side. Should they apologise to the fire spirit, or let the fire burn out and hope the magic goes with it?

Choice A: Apologise to the Fire
Choice B: Let It Burn Out

CHOICE A: APOLOGISE TO THE FIRE
First popup: The two of them, in each other's bodies, kneel down in front of the embers together. "We're sorry," says (name1), in (name2)'s voice. "We'll take turns," says (name2), in (name1)'s. "Fairly." They put a fresh log on, together. The fire crackles, thinking about it...

Ending A1 -- SATISFIED. Chance 50%. EFFECT: body swap, then swapped back (no lasting change)
The fire seems satisfied. It flares up warm and gold around the new log, gives one more crackle, and with a little puff of blue smoke, (name1) and (name2) are themselves again. They look down at their own hands. They look at each other. Without another word, they work out a rota for the fire, scratch it into the doorpost of the cooking hut, and stick to it for the rest of their lives.

Ending A2 -- NOT SATISFIED ENOUGH. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent)
The fire seems satisfied. Mostly. It flickers, and crackles, and a single blue spark spirals up and pops in the air. But nothing changes. (Name1) is still in (name2)'s body, and (name2) is still in (name1)'s. The elders say they'll stay swapped until they learn to share properly. They try. They really do try. But they never quite manage it, not entirely, so they stay swapped. They still argue about the fire. Now they each argue the other one's side, which is very confusing for everyone.

CHOICE B: LET IT BURN OUT
First popup: "Fine," says (name1), in the wrong voice. "Let it go out, then." "Fine," says (name2). "See if I care." They both fold their arms. And the fire, very slowly, dies down to embers, and to ash...

Ending B1 -- THE MAGIC GOES OUT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The last ember winks out. S060. The Swarm   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: no one picked (the whole village)
EVENT TEXT
At noon, the sky goes dark.
It isn't a storm. There are no clouds. The sound comes first: a dry, rattling hiss, rising from the far side of the island, louder and louder, as if the whole island were being shaken in a giant gourd full of seeds. Then the shadow comes over the hill, rolling across the fields, and everyone sees what it is.
Grasshoppers. Millions of them. A brown, whirring cloud so thick the sun can't be seen through it. They come down on the fields like rain, and the crops vanish under them in moments, and then, still hungry, they lift off again and start heading straight for the food store. Should the village try to smoke them away, or catch them?

Choice A: Light Smoky Fires
Choice B: Catch Them

CHOICE A: LIGHT SMOKY FIRES
First popup: "Smoke! They hate smoke!" one of the elders shouts. Everyone runs for wet leaves, green branches, damp thatch, anything that will burn badly, and piles it on fires all round the food store. Thick grey smoke billows up...

Ending A1 -- MOST OF THEM. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (small amount)
The smoke drives most of them away. The cloud wavers in the air above the store, whirring angrily, then turns and pours away over the hills towards the sea. Most of them. The rest get into the store through the gaps in the walls and eat a little of everything before the villagers can sweep them out. When it's over, everyone is coughing and soot-faced and hoarse from shouting, but the store is mostly full. Your village loses (award) food.

Ending A2 -- THE WIND TURNS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (large amount)
For a moment, it works. The cloud wavers. Then the wind turns. It swings round from the sea, and blows the smoke straight back over the villagers, into their eyes and down their throats, and drives the grasshoppers straight into the food store instead, in a great whirring wave. They eat and eat and eat. By the time the wind turns again and they finally leave, a great deal of the store is gone. Your village loses (award) food.

CHOICE B: CATCH THEM
First popup: "Catch them?!" "Catch them! They're FOOD!" Every basket, net, pot, cloth and bare hand in the village is pressed into service, and everyone runs out into the whirring cloud, scooping, grabbing, shrieking, laughing...

Ending B1 -- CRUNCHY NUTS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (normal amount)
The villagers catch them by the thousand, by the basketful, and tip them into the big pots, and roast them over every fire in the village. They taste, everyone agrees, a lot like crunchy nuts. With a bit of salt, they're actually delicious. By evening the fields are completely bare, stripped to the stalks. But the stores are full to bursting, and there's a whole new kind of snack that the children won't stop eating. Your villagers gain (award) food.

Ending B2 -- NOT ENOUGH. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (normal amount)
The villagers catch a lot of them. Basket after basket, pot after pot, until their arms ache. But there are millions, and only so many villagers, and while everyone is busy catching them in the fields, the rest of the cloud quietly settles on the food store and eats its way through it. By the time anyone notices, the swarm is lifting off again, fat and slow, and there's a lot less food than there was this morning. Your village loses (award) food.

S061. The Soft Yams   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: no one picked (the whole village); in ending B2, one random villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
Somebody opens the yam store first thing in the morning, takes one breath, and slams the door shut again. Then they stagger backwards, eyes watering, and sit down on the ground.
Inside, the yams have gone soft. And black. And wet. And they smell like something died in there. Probably several things, possibly on purpose. Rainwater has been seeping in under the back wall for days, and nobody noticed until now. The smell drifts out under the door and across the village, and people come out of their huts with their hands over their noses, asking what happened.
The flies have already moved in. Hundreds of them. They seem to be holding a meeting. Is any of it worth saving, or should the whole lot go?

Choice A: Throw Them Out
Choice B: Try to Save Some

CHOICE A: THROW THEM OUT
First popup: Nobody wants to do it. In the end, the whole village draws straws, ties wet cloths over their faces, and goes in together in a long chain, passing out the slimy black yams hand over hand to be dumped far away beyond the gardens...

Ending A1 -- EVERY LAST YAM. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (normal amount)
Every yam is thrown out. Every single one, even the ones that look all right, because nobody wants to risk it. The store is scrubbed out with sand and seawater and left open to the wind for three days. The smell lingers a little longer than that. Nobody in the village eats a yam for a month afterwards, and, rather surprisingly, nobody complains about it. Your village loses (award) food.

Ending A2 -- THE GOOD ONES AT THE BOTTOM. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (small amount)
They work their way down through the pile, throwing out the bad ones, gagging, passing them along. They were packed down in cool sand when the store was built, and the rot never reached them. It isn't much, but it's something. Your village loses (award) food.

CHOICE B: TRY TO SAVE SOME
First popup: "Wait," say the researchers. "Not all of it's gone. If we cut out the bad parts..." Everyone looks at them as if they're mad. The researchers tie cloths over their faces, take their sharpest knives, and go in...

Ending B1 -- NOT TASTY, BUT FOOD. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (small amount); tech gain (small amount)
The researchers spend all day cutting away the bad parts, slicing the good parts thin, and laying them out on hot rocks in the sun until they're dry and hard as bark. Ending B2 -- SOMEONE CHECKS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (normal amount); (name) has an ILLNESS (needs the healers)

(Name) says (he/she) knows exactly how, picks up one of the soft ones that doesn't look too bad, and takes a bite before anyone can stop (him/her). (He/She) chews thoughtfully. "Seems all right," (he/she) says. By the evening (he/she) is very, very sick, and stays that way for a week in the healers' hut, and everything in the store is thrown out after all. Your village loses (award) food.

S062. The Flood   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: no one picked (the whole village)
EVENT TEXT
It rains for nine days without stopping. The paths turn into brown streams. Frogs sit on every doorstep, looking very pleased with themselves. Nothing anybody owns is dry: not the mats, not the clothes, not the firewood, not the inside of anybody's ears.
On the tenth day, with a deep, groaning roar that everybody hears at once, the river comes over its banks.
It pours through the village in a brown, churning wave, knee-deep and rising, carrying away everything that isn't tied down, and quite a few things that are. Baskets go spinning past. A canoe floats by, upside down. There isn't time to save everything. There's barely time to save one thing: the food store, or the research hut and its years of notes. Which should the village save?

Choice A: Save the Food
Choice B: Save the Research Notes

CHOICE A: SAVE THE FOOD
First popup: "The store! The store!" Everyone wades for the food store, waist-deep in the brown water now, forming a chain to pass the baskets up the hill to the high ground, one after another, while the water climbs...

Ending A1 -- THE RESEARCH HUT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech loss (normal amount)
The food is carried to the high ground, every basket of it, dry and safe on the hilltop. But while everyone was busy at the store, the river reached the research hut, and went in through the door, and came out through the window, and took most of what was on the shelves with it. When the water goes down three days later, the researchers wade in and find their notes plastered across the floor in a brown, soggy paste. Your villagers lose (award) tech points.

Ending A2 -- THE BLACK MUD. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (small amount)
The food is saved. And then, at the very last moment, the water turns, just slightly, and runs round the research hut instead of through it. Everything is saved. When the river finally goes back down to its banks, it leaves behind a thick layer of rich, black, sweet-smelling mud all over the fields. The farmers are delighted. Everything they plant in it comes up twice as fast. Your villagers gain (award) food.

CHOICE B: SAVE THE RESEARCH NOTES
First popup: "The notes! Years of work!" The researchers and half the village wade for the research hut and carry out armful after armful of scrolls, holding them high above their heads, struggling up the hill with the water pulling at their legs...

Ending B1 -- THE FOOD STORE GOES. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (large amount)
The notes are saved, every one, stacked dry and safe on the hilltop. But down below, with a long, wet groan, the walls of the food store give way, and the river takes it. Baskets and pots and sacks go sailing off downstream towards the sea, bobbing and spinning, and there's nothing anyone can do but watch. It's a very hungry season afterwards. Your village loses (award) food.

Ending B2 -- ONE FAVOURITE HAT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
By some miracle, everything is saved. The notes, the food, the tools, the babies, the goats, and even most of the chickens. The only casualty is one villager's favourite hat, a big woven one with a feather in it, which is last seen floating gently down the river and out to sea, the right way up, as if it's going on a holiday. Its owner stands on the hill and waves it goodbye, and is never quite the same.

EVENT TEXT

S071. The Robe That Shrank   [VV3]

Choice B: Wear It Anyway

S072. The Tree Blossoms Early   [VV4]
WHO: no one picked (the whole village)
EVENT TEXT
One morning, the whole village wakes up to a smell so sweet and strong it's like walking into a wall of honey. Outside, the air is full of petals.
The Tree of Life has burst into blossom, a whole season early. The researchers blame the unusually warm rains; the elders say the Tree only does this when it is pleased with the village. Every branch, from the lowest to the very top, is covered in flowers the colour of sunrise: pink and gold and orange, so thick the leaves can't be seen. The petals drift down onto every roof, into every soup pot, into everyone's hair. The children are running about trying to catch them.
And bees are coming. From all over the island, it seems, in a great humming golden cloud, to the Tree. Should the village gather the blossoms, or leave them on the Tree?

Choice A: Gather the Blossoms
Choice B: Leave Them on the Tree

CHOICE A: GATHER THE BLOSSOMS
First popup: Out come the baskets and the long poles. The villagers spread cloths under the Tree and shake the lower branches, very gently, and the blossoms come tumbling down like warm snow, while the bees grumble overhead...

Ending A1 -- SUNRISE TEA. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (normal amount)
Somebody drops a handful of the blossoms into hot water, just to see, and the water turns the colour of a sunrise, and smells like the morning the Tree flowered. It tastes wonderful: sweet and soft and a little bit like honey. Everyone loves it. The cooks dry baskets and baskets of the blossoms in the sun, and there's sunrise tea at every meal for the whole season, and a sweet blossom bread that the children would fight over if they were allowed. Your villagers gain (award) food.

Ending A2 -- TOO DELICATE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The blossoms are too delicate. As soon as they're picked, they start to wilt, turning brown and limp in the baskets, losing their colour and their smell in minutes. By lunchtime the baskets are full of nothing but soggy brown petals. The villagers look up guiltily at the Tree. The Tree, still covered in flowers, doesn't seem to mind. The cooks tip the baskets out under it, and the petals sink into the roots.

CHOICE B: LEAVE THEM ON THE TREE
First popup: The elders say that something this rare should be left alone. So nobody picks a single blossom. They let them be. The village just stops and looks at them, every morning and every evening, for as long as they last...

Ending B1 -- EARLY FRUIT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (large amount)
The blossoms stay on the Tree for a week, humming with bees. Then, slowly, they fall, and where every blossom was, there's a tiny green bud of fruit. The fruit swells, and ripens, much earlier than it ever has before, and much more of it. By the time the ordinary fruiting season should be starting, the Tree has already given the village a whole harvest, heavy and sweet. Your villagers gain (award) food.

Ending B2 -- THE RESEARCHERS' WEEK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (normal amount)
The researchers set up a little camp under the Tree and watch the blossoms every hour of the day and night for a week. They count the bees. They measure the petals. They notice that the blossoms open at sunrise and close at sunset, all at once, every single one, as if someone had told them to. They notice that the Tree is warm to the touch all week. They learn something new about the Tree of Life, something nobody knew before, and write it all down in a very long and very excited scroll. Your villagers gain (award) tech points.

S075. Too Many Cooks   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: no one picked (the whole village); in Choice B, one random villager aged 14 or older (not protected) is the chosen cook; (elder name) is any elder
EVENT TEXT
Everyone in the village has decided, all at the same time, to help with tonight's stew. Nobody asked them to. Nobody knows how it happened. But there are now twelve people standing round the big pot, and every one of them is stirring.
Nobody agrees on anything. Someone has added fish. Someone else, horrified, has added fruit to "balance out the fish." Someone has added a great deal of salt, and someone else has added water to fix the salt, and someone else has added more salt to fix the water. There may be a sandal in it.
The pot is so big that the smallest stirrer is standing on a log to reach. Should the elders let them carry on, or pick one cook and send everyone else to sit down?

Choice A: Let Them Carry On
Choice B: Pick One Cook

CHOICE A: LET THEM CARRY ON
First popup: Nobody wants to be the one to tell twelve people with spoons to stop. So the cooking goes on. And on. More things go in. Some things come out. One of them is definitely a sandal. The pot bubbles ominously...

Ending A1 -- A DISASTER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food loss (small amount)
The stew is a disaster. It's brown. And purple. And green in places. It tastes of fish, and fruit, and salt, and smoke, and something nobody can identify and nobody wants to. But everybody made it, so everybody eats it, sitting round the fire pulling faces at each other and trying very hard not to laugh. They fail. The whole village laughs until they cry. Years later, people still say "it's a twelve-cook stew" about anything that's gone horribly wrong. Your village loses (award) food.

Ending A2 -- SOMEHOW THE BEST. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (small amount)
The stew is, somehow, the best stew anyone has ever eaten. Nobody knows why. The fish and the fruit and the twelve different handfuls of herbs have all come together into something warm and rich and perfect. People go back for thirds. People go back for fourths. S077. The Mask Seller   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
A traveller has laid out a long cloth on the grass by the meeting hut, and on it, in rows, are masks. Dozens of them, carved from wood and painted in every colour: bird faces with long beaks, fish faces with round staring eyes, laughing faces, sleepy faces, cross faces, faces nobody can quite describe. Bright ribbons tied to the corners of the cloth flutter in the wind.
A crowd has gathered in no time. "Try one," the seller says, smiling, to anyone who comes close. "Go on. Anyone can be anything, for a little while." The masks were carved from a lightning-struck tree on the seller's home island, the seller says, "and lightning always leaves a little of itself behind."
(Name) has been standing at the front for a long time, trying to decide. Two of them keep catching (his/her) eye: a bird mask with blue and green feathers, and a big, round, painted laughing face. Which one should (he/she) try?

Ending A1 -- EVERY FESTIVAL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: NEW LOOK for (name) (a bird-feather look)

(He/She) runs home and comes back with (his/her) very best basket, the one (his/her) grandmother made, and trades it on the spot. (Name) doesn't mind one bit.

Ending B1 -- AN HOUR OF LAUGHING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: loses one dislike (at random)

EVENT TEXT

Choice B: Hope Nobody Notices

S084. The Riptide   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
The afternoon is bright and lazy, and the sea glitters like a cloth scattered with beads. The water looks calm. It always looks calm, the old fishers say, right before it isn't.
(Name) is a strong swimmer, one of the best in the village, and has been out past the breakers for an hour, floating on (his/her) back, watching the clouds. That's exactly why (he/she) doesn't notice how far out (he/she) has drifted until (he/she) turns over to swim back, and the beach looks very, very small.

CHOICE A: SWIM STRAIGHT BACK

Ending A1 -- EVERYTHING (HE/SHE) HAS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
For a long, terrible time, nothing happens. (Name) swims and swims and the beach stays exactly where it is. Then, slowly, so slowly, (he/she) starts to gain. A stroke at a time. A breath at a time. Two days later, (his/her) body washes up on the beach on the far side of the island. The village carries (him/her) home and lays (him/her) to rest above the bay, facing the water (he/she) loved to swim in.

S085. The Elder from the Sea   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: no one picked (the newcomer is a new villager)
EVENT TEXT
A leaky little canoe comes paddling right up onto the beach one morning, so slowly that the children see it coming for an hour. In it is a small, very old person, wrapped in a faded cloak, with a face as wrinkled as a dried fig. The canoe has a pair of faded eyes painted on the prow, and a small grey crab is riding on the paddle.
The old one climbs out, slowly, onto the sand. Straightens up, slowly. Looks around at the beach and the village and the hills behind it, and nods, very satisfied.
"Ah," (he/she) says. "This must be the place."
Nobody knows what place. The old one seems quite sure. Should the village ask where (he/she) has come from, or feed (him/her) first?

Choice A: Ask Where (He/She) Came From
Choice B: Offer Food First

CHOICE A: ASK WHERE (HE/SHE) CAME FROM
First popup: The elders come down the beach and greet the visitor politely, and ask where (he/she) has come from, and where (he/she) is going. The old one sits down on the edge of the canoe, crab and all, to answer...

Ending A1 -- NOT GOING BACK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: NEW VILLAGER (an elder) arrives and stays
"Far away," says the old one, waving a hand vaguely at the whole of the ocean. "Very far. And I'm not going back." That's all (he/she) will say. Then (he/she) gets up and walks straight up the beach to the little empty hut at the top of the sand, the one nobody has lived in for years, and goes in, and puts (his/her) bag down on the mat as though (he/she) has always lived there. The crab moves in too. Nobody has the heart to argue.

Ending A2 -- THE STORIES. Chance 50%. EFFECT: NEW VILLAGER (an elder) arrives and stays; tech gain (small amount)
"Oh, where to begin," says the old one, and settles in, and begins. And keeps going. (He/She) tells them about islands made of black glass, and islands where the trees walk, and islands where the fish talk and the people don't, and a great city where... The stories are so amazing that the researchers come running with bark and charcoal and start writing them all down. They're still writing at sunset. They're still writing a month later, because the old one, of course, has stayed. Your villagers gain (award) tech points.

CHOICE B: OFFER FOOD FIRST
First popup: Questions can wait. The village brings the old one a warm bowl of stew and a cup of fresh water, and sits (him/her) down by the fire, and lets (him/her) eat in peace...

S086. The Two (Name)s Problem   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
It's the height of the dry season. Dust lies thick and yellow on all the hill paths, and gets in everything: eyes, food, teeth, dreams. (Name) has walked up past the old carved stones on the hill, the ones with the faces that nobody remembers carving. The elders say they were carved long ago to keep the island's spirits company, and that the spirits get restless in the dry season. The dust is getting right up (his/her) nose.
(He/She) sneezes. A huge one, a real thunderclap of a sneeze, that echoes off the stones.
And something sneezes back.
(Name) wipes (his/her) eyes and looks round. Standing right beside (him/her), dusty from head to foot, is another (name). Or someone who looks exactly like (him/her), down to the last hair. It's already complaining, loudly, about the dust. "What am I supposed to do with... me?" (name) thinks.

Choice A: Make the Best of It
Choice B: Ask the Elders

CHOICE A: MAKE THE BEST OF IT
First popup: (Name) is too surprised to be frightened. "Bless you," (he/she) says, automatically. "Thanks," says the other one. "Awful, isn't it? The dust." They look at each other. Then, because there's nothing else to do, they walk back down to the village together...

Ending A1 -- DIFFERENT INSIDE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: DUPLICATE of (name), named (made1); joins the village

S087. The Swapping Mango   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: two villagers aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
The elders tell of a mango tree on the island that fruits only once in a lifetime, one single mango, and that whoever eats it will never taste anything sweeter. The tree drinks from the island's oldest spring, they say, and whoever shares its fruit shares a little more than fruit. (Name1) and (name2) have been searching for it for years, on and off, just for fun.
Today, at last, they find it. It stands alone on a windy cliff at the far end of the island, twisted almost flat by the wind, and among its few tough leaves hangs one perfect mango, glowing red and gold in the late sun like a little lamp.
There's only one mango. So they share it, fairly, half each, cutting it down the middle with (name1)'s knife. And with the very first bite, sitting side by side on the cliff, they feel their minds slip, like stepping onto a wet rock, and trade places. Should they finish the mango, or spit it out before it's too late?

Choice A: Finish the Mango
Choice B: Spit It Out

CHOICE A: FINISH THE MANGO
First popup: (Name1) looks down at (name2)'s hands holding (name1)'s half of the mango. (Name2) looks down at (name1)'s. They look at each other's faces. Then, because it is, after all, the best mango either of them has ever tasted, they both take another bite...

Ending A1 -- MAKE THE MOST OF IT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent)
They each eat their half, down to the stone, sticky to the elbows, and lick their fingers, and sit there in the sunset, and stay swapped. Completely. "I suppose I'm you now," says (name1), in (name2)'s voice, looking down at (name2)'s knees. "Make the most of it," says (name2), with (name1)'s grin. They walk home in each other's bodies, and live each other's lives from then on, and agree, years later, that it was worth it, for that mango.

Ending A2 -- THE LAST BITE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: body swap, then swapped back (no lasting change)
They finish it, bite by sticky bite, swapped, laughing at each other's faces. And with the very last bite, the last sweet scrap from around the stone, their minds slip again, and swap back, and they're themselves, sitting on a cliff with juice running down their chins. It was the best mango either of them ever tasted, or ever will. They plant the stone right there on the cliff, side by side, and promise to come back in a lifetime to see if it's grown.

CHOICE B: SPIT IT OUT
First popup: "Spit it out!" shouts (name1), in (name2)'s voice, and they both do, at once, spitting the mouthfuls of sweet gold mango over the edge of the cliff...

Ending B1 -- A LITTLE DISAPPOINTED. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The magic stops the moment the mango leaves their mouths. They're themselves again, instantly, kneeling on the cliff edge, coughing. They look at each other. Then they look at the two halves of the once-in-a-lifetime mango, lying in the grass. They're both a little disappointed, actually. They pick up the halves, and look at them, and put them down again, and walk home, wondering, for the rest of their lives, what the second bite would have tasted like.

Ending B2 -- STICKY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: BODY SWAP between (name1) and (name2) (permanent)
Too late. The first bite was enough. They spit out what's left, but they stay swapped, kneeling there on the cliff in each other's bodies with mango juice all over each other's faces. And the juice is everywhere: on their hands, their chins, in their hair, all down their fronts. They walk all the way home swapped, and sticky, and cross, and stay that way, swapped at least, for good. The stickiness wears off by morning.

S091. The Fever Dream   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected) who is ill
EVENT TEXT
For three days, (name) has had a fever so high that (he/she) hasn't known where (he/she) is. And for three days, (he/she) has been talking. Not to the healers, or (his/her) family sitting by the mat. To someone else. To several someones, it seems, that nobody else can see. Spirits, (he/she) says, when (he/she) can say anything at all.
This morning the fever has finally broken, and (name) is sitting up, pale and sweaty and wide-eyed, and (he/she) remembers everything they told (him/her).
None of it makes any sense. (He/She) keeps talking about a lizard wearing a crown. And a song about rain that falls upwards. And a door in the sea. And a number, which (he/she) repeats over and over, very urgently, as if it's important. Should (name) tell the researchers everything, or rest and let it fade?

Choice A: Tell the Researchers
Choice B: Rest

CHOICE A: TELL THE RESEARCHERS

Ending A1 -- QUITE A LOT, IN FACT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (normal amount)

The number (name) kept repeating turns out to be exactly how many days there are between one big tide and the next, something they've been trying to work out for years. The lizard in the crown turns out to match an old carving nobody understood. The song about upward rain, when they think about it, describes how water rises from the sea into the clouds. Ending A2 -- POLITELY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

(Name) is sure, for the rest of (his/her) life, that it all meant something.

CHOICE B: REST

Ending B1 -- BETTER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: illness cured

Every day after that (he/she) gets a little stronger, and the strange memories fade a little more, like a dream after waking, until (he/she) can't quite remember the lizard's crown or the words of the upward song. Within a fortnight (he/she) is back at work, completely well. Sometimes, when it rains, (he/she) looks up, just in case.

Ending B2 -- WEAK FOR GOOD. Chance 50%. EFFECT: PERMANENT DISABILITY (health loss 60%); now dislikes learning (VV2-VV5: learning; story only in VV1); "old" head look
(Name) rests. The fever breaks, and doesn't come back. But it was too high for too long, and it has taken a great deal out of (him/her) on its way out. (Name) is left weak, for good. (He/She) tires after the shortest walk. (His/her) hair has gone grey at the front, and (his/her) face looks years older. And (his/her) mind, which the fever burned so hot, gets tired and foggy whenever (he/she) tries to learn anything new. The healers say (he/she) is lucky to be alive. On good days, (name) agrees.

S092. The Big Wind   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: no one picked (the whole village); some endings name the builders (every villager whose best skill is Building)
EVENT TEXT
A great wind blows all night, howling round the huts like something trying to get in. Nobody sleeps. Things bang and crash and clatter in the dark, and every so often there's a long tearing sound, and everyone flinches.
In the morning, the village comes out blinking into a still, clear dawn, and looks around. Three huts have lost their roofs entirely. The fences are flat. Torn leaves are plastered over every wall like green paint. The cooking pots are halfway down the beach.
And somebody's hammock is hanging from the very top of the tallest palm on the island, swinging gently, as if it's been put there on purpose. Should the builders start rebuilding right away, or should everyone clear up the mess first?

Choice A: Rebuild Right Away
Choice B: Clean Up First

CHOICE A: REBUILD RIGHT AWAY
First popup: The builders don't wait. Before breakfast they're up on the walls with fresh thatch and new poles and rope, and soon everyone who can carry anything is carrying it to them, while the children are sent to fetch the cooking pots back from the beach...

Ending A1 -- MUCH BETTER AT IT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: every builder gains 10 Building; the damaged huts are repaired (stock island-event effect)
The builders work day and night, by sunlight and then by torchlight, eating on the roofs, sleeping in turns. By the end of the week every roof is back on, every fence is standing, and the village looks better than before the wind. And the builders, who had to work faster and harder than ever, have learned more in one week than in a whole season: how to lash a roof pole so it holds, how to set a fence post so the wind can't pull it. They're all much better at their work for it.

Ending A2 -- THE BETTER KNOT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: the damaged huts are repaired (stock island-event effect); tech gain (small amount)
The builders mend everything in three days. And while they're doing it, one of them, cursing at a roof pole that keeps slipping, comes up with a new way to tie a roof down: a clever double knot round the rafters, pinned with a wooden peg, that the wind just can't pull loose. It works so well that they use it on every hut. The researchers come and watch, and draw it, and write it up very carefully, so it's never forgotten. Your villagers gain (award) tech points.

CHOICE B: CLEAN UP FIRST
First popup: Before anyone can build anything, the village has to be cleared. Everyone starts at one end and works to the other, hauling away the fallen branches, the broken poles, the torn thatch, the smashed baskets and the goats that have got into places goats shouldn't be...

Ending B1 -- USEFUL WOOD. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none (the damaged huts still need repair, as in the stock game)
The cleanup takes the whole day, and most of the next. But it turns up piles of good wood among the wreckage: straight poles, solid branches, planks from a fence, all neatly stacked and ready for the builders. Nothing is wasted. The roofs still have to be mended afterwards, of course, and that's a job for the builders over the following days. The hammock comes down from the palm on the third day. Nobody will admit to having climbed up for it.

Ending B2 -- EGGS AND COCONUTS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (small amount) (the damaged huts still need repair, as in the stock game)
Under one of the biggest fallen branches, the clearing party find a nest of big speckled eggs, blown down from the treetops, somehow still whole. Then they find another. Then they find that the wind has shaken every coconut off every palm on the island, and they're lying everywhere, in heaps, in drifts, in the paths and the gardens and the doorways. By evening the store is full of eggs and coconuts. The roofs still have to be mended afterwards, but nobody minds as much on a full stomach. Your villagers gain (award) food.

S093. The Wise Old Tortoise   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
A huge old tortoise has come up out of the sea, walked up the beach and into the village, very slowly, all morning, and is now sitting in the middle of the main path. Everyone has to squeeze round it. Nobody wants to move it.
It's enormous: bigger than a cooking pot, older than anybody can guess. Its shell is scratched all over with marks and grooves that look older than the village, and from one crack near the top, a small yellow flower is growing.
It is looking at (name). Only at (name). With deep, slow, ancient eyes, as if it has a great deal to say and all the time in the world to say it. Should (name) sit with it and see, or follow it wherever it goes?

Choice A: Sit with It
Choice B: Follow It

CHOICE A: SIT WITH IT
First popup: (Name) sits down cross-legged in the dust in front of the tortoise, and looks back at it. The tortoise blinks, very slowly. (Name) blinks back. People walk round them, carefully, and the afternoon goes on...

Ending A1 -- PATIENCE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: gains 20 to 30 Parenting
(Name) sits there all afternoon. The tortoise says nothing at all. It doesn't move. Once, it slowly stretches out its neck, and slowly draws it back in. That's all. But somewhere in the middle of the long, hot, quiet afternoon, (name) understands something about patience that (he/she) never understood before: about waiting, and listening, and letting things take the time they take. At sunset the tortoise turns round and walks away. And from then on, (name) is the gentlest, most patient person with the little ones in the whole village.

(Name) sits so long that (he/she) completely forgets about work. When the farmers come back in the evening and find (him/her) still sitting there, they are very annoyed. The tortoise, as far as anyone can tell, is not sorry at all. Your village loses (award) food.

CHOICE B: FOLLOW IT
First popup: At last, the tortoise turns, very slowly, all the way round, and starts to walk away, and looks back over its shell at (name). Clearly, unmistakably, it wants (him/her) to come. So (name) follows. Very, very slowly...

Ending B1 -- THE HIDDEN GROVE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: gains 20 to 30 Healing
The tortoise leads (name) very, very slowly, all afternoon, out of the village, along a stream (he/she) has never followed, up into the hills, through a gap in the rocks (he/she) has walked past a hundred times without seeing. (Name) watches what it eats, and what it doesn't, and picks a little of everything, and comes home knowing more about healing plants than anyone in the village.

Ending B2 -- BACK TO THE SEA. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The tortoise leads (name) very, very slowly, all afternoon, out of the village, down the path, across the beach, all the way to the edge of the water. Then it walks straight into the sea, and swims away. That's it. That's where it was going. (Name) stands there in the shallows at sunset, feeling slightly foolish. The little yellow flower on its shell is the last thing to disappear under the waves.

S095. The Lucky Harvest   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: no one picked (the whole village)
EVENT TEXT
Everything has grown at once. Every field, every tree, every vine, every garden on the island, all ripe on the very same morning. The elders have never seen anything like it. The researchers think the long rains followed by the hot dry spell set everything off at once.
The fields are bursting. The fruit trees are bent so low with fruit that their branches touch the ground. Vines climb over the fences and across the paths, and fat gourds roll into the doorways. The air is thick and sweet and heavy, and humming. The bees are so busy and so happy that they can't even be bothered to sting anyone.
It's going to take everybody in the village to bring it all in. Maybe more than everybody. Should the village harvest everything, or leave some for the island?

Choice A: Harvest Everything
Choice B: Share with the Island

CHOICE A: HARVEST EVERYTHING
First popup: Every single villager who can walk heads for the fields with a basket. Children, elders, healers, researchers, the chief. They pick from dawn to dark, and carry, and pick again, singing to keep going...

Ending A1 -- OVERFLOWING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (huge amount)
It takes a whole week, and every basket, pot, bowl, net, cloth and hat in the village, and in the end they're piling the harvest in heaps on the floor of the meeting hut because there's nowhere else to put it. The stores are full to the brim and overflowing. Nobody in the village has ever seen so much food in one place. The children lie on top of the pile of melons and refuse to get off. Your villagers gain (award) food.

Ending A2 -- SOME FOR THE BIRDS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (large amount)
The village harvests so much, so fast, that they simply can't carry it all. Baskets fill up faster than anyone can take them to the store. Heaps of fruit sit waiting in the fields, and the birds come, in great happy flocks, and help themselves. By the time the last basket is carried in, the birds have had a good share. But even so, it's the biggest harvest the village has ever had. Your villagers gain (award) food.

CHOICE B: SHARE WITH THE ISLAND
First popup: The elders say that a gift this big should be shared. So the village harvests what it needs, and then, on purpose, leaves the rest: whole rows in the fields, whole trees in the orchards, left standing, untouched...

Ending B1 -- THE ANIMALS ARE GRATEFUL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (normal amount)
They leave the rest for the animals. And the animals come: birds, pigs, goats, the little striped forest creatures nobody usually sees, all eating side by side in the fields as the sun goes down. It's a strange and lovely sight. And the animals seem grateful, in their way: the pigs root up the leftover stalks and turn the soil, the birds leave their droppings on the fields. The next harvest is just as good as this one. Your villagers gain (award) food.

S097. The Ghost Light   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: one villager aged 14 or older (not protected)
EVENT TEXT
For three nights now, a soft light has been bobbing among the trees beyond the edge of the village. It's pale green, about the size of a cooking pot, and it moves in a slow, bobbing way, up and down, back and forth, almost as if it were walking.
Everyone has seen it. Nobody has gone to look. The elders have said, very firmly, that nobody is to go to look. They say it's a spirit searching for someone, and that it's best not to be the one it finds.
On the fourth night, (name) can't stand it any more. Long after everyone else has gone to sleep, (he/she) slips out of (his/her) hut and walks to the edge of the trees. The light is there, waiting, a little way in among the dark trunks. As (name) watches, it bobs once, as if it's nodding. Should (name) follow it into the trees, or stay at the edge and call out to it?

Choice B: Call Out to It

CHOICE A: FOLLOW THE LIGHT

Ending A1 -- THE GLOWING MUSHROOMS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (normal amount)
The light leads (name) through the forest for a long time, and at last into a small clearing (he/she) has never seen. The ground is covered, every inch of it, in mushrooms that glow the same soft green as the light. Hundreds of them. Thousands. The whole clearing is lit up like a pool of green fire. The light hangs in the middle of it for a moment, and then, slowly, fades away to nothing. (Name) gathers a basketful of the glowing mushrooms and finds (his/her) way home by their light. The researchers are absolutely thrilled. Your villagers gain (award) tech points.

Ending B1 -- ODDLY COMFORTED. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

(He/She) can't explain it, but (he/she) feels oddly comforted, as if somebody (he/she) once knew has just said goodbye. (He/She) goes back to bed and sleeps better than (he/she) has in weeks. The village keeps a fire burning at the edge of the trees for a whole season, in case.

S100. The Last Sunset of the Year   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: no one picked (the whole village)
EVENT TEXT
The last sunset of the year is always the most beautiful. Everybody knows it. Nobody knows why. The elders say it's the sky saying goodbye to the old year properly.
Tonight, the whole village climbs to the top of the hill together to watch it. Every single one of them: the elders on sticks, helped by the young ones; the babies on their parents' backs; the children running ahead and back and ahead again. They sit down together in the long grass, shoulder to shoulder, looking out over the sea.
The sky turns orange. Then pink. Then a purple deep enough to swim in. The sea holds every colour, and the first star comes out over the water. Should the village watch in silence, or sing together?

Choice A: Watch in Silence
Choice B: Sing Together

CHOICE A: WATCH IN SILENCE
First popup: Nobody says a word. Nobody needs to. The whole village sits on the hill together, quiet, watching the colours change, while the sun slides down, slowly, into the sea...

Ending A1 -- PEACEFUL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Nobody says a single word. The sun goes down. The last red line of it slips under the water. The stars come out, one by one and then all at once, until the sky is thick with them. Somebody's baby gives a little sleepy sigh. And then, still without a word, the village gets up, and helps each other up, and walks home together down the hill in the starlight, feeling peaceful, every single one of them, all the way to their beds.

Ending A2 -- WILL IT COME BACK? Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Nobody says a word. Right up until the very last sliver of sun is slipping under the sea, and a very small child, sitting on a parent's lap, looks up and asks, in a very worried little voice that carries across the whole silent hillside, "Will it come back?" There's a pause. Then everybody laughs, the whole village at once, warm and loud, and everyone says yes, all together, "Yes!", and the child is very relieved. They walk home laughing.

CHOICE B: SING TOGETHER
First popup: One of the elders starts it, softly, the old song for the end of the year. Then another voice joins, and another, and another, until the whole hillside is singing...

Ending B1 -- A NIGHT NOBODY FORGETS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: every villager is happier (stock island-event effect)
The whole village sings the old songs, one after another, as the sun goes down and the stars come out. The songs the elders learned from their grandparents, and the ones the children made up last week, and the one about the turtle that everybody knows. Their voices roll down the hill and out over the dark sea. It goes on until the moon is high. It's a night nobody ever forgets, and years later, people still say "Do you remember the last sunset, when we sang?"

Ending B2 -- SINGING BADLY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Somebody starts singing. Badly. Very badly, completely off-key, and too loud, and getting the words wrong. A few people start to laugh. Then somebody else joins in, just as badly, on purpose. And then everybody does, the whole village, at the top of their lungs, as out of tune as they can possibly manage, howling at the purple sky. The goats in the valley start bleating along. It's terrible. It's wonderful. It's the happiest anyone has been all year, and the perfect way to end it.

NEW-101. The Spring That Reflected Tomorrow   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (name1) any villager 14+. (name2) a second villager 14+ (the volunteer). (elder name) the oldest villager in the village, never (name1) or (name2).
EVENT TEXT

Grey at the temples. Deep laugh lines. And a long scar across the cheek that (name1) has definitely not earned yet.
A leaf drifts down and lands on the surface. The water does not even ripple. The older face just keeps looking at (him/her), patient, as if it has been waiting a long time for (name1) to show up.

Choice B: Let Someone Take a Long Look
Choice C: Ask the Oldest Villager

...but by the time (he/she) has the charcoal sharpened, a breeze wrinkles the water. The older face breaks into a hundred wobbling pieces and never comes back together. "...although," (elder name) adds with a shrug, "she mostly said it to keep us children from falling in. It worked. I never went near it." The elder cannot say if any of it is true, and seems to find the whole affair very funny. (Name1) goes to bed with more questions than (he/she) started with.

"...and she taught me how to watch it properly." (Elder name) shows (name1) how to visit the spring at dawn and dusk and tie a knot in a cord for every change seen in the water: big knots, small knots, double knots. NEW-102. The Second Shadow   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) any villager 14+. (elder name) the village's keeper of tales: any elder, never (name).
EVENT TEXT
At sunset on the beach, (name) looks down and notices (he/she) has two shadows.
One moves the way a shadow should. The other copies every move a heartbeat late, like a shy dancer trying to keep up with the music. When (name) raises an arm, it raises an arm... eventually. When (he/she) turns to run, it stumbles after (him/her).
The children have already started waving at it. It waves back, a little late, and they shriek with delight. (Name) does not shriek, but only because (he/she) is too busy trying not to. What should (he/she) do about it?
Choice A: Time the Delay
Choice B: Let the Shadow Step Forward
Choice C: Question the Keeper of Tales
Choice D: Walk Home Before Dark

CHOICE A: TIME THE DELAY
First popup: (Name) decides that if (he/she) is going to be haunted, (he/she) might as well be haunted precisely. (He/She) claps once, then counts heartbeats until the shadow claps back. One... two...
Ending A1 -- THE STEADY COUNT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
Every clap comes back after exactly the same count, as steady as a drum. (Name) practices until (he/she) can keep the beat without thinking, and the fishers later borrow the trick for timing when to haul their nets. Nobody asks where (he/she) learned it. (He/She) does not volunteer the answer.
Ending A2 -- THE SUNSET. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Halfway through the count, the sun slips into the sea, and the second shadow goes down with it like someone sinking into deep water. (Name) waits a long time on the darkening sand. It does not come back up. (He/She) is surprised to find (he/she) is a little sad about that.

CHOICE B: LET THE SHADOW STEP FORWARD
First popup: (Name) takes a deep breath and steps aside, leaving room on the sand. "Well? Go on then." The second shadow hesitates... and then peels up off the beach like a wet leaf lifting from a rock...
Ending B1 -- THE NEW VILLAGER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: clone of (name) (different name)
It fills out, gains colour, and stands up as a whole person with (name)'s exact face and build, right down to the freckle (name) always thought nobody noticed. The newcomer looks around at the gaping crowd, clears (his/her) throat, and politely asks to be called by a different name so as not to cause any confusion. Then (he/she) asks where supper is. It turns out (he/she) has a mind entirely of (his/her) own, and the village has one more mouth to feed.
Ending B2 -- SECOND THOUGHTS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The shadow rises halfway, a dark shape the size of a person, and (name) loses (his/her) nerve completely. "No. No, sorry, I changed my mind!" (He/She) steps out of the sunset, and the shape slumps back down onto the sand. No one argues with (him/her). The shadow just goes on being late, every evening, for about a week, and then stops.

CHOICE C: QUESTION THE KEEPER OF TALES
First popup: (Elder name) hears the whole thing with (his/her) eyes closed, nodding slowly. "Shadows that ran off to be people. Yes. I know that one..."
Ending C1 -- A GOOD WAY TO GET CHILDREN INDOORS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
"...but I could never tell you if it is a true story or just a very good way to get children inside at dusk." (Elder name) opens one eye. "Is it working?" It is. The children are all suddenly very keen to be indoors.
Ending C2 -- THE SHADOW STICKS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
"...and here is what my teacher did with it." (Elder name) shows (name) how to push sticks into the sand at the tip of a shadow through the day, an old method for telling the hour and the turning of the seasons. By the end of the week there is a neat arc of sticks on the beach, and the researchers are measuring it with great excitement.

CHOICE D: WALK HOME BEFORE DARK
First popup: (Name) decides this is not (his/her) problem and walks briskly up the beach without looking back. (He/She) can hear the children giggling behind (him/her)...
Ending D1 -- A STORY FOR THE FIRE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
...and by the time (he/she) reaches the fire, (he/she) has turned it into a pretty good story. The village decides the second shadow will be something to tell tales about, not a project. (Name) still checks the sand behind (him/her) every sunset.
Ending D2 -- ONE SHADOW. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The next evening, (name) casts only one shadow. The beach shows nothing but footprints. The story rests on the word of the few who saw it, and they tell it so often and so loudly that nobody quite believes them anymore.

NEW-103. The Twin in the Mist   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) any villager 14+. (elder name) any elder, never (name).
EVENT TEXT
Morning mist rolls up from the lagoon, thick and white, and out of it walks... (name).
Same face. Same hair. Same walk, right down to the way (he/she) scratches behind one ear when (he/she) is thinking. The trouble is that the real (name) is standing a few steps away holding a basket of fish, and (he/she) is looking very, very unsettled.
The double spots (him/her) and smiles warmly, the way someone smiles at an old friend not seen in years. Then it waves. What should (name) do?
Choice A: Study the Double from Afar
Choice B: Offer the Double a Seat by the Fire
Choice C: Bar the Doors Until It Lifts

CHOICE A: STUDY THE DOUBLE FROM AFAR
First popup: (Name) puts the fish basket down very slowly and crouches behind a palm, watching. The double crouches behind the next palm and watches (him/her) back...
Ending A1 -- THE BENDING LIGHT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
For an hour they copy each other, gesture for gesture, until the mist starts to thin. As it does, (name) notices the double wobbles and stretches whenever the fog gets thicker, the same way the far shore wobbles on hot days. (He/She) brings a careful description of how fog bends light along the water back to the researchers. It is a small piece of new knowledge, and a large piece of new nightmares.
Ending A2 -- BURNED AWAY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The sun comes up over the trees, and the double thins with the mist. It gives (name) one last friendly wave as it fades, until nothing is left but wet grass and a single, perfectly ordinary footprint. (Name) puts (his/her) own foot next to it. It is an exact match. (He/She) goes home and does not mention this to anyone for three days.

CHOICE B: OFFER THE DOUBLE A SEAT BY THE FIRE
First popup: "Well," says (name) weakly, "you'd better come and have breakfast, I suppose." The double beams and follows (him/her) up the path. The whole village stops what it is doing to stare...
Ending B1 -- THE STAYING GUEST. Chance 50%. EFFECT: duplicate of (name) (different name)
The double sits, eats two bowls of porridge, and simply... stays. By midday it is a real, solid person, laughing at jokes and helping to scrub the pot. (He/She) has (name)'s face, but picks a different name for (himself/herself) so nobody mixes the two of them up at dinner. (Name) is not sure whether (he/she) has gained a twin or lost an argument, but the village has gained a villager.
Ending B2 -- NOT AT MY FIRE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
At the edge of the village, (name) stops dead. "No. I'm sorry. I can't share a fire with my own face." The others honour that, and nobody presses. The double looks only a little hurt. It bows, turns, and drifts back down the path into the mist, scratching behind one ear.

CHOICE C: BAR THE DOORS UNTIL IT LIFTS
First popup: (Name) runs. The whole village, hearing (his/her) shouting, decides that running is a fine idea, and every door flap is tied shut. Then the long wait begins...
Ending C1 -- THE REED TRICK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
Crammed into one hut, (elder name) passes the time by showing (name) how to tell when fog will lift by watching which way the reeds bend at the water's edge. "Mist walkers," (elder name) mutters, "never stay past the reeds standing up." Whether that is true or not, the trick works on ordinary fog, and saves the fishers many wasted mornings afterwards.
Ending C2 -- GONE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
When the doors finally open, the double is gone. Only the people who saw it can say it was ever there, and they do, often, loudly, and with more detail every time. By the end of the season, the double has apparently juggled fish and sung a song. It did neither.

NEW-104. The Charm That Forgot   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (name1) any villager 14+ (the wearer). (name2) a second villager 14+ (the volunteer). (elder name) the weaving elder: any elder, never the others.
EVENT TEXT
The memory charm, a braid of hair and little shell beads, was made to help forgetful villagers remember their chores. It has worked well for years. Mostly.
This morning (name1), who was wearing it, opened (his/her) mouth to say good morning and could not remember (his/her) own name. Not for long, just for one horrible breath, but long enough. And when the others look closely at the charm, one of the shell beads now shows a tiny carved name that nobody in the village recognizes.
The charm sits on its cord looking completely innocent. What should (name1) do with it?
Choice A: Unpick the Charm's Knots

The charm is plain string now. (Name1) cannot decide if (he/she) is relieved or not, and keeps checking that (he/she) still knows (his/her) name.

CHOICE B: LET SOMEONE WEAR IT OVERNIGHT

(Name2) asks why everybody is staring. Someone hands (him/her) a bowl of water to look into. There is a long silence, and then, to everyone's relief, (name2) laughs.
Ending B2 -- ON THE PEG. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

"Here. I'll show you how they tested a weave." (Elder name) soaks a strand in seawater and has (name1) watch how it dries: tight weaves curl, loose ones sag, and good ones dry straight as an arrow. It is an old method worth keeping, and (name1) writes it down so the village will not forget it, then checks the bark twice to make sure the writing has not forgotten anything either.

NEW-105. The Night of Exchanged Voices   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (name1) and (name2) two villagers 14+ who woke up with swapped voices. (name3) a third villager 14+ (the volunteer). (elder name) the elder who hears spirits: any elder, never the others.
EVENT TEXT
(Name1) and (name2) wake up in neighbouring huts, step outside, and wish each other good morning.
Each of them hears the other's voice come out of (his/her) own mouth.
(Name1), who usually has a voice like a rumbling drum, now squeaks like a startled bird. (Name2), who usually speaks so softly people lean in to hear, now BOOMS across the clearing loud enough to make the babies cry. They stare at each other. Then they both try to say "what" at the same time, and it comes out as a squeak and a boom.
Breakfast is loud, confusing and very, very funny for everyone who is not them. (Name1) and (name2) just want their own voices back. What should they do?
Choice A: Record How Each Voice Sounds
Choice B: Have Someone Sleep Where They Slept
Choice C: Ask the Elder Who Hears Spirits

CHOICE A: RECORD HOW EACH VOICE SOUNDS
First popup: A researcher sits the two of them down and has them sing the same chant over and over, marking each high and low note on a stick. (Name1) squeaks. (Name2) booms. The children gather to watch, giggling into their hands...
Ending A1 -- THE PITCH STICK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
By noon the stick is covered in marks, and the researcher has learned a surprising amount about how high and low sounds carry across the clearing, and why a booming voice reaches the far huts while a squeaky one gets lost in the trees. It is useful knowledge. (Name1) and (name2) are not consulted about whether they found it useful.
Ending A2 -- GONE BY MIDDAY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Halfway through the third chant, (name1)'s voice drops back into a rumble, mid-note. (Name2) gasps softly, in (his/her) own soft voice. Both voices have slipped back to their owners as if nothing happened, and there is nothing left to study. The children are very disappointed. (Name1) and (name2) are not.

CHOICE B: HAVE SOMEONE SLEEP WHERE THEY SLEPT
First popup: (Name3) is curious, and possibly a little bored. "If something swapped them in the night, I want to see it." (He/She) drags a sleeping mat to the spot between the two huts and lies down, grinning at the stars...
Ending B1 -- THE NEW FACE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: new look (head) for (name3)
In the morning (name3) wakes up and says "Well? Did it work?" in (his/her) own perfectly normal voice, and everyone is about to be disappointed... until they see (his/her) face. Whatever did the swapping kept (his/her) voice but changed everything else: a new face and new hair, changed for good. The village has to learn (his/her) look all over again. (Name3) seems rather pleased about it.
Ending B2 -- NO GAMBLERS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name3) lies there for about as long as it takes to hear an owl hoot twice, then picks up the mat and goes home. "I like my voice," (he/she) explains the next day. Nobody presses anyone else to try, and the spot between the huts gets a lot of nervous looks.

CHOICE C: ASK THE ELDER WHO HEARS SPIRITS
First popup: (Elder name) listens to (name1) squeak the story and (name2) boom the ending, and manages to keep a straight face for almost the whole thing...
Ending C1 -- A TRADING GAME. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
"Spirits sometimes play trading games with sleepers," (elder name) says gravely, and then, less gravely: "Or so I'm told. I've never seen one myself." (He/She) suggests they each eat something they dislike, "to show the spirits you mean business." They do. It does not help. By night the voices drift home on their own anyway.
Ending C2 -- LISTENING THROUGH THE FLOOR. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
(Elder name) presses an ear to the hut floor. "Spirits move through hollow places. Listen." (He/She) teaches (name1) an old way of tapping and listening for echoes through the floor. They find no spirits, but they do find two hollow, rotting floor posts that nobody knew about. The builders start using the trick everywhere. The voices come home that night.

NEW-106. The Blessing of the Old Tree   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (name1) and (name2) a couple, both 18+, partners (married or in love, as the game records it), neither nursing nor already pregnant, (ANY BIRTH SEX): the magic decides which of them carries the baby. (elder name) the tree's keeper: any elder, never the couple.
EVENT TEXT
(Name1) and (name2) have hoped for a child for a long time. They do not talk about it much anymore. They just sit together most evenings beneath the oldest tree on the island, the huge one with roots like folded arms, and watch the light go.
Tonight, a single leaf drifts down and lands in their joined hands.
It glows. A soft, warm gold, like a coal in a fire, and it stays as warm as a hearthstone even as the night cools. The two of them sit absolutely still, not daring to breathe.
Everyone in the village has an opinion about it before sundown the next day. What should (name1) and (name2) do with the leaf?
Choice A: Keep Notes on the Leaf
Choice B: Accept the Tree's Blessing
Choice C: Ask the Tree's Keeper

CHOICE A: KEEP NOTES ON THE LEAF
First popup: (Name1) decides that before anyone gets their hopes up, someone should watch this leaf very carefully. (He/She) sets it on a flat stone and checks it every hour, scratching notes into bark...
Ending A1 -- THE GLOWING HOURS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
The leaf glows brightest at dawn, dimmest at noon, and pulses gently whenever it rains. (Name1) takes the notes to the researchers, who are fascinated, and who learn a good deal about the old tree from watching its leaf. Whatever the leaf meant, it has taught the village something. (Name2) keeps the notes in a safe place.
Ending A2 -- AN ORDINARY LEAF. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
By evening the glow has faded completely, leaving an ordinary dry leaf that crumbles a little at the edges. (Name1) and (name2) sit looking at it for a long time, not sure what to feel. Then (name2) quietly presses it between two pieces of bark to keep, and takes (name1)'s hand.

CHOICE B: ACCEPT THE TREE'S BLESSING
First popup: (Name1) and (name2) look at each other. Then, together, they close their hands around the leaf and say thank you to the tree, out loud, feeling a little silly and very hopeful. The glow sinks slowly into their hands, warm all the way up to their elbows...
Ending B1 -- EXPECTING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: pregnant with one baby: one of the couple (ANY BIRTH SEX, the magic chooses) with the other
Within the month, one of them is expecting a baby. The healers confirm it twice, because the couple ask them to check twice. The two of them can hardly stop smiling, and they go back to the old tree to say thank you again, this time with a basket of the best fruit in the village, which they leave among the roots.
Ending B2 -- IN OUR OWN TIME. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
As the warmth fades, (name2) shakes (his/her) head gently. "If it happens, I want it to happen because it happens. Not because a tree said so." (Name1) understands. They set the leaf among the roots with a word of thanks, and the village respects their choice, though one or two of the more nosy aunts are very disappointed.

CHOICE C: ASK THE TREE'S KEEPER
First popup: (Elder name), who has tended the old tree's roots for decades, listens with (his/her) hand resting on the bark, as if checking the tree's side of the story...
Ending C1 -- MY AUNT SWORE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
"It has blessed families before," (elder name) says at last, "or so my aunt swore. She also swore she once saw it walk, so." (He/She) cannot promise them anything, and is honest enough not to try. The couple thank (him/her) and decide to just enjoy the warm leaf while it lasts.
Ending C2 -- READING THE BARK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
"I can't tell you what the tree means. But I can teach you to read it." (Elder name) shows (name1) how to judge the tree's health from the colour of its bark and the pattern of its fallen leaves, an old way of watching that the village is glad to keep. Whatever the leaf was saying, (name1) is now one of the few people who can listen to the tree properly.

NEW-107. The Mirror of Other Years   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) any villager 25+ (so five years younger is still an adult). (elder name) any elder, never (name).
EVENT TEXT
Builders clearing the rubble of the old healer's collapsed hut, empty since before most villagers were born, find a disc of polished black stone, perfectly round and cool to the touch. (Name) picks it up to brush off the dust and catches (his/her) reflection.
It is (him/her), all right... but much younger. Gap teeth and all. The haircut (his/her) mother gave (him/her) the year of the big storm. The bruise from falling out of that mango tree.
Stranger still: the longer (name) looks, the less (his/her) knees and back ache. (He/She) has not felt this limber in years. What should (he/she) do with the stone?
Choice A: Compare the Reflection
Choice B: Gaze Into It Willingly
Choice C: Wrap It and Set It Aside

CHOICE A: COMPARE THE REFLECTION
First popup: (Name) sits down with a few old friends and the stone, and goes through it carefully: old scars, the missing tooth, the shape of that bruise. "Was it the left knee or the right one?" "The right. You cried for a day."...
Ending A1 -- EVERY DIFFERENCE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
(Name) notes every difference between the reflection and (his/her) friends' memories. They match far too well. The researchers pore over the notes and the stone, and learn a little about how this strange black rock was polished and where it might have been quarried. Nobody can explain the knees.
Ending A2 -- CLOUDED. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Halfway through, the stone clouds over like breath on a cold morning. When it clears, it shows only (name)'s face as it is today, wrinkles and all. The young face never comes back. Neither does the feeling in (his/her) knees. (He/She) puts the stone down gently and goes for a walk, slowly.

CHOICE B: GAZE INTO IT WILLINGLY
First popup: (Name) sits cross-legged in the shade and stares into the stone, deeper and deeper, ignoring the voices around (him/her). The young face in the stone stares back, and slowly begins to grin...
Ending B1 -- FIVE YEARS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: changes age: (name) becomes 5 years younger
The stone flashes white, bright enough that the others cry out and cover their eyes. When (name)'s eyes clear, (his/her) body is five years younger, with a little less grey and a lot more spring in (his/her) step. (His/Her) memories are all exactly the same, including every one of the jokes (his/her) friends now make about it. (Name) celebrates by running up the hill to the fields. Just because (he/she) can.
Ending B2 -- EVERY YEAR EARNED. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
After a long while, (name) blinks, sighs, and turns the stone face down on the ground. "No," (he/she) says. "I've earned every one of my years. I'd like to keep them." (His/Her) knees start aching again almost at once. (He/She) does not seem to mind as much as everyone expected.

CHOICE C: WRAP IT AND SET IT ASIDE
First popup: (Name) wraps the stone in bark cloth without looking at it again and carries it to (elder name), who unwraps one corner, peers inside, and quickly wraps it up again...
Ending C1 -- POLISHING STONE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
"Hmph. Nice work, whoever made it." (Elder name) refuses to look into it, but teaches (name) the old way of polishing stone with wet sand and coconut oil, and how to tell good stone from bad by its sheen. The disc goes up on a high shelf, still wrapped, and the village's stone tools get noticeably shinier.
Ending C2 -- THE EMPTY CLOTH. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The stone is set on a high shelf, still wrapped, a thing to tell stories about rather than use. The next morning the bark cloth is empty and neatly folded. The stone is gone without a trace, and nobody, as far as anyone can tell, looks a day younger.

NEW-108. The Spirit's Unfinished Song   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) the village's best singer: any villager 14+ (prefer one with high Research or any villager if none stands out). (elder name) any elder, never (name).
EVENT TEXT
For three nights now, a melody has drifted out of the empty hut at the edge of the village. Nobody lives there. Nobody has lived there for years.
It is a beautiful tune: slow, sweet, a little sad. And every time, it stops one note short of the end, like a question left hanging in the air.
(Name), who has the best voice in the village, cannot stop humming it. While cooking. While fishing. While asleep, according to (his/her) family, who are being driven slowly up the walls. "Just FINISH it!" one of them begged this morning. "I CAN'T," (name) said. "I don't know the last note." What should (name) do?

Choice B: Sing the Missing Note
Choice C: Ask Who Lived There

CHOICE A: SCRATCH THE TUNE ONTO A BOARD

Ending A1 -- THE WRITTEN SONG. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
By dawn (name) has the whole melody on the board, every note except the last. It is the first time anyone in the village has written a song down this way, and the researchers are thrilled; other singers start copying the method for their own chants. (Name)'s family is less thrilled, because now (he/she) can hum it while reading it.
Ending A2 -- HALFWAY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

CHOICE B: SING THE MISSING NOTE

"...and she taught me this, before she died." (Elder name) shows (name) the old breathing method that the hut's owner used to hold long notes: breathe low, into the belly, and let it out like a slow tide. (Name)'s chants grow steadier, and (he/she) teaches it to the other singers. The song from the hut keeps playing, but somehow it sounds happier.
