NEW-109. The Blue Flame   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (name1) the observer: any villager 14+. (name2) the volunteer: another villager 14+. (elder name) the fire keeper: any elder, never the others.
EVENT TEXT
On a flat stone beside the volcano path, a little blue flame has been burning all day.
There is no wood under it. No oil, no moss, nothing. It just sits there on bare rock, flickering politely, the colour of the sky right before dark. The moss around it is not even singed. Stranger still, it is cool enough to hold a hand over.
Three children have already tested this. Their parents found out. There was shouting.
(Name1) is supposed to be walking the children home. Instead (he/she) has sat down on a log, staring at the flame, and has not moved for an hour. What should (name1) do about it?
Choice A: Sit Up with the Flame
Choice B: Pass a Hand Through the Fire
Choice C: Fetch the Fire Keeper

CHOICE A: SIT UP WITH THE FLAME
First popup: (Name1) sends the children home with someone else, wraps (himself/herself) in a blanket, and settles in for the night beside the blue flame, scratching notes onto bark by its strange cold light...
Ending A1 -- THE VOLCANO'S BREATH. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
All night (name1) watches. The flame leans away from the wind instead of with it. It brightens just before the rain comes and dims when the rain stops. There is a faint smell like rotten eggs whenever it flares. By morning (name1) has learned a good deal about the volcano's breath seeping through the rocks, and the researchers decide that the volcano path should not be a place for napping.
Ending A2 -- GUTTERED. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Around midnight, the flame gutters, shrinks to a blue speck, and goes out. (Name1) waits and waits, holding (his/her) breath, but it will not come back. In the morning (he/she) walks home stiff, cold and empty-handed, and has to explain to (his/her) family why (he/she) spent the night talking to a rock.

CHOICE B: PASS A HAND THROUGH THE FIRE
First popup: (Name2) shoulders through the crowd. "Children did it. How bad can it be?" Before anyone can stop (him/her), (he/she) holds out a hand and passes it straight through the blue flame...
Ending B1 -- BLUE LIGHT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: new look (head) for (name2)
Blue light runs up (his/her) arm like water up a reed, over (his/her) shoulder and across (his/her) face. The crowd screams. (Name2) does not; (he/she) just stands there with (his/her) mouth open. When the light fades, (he/she) is completely unhurt, but (his/her) look has changed for good: new hair, new features, same grin. "That," (name2) announces, "was AMAZING."
Ending B2 -- THE SENSIBLE CROWD. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name2)'s fingertips touch the edge of the flame, and it flares up tall and bright. (He/She) yanks (his/her) hand back with a yelp. It does not hurt. NEW-110. The Dream of Two Selves   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (name1) and (name2) two villagers 14+ who are not close friends (any sex, any relation except spouse). Neither is nursing or pregnant. (elder name) the dream reader: any elder, never the two.
EVENT TEXT
(Name1) and (name2) barely speak to each other. They are not enemies, exactly; they just have nothing in common and both like it that way.
So it is a shock to everybody when, at breakfast, they both describe the same dream.
They woke up in each other's bodies, in each other's huts, and spent the whole day faking it. (Name1) describes (name2)'s sleeping mat perfectly. (Name2) knows which of (name1)'s pots has the chipped handle. They both mention a cracked water jar by the door, right down to the shape of the crack.
They look at each other across the fire. Neither of them is eating anymore. Was it just a dream? (name1) wonders. Or something more?
Choice A: Compare the Two Accounts
Choice B: Sleep Side by Side Tonight
Choice C: Ask the Dream Reader

CHOICE A: COMPARE THE TWO ACCOUNTS
First popup: A researcher takes (name1) to one side and (name2) to the other, and has each tell the dream in every detail, without the other listening. The two lists get longer, and longer...
Ending A1 -- MATCHING DETAILS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
Set side by side, the two accounts match in ways nobody could have guessed, down to what was for lunch. The researchers learn a little about dreams and memory, and come up with a careful way of questioning witnesses separately that turns out to be useful for all sorts of disputes. (Name1) and (name2) start nodding to each other at the well. It is a start.
Ending A2 -- FADING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The dreams stop the next night. By the time the researcher sits down with them, the details have already started to fade, the way dreams do. Was the jar cracked on the left or the right? Neither of them is sure anymore. The matter is dropped, but (name1) and (name2) keep giving each other odd, thoughtful looks.

CHOICE B: SLEEP SIDE BY SIDE TONIGHT
First popup: Against all common sense, and mostly because the whole village is dying to know, (name1) and (name2) agree to sleep in the same hut, mats side by side. They lie there in the dark, very stiff, very polite. "Good night." "Good night."...
Ending B1 -- FOR REAL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: body swap (name1) with (name2)
In the morning, (name1) opens (his/her) eyes, sits up, and looks down at hands that are not (his/hers). Across the hut, (his/her) own face is staring back at (him/her) in horror. This time it is not a dream: they really are in each other's bodies. Each keeps (his/her) own memories and mind, so each must now learn to live in the other's skin. The first thing they discover is that they will have to talk to each other a great deal more from now on.
Ending B2 -- NOT WORTH IT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Halfway through the night, (name2) sits up, grabs (his/her) mat, and walks out. "I'm not risking it." A moment later (name1) follows, going the other way. Neither of them sleeps a wink, but both wake up in their own bodies, and the village lets the dream stay a dream.

CHOICE C: ASK THE DREAM READER
First popup: (Elder name), who reads dreams for anyone who brings (him/her) a fish, listens to both of them very gravely, chewing on the fish...
Ending C1 -- TWO PATHS CROSSING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
"A shared dream means two paths crossing," (elder name) announces. Then, honestly: "I say that about most dreams. It's usually true enough." (Name1) and (name2) look at each other and laugh for the first time, and the cracked jar, when they check, turns out to be perfectly whole.
Ending C2 -- THE DREAM TALLY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
"Here's what you do." (Elder name) gives them each a stick and teaches them the old way of keeping a dream tally: a notch for each dream, a different notch for each place, a cross for each face. Over many nights the pattern shows things that no single dream could. The researchers adopt the method, and the dream reader gets a lot more fish.

NEW-111. The Fishing Line Dispute   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (leader name) leads the evening gathering: any villager 25+ (in The Secret City this may be the Tribal Chief; in New Believers never the Chief role, who is not sent on events). (name1) and (name2) the eldest fishers of the two households: two villagers 18+, not in the same family. (name3) a quiet young net-mender: any villager 14 to 20.
EVENT TEXT
Two households both say the rocky stretch past the reef is theirs to fish. Both have scratched marker stones to prove it. Both stones, annoyingly, look exactly alike.
Twice now, nets have been moved in the night. The first time, (name1)'s family found their net tangled on the rocks. The second time, (name2)'s family found theirs floating halfway to the horizon. Accusations have been flying across the cooking fires ever since, and yesterday somebody threw a fish. Not AT anyone. Near them. Pointedly.
(Leader name) wants this settled before somebody's whole net ends up in another village. How should (he/she) settle it?
Choice A: Let Both Households Speak
Choice B: Walk the Reef at Low Tide
Choice C: Split the Day Between Them

CHOICE A: LET BOTH HOUSEHOLDS SPEAK

The gathering listens without interrupting. Even (name2) uncrosses (his/her) arms. Nothing is decided tonight, but nobody throws anything either, and the two families walk home side by side.
Ending A2 -- THE ROLLED STONE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Before (name2) can start, (name3), who mends nets for both families and has never spoken at a gathering in (his/her) life, stands up, goes bright red, and blurts it out: the stretch was always shared, until a storm rolled one of the marker stones two summers ago. CHOICE B: WALK THE REEF AT LOW TIDE

Halfway along, (leader name) stops and points. The fish are all gathered on the north side of the rocks this early in the morning. By evening, when they come back to check, the fish have moved around to the south side. Neither family has been fishing the best spot at the best time! Ending B2 -- THE TIDE DID IT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

CHOICE C: SPLIT THE DAY BETWEEN THEM

Ending C1 -- WORKS WELL ENOUGH. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
It works well enough to keep. The mornings are calm, the evenings are calm, and the nets stay exactly where they were left. (Leader name) promises to look at the arrangement again after the big tides, and the fish-throwing is never mentioned again, except as a joke.
Ending C2 -- STANDING AROUND. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
By the end of the week, both families have spent half of every day standing on the beach with nothing to do, glaring at the other family fishing. "This is worse!" (name1) complains. "For once I agree with (him/her)!" says (name2). (Leader name) calls the whole thing off, and they go back to arguing, though somehow a little more cheerfully than before.

NEW-112. The Watch at Night   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]

EVENT TEXT
Someone has to sit the watch between midnight and dawn. It is the worst watch there is: the fire burns low, the insects bite their hardest, and the jungle is at its noisiest, full of cracks and rustles and things that go "hoo" in a way that sounds personal.
Nobody wants it. Over supper, three different villagers have already "volunteered" each other, loudly, and with increasing creativity. ("(He/She) has the best ears!" "(He/She) snores anyway, (he/she) won't miss the sleep!")
(Name1), who has ended up with the late watch more often than anyone, is sitting very quietly, which is a bad sign. How should (leader name) decide who sits it?
Choice A: Hear the Night Guards Out
Choice B: Count the Notches on the Watch Post
Choice C: Rotate the Worst Watch Each Moon

CHOICE A: HEAR THE NIGHT GUARDS OUT

Ending A1 -- THE WRECKED SLEEP. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name1) tells them. How the late watch wrecks (his/her) sleep for days afterwards. How (he/she) snapped at (his/her) own children last week over nothing, and how bad (he/she) felt. Ending A2 -- THE NIGHT OWL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

CHOICE B: COUNT THE NOTCHES ON THE WATCH POST

Ending B1 -- TWICE A NIGHT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)

Ending B2 -- NOBODY DODGED. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

CHOICE C: ROTATE THE WORST WATCH EACH MOON

Ending C1 -- FAIR ENOUGH. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

Ending C2 -- NOBODY SHOWS UP. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

On the second night, nobody comes at all, and the fire goes out, and a curious pig wanders straight through the village. The idea is dropped, and (name1) sighs and picks up the watch stick again.

This was supposed to be the morning the storehouse roof repair finally began. The builders have been planning it for weeks. They turn up at the tool shelter at first light, rolling up their sleeves...

The builders stand around with empty hands. Somebody mentions that somebody else was "acting strange" last night. Somebody else mentions that the first somebody always acts strange. Fingers are starting to point, and (name1), the head builder, looks ready to chew through the roof beams with (his/her) own teeth. What should (leader name) do?

Choice C: Lend Tools by Tally Stick

CHOICE A: ASK THE BUILDERS WHAT IT COSTS THEM

(Name1) explains: without the adze and rope, the roof won't be finished before the rains, and the rains will soak every basket in the storehouse. Suddenly everyone understands why the builders are so upset, and half the village offers to help search. The tools turn up by evening, and nobody ever finds out who moved them. The builders decide they don't much care.
Ending A2 -- THE CANOE ROPE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

CHOICE C: LEND TOOLS BY TALLY STICK

Ending C1 -- IT WORKS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
It works well enough to keep. The tally sticks hang neatly where the tools should be, and the builders always know whose door to knock on. The storehouse roof is finished two days before the rains, and (name1) hangs a little tally stick of thanks on (leader name)'s door.
Ending C2 -- THE TALLY STICKS VANISH. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The tally sticks go missing faster than the tools ever did. Children use them as swords. A goat eats two. Within a week, nobody knows where any tool or any stick is, and the scheme is dropped. The builders go back to shouting "WHO HAS THE ADZE?" across the village, which at least is traditional.

NEW-114. The Council's Empty Seat   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (leader name) any villager 25+ (not the VV5 Chief role). (name1) the gardener: any villager 18+. (name2) the gardener's quiet nephew or niece: any villager 14 to 20.
EVENT TEXT
The gathering has been arguing for an hour about moving the fish drying racks. The new spot everyone likes best is a nice flat patch of ground... which happens to be (name1)'s garden.
(Name1) is not there. (He/She) is out fishing, blissfully unaware that half the village is deciding what to do with (his/her) taro.
The vote is about to happen when someone finally points at the empty mat where (name1) usually sits and says, "Er. Shouldn't we wait?"
There is a very long, very awkward silence. What should (leader name) do?
Choice A: Fetch the Gardener from the Beach
Choice B: Pace Out the Ground
Choice C: Tell the Gardener First

CHOICE A: FETCH THE GARDENER FROM THE BEACH
First popup: A runner sprints down to the beach. Some time later, (name1) is hauled into the gathering still dripping, still holding a fish, and extremely confused. "What about my garden?!"...
Ending A1 -- THREE HOUSEHOLDS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Once (he/she) understands, (name1) explains that the plot doesn't just feed (his/her) family: it feeds three households, including two elders who can't farm anymore. The gathering listens, and nobody looks at the flat patch of ground the same way again. The racks stay where they are. (Name1) sits down on (his/her) mat, still holding the fish, and refuses to leave until the meeting ends.
Ending A2 -- THE CLEARING BEHIND. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Before (name1) can finish catching (his/her) breath, (name2) speaks at a gathering for the first time. (His/Her) voice shakes. There's an unused clearing just behind the current racks, (he/she) says, if somebody would only cut back the vines. The whole discussion turns. The racks move there instead, and (name1) gives (name2) the fish.

CHOICE B: PACE OUT THE GROUND
First popup: (Leader name) decides that before anyone votes on anything, they should actually go and look. The whole gathering troops out to the garden in the late afternoon sun...
Ending B1 -- THE SUNNY SLOPE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
Pacing the ground, they notice that the flat patch is shaded by palms half the day, which is terrible for drying fish. The slope just above the garden, though, catches sun from dawn to dusk. That practical detail settles the matter: the racks go on the slope, the garden stays a garden, and the fish dry faster than they ever have. The drying team works out a better way to angle the racks to the sun as well.
Ending B2 -- THE HEALTHY TARO. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Someone at the gathering claimed (name1) had let the plot go to weeds. Standing in it, everyone can see the taro is the healthiest on the island, tall and glossy and neatly weeded. The claim is dropped, very quickly, and the person who made it suddenly remembers urgent business elsewhere.

CHOICE C: TELL THE GARDENER FIRST
First popup: (Leader name) calls off the vote and walks down to the beach alone, sits on the sand beside (name1), and explains what was being decided, before anyone else does...
Ending C1 -- UNDERSTOOD. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name1) does not love it. (He/She) says so, at length, while gutting a fish with unnecessary force. But (he/she) understands why the racks need a new home, and (he/she) is grateful to hear it first, face to face, instead of from gossip. They agree to move only one corner of the garden, and (name1) chooses which.
Ending C2 -- TOO HASTY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Halfway through explaining, (leader name) hears how it sounds and stops. "No. We were wrong to decide this without you. I'm sorry." (He/She) promises to bring the whole matter back to the gathering with (name1) present. (Name1) blinks, surprised, and offers (leader name) half of today's catch.

MIXER SEED NEW-114
Premise: The gathering is about to vote on moving the fish drying racks onto a nice flat patch of ground, which happens to be (name1)'s garden, and (name1) is out fishing, blissfully unaware.
Roles: leader: any villager 25+ (not the VV5 Chief role) | gardener: 18+ | quiet nephew or niece: 14 to 20

NEW-115. The Water Jar Rule   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (leader name) any villager 25+ (not the VV5 Chief role). (name1) a caregiver: any villager 18+ (prefer a parent or a healer). (elder name) any elder.
EVENT TEXT
The new rule seemed so sensible: water jars may only be filled at the morning spring call, all together, so the spring doesn't get churned into mud by people wandering down all day.
It was sensible, right up until noon.
That was when the parents with babies, and the villagers nursing the sick, found themselves standing in their huts with empty jars, a crying baby or a feverish patient, and a long wait until tomorrow morning. (Name1) has just marched into the middle of the village with an empty jar under each arm and an expression that could curdle milk. How should (leader name) answer?
Choice A: Listen to the Caregivers
Choice B: Watch the Spring for a Day
Choice C: Allow Caregivers a Midday Fill

CHOICE A: LISTEN TO THE CAREGIVERS
First popup: (Leader name) takes one look at (name1)'s face and calls a gathering right then and there, before lunch...
Ending A1 -- ALL DAY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name1) explains that the sick need fresh water all day long, for drinking, for washing, for cooling fevers, not just at dawn. The gathering listens. Several people who voted for the rule look at their feet. By evening the rule has a sensible exception for anyone caring for the sick or the very young.
Ending A2 -- THE SECOND SPRING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
In the middle of it, (elder name), who rarely speaks at gatherings, clears (his/her) throat. "When I was young there was a second, smaller spring behind the rocks. Nobody's used it in years." The discussion changes course entirely. By sunset, a group has cleared the old spring, and the caregivers have water of their own.

CHOICE B: WATCH THE SPRING FOR A DAY
First popup: (Leader name) sits beside the spring from dawn to dusk with (name1), watching every single villager who comes to fill a jar...
Ending B1 -- THE FLAT ROCK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
By evening, they have seen the problem: the spring only muddies when people wade into the shallows to fill their jars. When they fill from the big flat rock at the edge, the water stays clear. That practical detail reshapes the whole rule. Now anyone can fill a jar at any time, as long as they use the flat rock, and the village builds a second flat stone step so there's never a queue.
Ending B2 -- THE HILL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Nobody muddies the spring all day. Then, late in the afternoon, a light rain starts, and they watch muddy water come trickling straight down the hill and into the spring. Nobody was breaking the rule on purpose; the mud came from the rain all along. Nobody is scolded, and the rule is quietly dropped.

CHOICE C: ALLOW CAREGIVERS A MIDDAY FILL
First popup: (Leader name) announces a compromise: caregivers may make one extra fill at midday...
Ending C1 -- IT HOLDS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
It works well enough to keep. The midday fill is quiet and quick, the spring stays clear, and (name1) stops looking as if (he/she) wants to curdle anything. (Leader name) promises to change it again if it stops working.
Ending C2 -- THE MIDDAY CROWD. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Somehow, by the third day, the "caregivers' midday fill" draws a crowd of nearly everyone in the village, each with a very creative reason for being a caregiver. ("I'm caring for my thirst!") There is a squabble at the spring, a jar is broken, and the rule is withdrawn.

MIXER SEED NEW-115

NEW-116. The Refused Duty   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (leader name) any villager 25+ (not the VV5 Chief role). (name1) the worker who refused: any villager 18+. (name2) a friend of (name1): any villager 14+. (name3) a strong climber: any villager 18+.
EVENT TEXT
(Name1) was asked to climb the cliff behind the village and cut fresh vines for rope. It is a long, hard climb, but someone has to do it, and it was (his/her) turn.
(Name1) said no. Just "no", flatly, and walked away.
By evening, the word "lazy" is drifting around the cooking fires, getting a little louder every time it passes from one fire to the next. (Name1) is sitting alone on the edge of the village with (his/her) jaw set, not eating, not looking at anyone. What should (leader name) do?
Choice A: Hear Why They Refused
Choice B: Inspect the Cliff Face
Choice C: Pair Them with a Climber

CHOICE A: HEAR WHY THEY REFUSED
First popup: (Leader name) brings two bowls of stew and sits down beside (name1) without a word. After a while, (name1) starts eating. After a longer while, (he/she) starts talking...
Ending A1 -- THE OLD SHOULDER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name1) explains that an old shoulder injury gives out without warning on hard climbs. If it went halfway up that cliff, (he/she) would fall, and (his/her) family would be left without help for a season, or forever. (He/She) was too proud to say it in front of everyone. When (leader name) repeats it at the fire, the word "lazy" stops going around very quickly.
Ending A2 -- THE ROCKFALL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Before (name1) can answer, (name2) hurries over. "Did you tell them about the rockfall?" Last week, the two of them watched a slab of that cliff break loose and smash onto the path below. (Name1) didn't want to frighten anyone. Suddenly the talk at the fires is about the cliff, not about (name1), and nobody else wants to climb it either.

CHOICE B: INSPECT THE CLIFF FACE
First popup: At first light, (leader name) and a few climbers walk to the foot of the cliff to see what (name1) was so afraid of...
Ending B1 -- VINES AT THE BASE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
Poking around the shady base of the cliff, the climbers find thick, strong vines growing in the damp, every bit as good for rope as the ones at the top, and much easier to reach. The risky climb is no longer necessary at all. The rope makers learn which shady spots grow the best vines and save themselves a great deal of climbing from then on.
Ending B2 -- CRUMBLING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The cliff is crumbling exactly as (name1) feared: loose stones, fresh cracks, a rock that wobbles when a climber touches it. Laziness was never the issue. Nobody is punished, and the cliff is marked as off-limits with a row of white stones.

CHOICE C: PAIR THEM WITH A CLIMBER
First popup: (Leader name) suggests a compromise: (name3) climbs, while (name1) holds the ropes at the bottom and hauls the vines down...
Ending C1 -- A GOOD TEAM. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
It works well enough to keep trying. (Name3) climbs fast and light, (name1) is strong and steady on the ground, and by midday they have more vines than anyone has ever brought back in one trip. They start doing the job together every season.
Ending C2 -- TANGLED. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The pairing slows everyone down. (Name3) shouts instructions that (name1) can't hear, (name1) pulls when (he/she) should let go, and by noon three ropes are so tangled together that they have to be cut apart. Nobody is hurt, but the plan is dropped, and they go home with fewer vines than they started with.

NEW-117. The Storehouse Key   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (leader name) any villager 25+ (not the VV5 Chief role). (name1) the storehouse keeper: any villager 25+. (name2) the young storehouse sweeper: any villager 10 to 17.
EVENT TEXT
The storehouse "key" is a carved wooden peg that holds the door bar shut. It hangs on a cord around the neck of (name1), the storehouse keeper, and in all the years (he/she) has kept it, (he/she) has never once refused to open the door.
Until today. The feast is tonight. The feast cooks are lined up outside the storehouse with empty baskets and growing impatience. And (name1) is standing in front of the door with (his/her) hand closed tight around the peg, refusing to hand it over, and refusing to say why.
Somebody's stomach growls loudly. Nobody laughs. How should (leader name) handle this?
Choice A: Ask the Keeper Privately
Choice B: Count Every Basket
Choice C: Release One Basket at a Time

CHOICE A: ASK THE KEEPER PRIVATELY
First popup: (Leader name) sends the cooks off to "check the fire" and takes (name1) behind the storehouse, where no one can hear...
Ending A1 -- LOWER THAN ANYONE KNOWS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Away from the crowd, (name1)'s shoulders slump. The stores are much lower than anyone realizes. A big feast tonight could leave the village short before the next harvest. (He/She) didn't want to be the one to ruin the celebration. (Leader name) thanks (him/her), and the feast goes ahead, smaller, with fish from the morning's catch instead of the stores.
Ending A2 -- THE RATS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Before (name1) can say anything, (name2), the young helper who sweeps out the storehouse, peeks around the corner. "Is this about the rats?" Rats got into the yams last week, and (name1) didn't want to start a panic before (he/she) had dealt with them. Now everyone knows. Within an hour, the village's best trap-setters are at work, and the feast goes ahead.

CHOICE B: COUNT EVERY BASKET
First popup: (Leader name) suggests that everyone go in together, the keeper included, and count every basket in the storehouse, out loud...
Ending B1 -- OLDEST FIRST. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
Counting the baskets together, they find that the newest food has been stacked at the front and the oldest pushed to the back, where some of it is starting to go soft. They work out a better way to stack them, so the oldest food is always eaten first. It is a practical improvement that saves a great deal of spoiled food in the seasons to come, and (name1) finally hands over the peg, smiling for the first time all day.
Ending B2 -- THE COUNT MATCHES. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The count matches (name1)'s tally exactly, down to the last coconut. Nobody has been sneaking food, and no one is punished. It turns out (name1) simply forgot to tell the cooks that half the feast food was already set aside in a different hut. There is a lot of embarrassed laughter, and the cooks fill their baskets.

CHOICE C: RELEASE ONE BASKET AT A TIME
First popup: (Leader name) proposes that (name1) open the door, but let out only one basket at a time, and only when the cooks bring the last one back empty...
Ending C1 -- IT WORKS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
It works well enough for the feast. Nothing is wasted, (name1) can see exactly what is being used, and the cooks discover they needed far less than they thought. Everyone eats well, and there is still plenty in the storehouse in the morning.
Ending C2 -- THE GRUMBLING LINE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The one-basket rule turns the feast into a slow, shuffling line of grumbling cooks, each waiting for the last one to finish. The fish is cold before the yams are hot. By the time dinner is served, the moon is high. The rule is dropped the next day, to loud cheers.

NEW-118. The Stranger's Complaint   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (leader name) any villager 25+ (not the VV5 Chief role). (name1) a villager who once travelled with traders: any villager 25+. The trader is a visitor and not a villager (sex picked at random).
EVENT TEXT
A visiting trader has paddled in with a canoe full of shells, dyes and carved combs. The children are thrilled. The trader is not.
"I mean no offence," the trader says, very politely, to (leader name), "but your rule, that outsiders may only trade on the beach and never among the huts, treats people like me unfairly." The trader has been polite about it all morning. But the trader has also started packing up, early, and the beautiful dyes are going back into their pots.
The village's dyers look stricken. How should (leader name) respond?
Choice A: Hear the Trader Out
Choice B: Study the Tide Marks
Choice C: Open the Edge Huts to Trade

CHOICE A: HEAR THE TRADER OUT
First popup: (Leader name) asks the trader to sit, offers a cup of coconut water, and listens...
Ending A1 -- LOST TWICE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The trader explains that the beach floods at high tide. Twice now, the trader has lost a whole pot of costly dye to a sudden wave, and that is a season's work gone. The gathering listens, and several people who thought the trader was just being difficult go quiet. The trader stays one more day, trading from a dry spot above the high-tide line that the villagers clear especially.
Ending A2 -- HOW OTHERS DO IT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name1), who travelled with traders when (he/she) was young, speaks up about how other villages handle it: a special hut for visitors' goods, right at the edge of the village, with a roof and a door. The talk takes a whole new direction. The trader unpacks the dyes again and stays to hear the end of the discussion.

CHOICE B: STUDY THE TIDE MARKS
First popup: (Leader name) walks the beach with the trader, looking at the old lines of seaweed and shell left behind by high tides...
Ending B1 -- THE NEW MOON. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
The tide marks show that the beach floods badly mostly around the new moon, and hardly at all in between. That useful detail lets the village set proper trading days, when the beach will be safe, and the fishers start using the same knowledge to plan when to pull canoes higher. The trader promises to come back on the right days.
Ending B2 -- CRAB TRACKS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The trader confides a suspicion: someone in the village kicked over a pot of dye yesterday. But the tracks around the spilled dye are crab tracks, hundreds of tiny ones, and a very blue crab is hiding under the next rock. No one is blamed. The trader laughs until the tears come, and has to sit down.

CHOICE C: OPEN THE EDGE HUTS TO TRADE
First popup: (Leader name) agrees to try letting traders set up beside the first row of huts, just for this visit...
Ending C1 -- IT WORKS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
It works well enough to keep, with room for changes. The dyes stay dry, the villagers can browse in the shade, and the trader sells out by evening. "I'll be back," the trader promises, "and I'll tell the others."
Ending C2 -- THE CROWDED PATH. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The stalls crowd the path, children run between them shrieking, and the families who live in the edge huts can't get out of their own doors without buying a comb. By midday they have had enough, and the trial ends. The trader goes back to the beach, a little less annoyed than before, since at least the village tried.

Nothing ever arrived.
Today, the family's eldest walked all the way in, through the swamp, on bad feet, to ask why. (He/She) is standing at the edge of the village now, mud to the knees, leaning on a stick, not angry exactly, just tired. Very, very tired.
(Leader name) feels (his/her) face go hot. What should (he/she) do?

Choice B: Retrace the Delivery Route
Choice C: Send Half Now and Half Later

WHO: (leader name) any villager 25+ (not the VV5 Chief role). (name1) a fisher: any villager 18+. (name2) the cook's young helper: any villager 10 to 17. (elder name) the elder who slept through it: any elder.
EVENT TEXT
Should the village build a new fishing canoe, or a second cooking hut?
The argument has gone on all evening. The fishers have made speeches. The cooks have made speeches. One fisher made a speech so long that a cook fell asleep in the middle of it and had to be poked.
Finally, the hands go up. (Leader name) counts. Then counts again.
Exactly half and half.
The only villager who has not voted is (elder name), who slept peacefully through the entire evening and is still snoring gently by the fire, with a small lizard sitting on (his/her) knee. How should (leader name) break the tie?

Choice B: Tally the Logs and Thatch
Choice C: Wake the Elder and Explain

CHOICE A: ASK WHO EACH CHOICE HELPS

(Name1) explains simply that the old canoe leaks so badly now that every trip past the reef is a risk. Last week (he/she) bailed water the whole way home, and one big wave could have sunk it. The gathering listens. The cooks look at each other. A second vote is taken, and this time the canoe wins easily.
Ending A2 -- THE ROOF. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name2), the cook's young helper, who has never said a word at a gathering, stands up and points out that the old cooking hut's roof is about to fall in anyway. "I can see the stars through it. Ending C2 -- NOT LIKE THIS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Elder name) listens, then waves the whole thing away. "You're not going to let one old person who was asleep decide this. Vote again tomorrow when you've all slept as well as I have." (Leader name) admits declaring a winner tonight would have been too quick, and the gathering agrees to vote again next evening.

(He/She) beams at being taken seriously by a grown-up, and for the rest of the day follows (adult name) around explaining the faces to anyone who will stand still.

Ending B2 -- ALONE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

So (adult name) sits close by and pretends to be very busy whittling a stick, while sneaking glances at the board. Ending C2 -- THE BIRD. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

WHO: (Name) a child: any villager 4 to 13. (adult name) a fisher: any villager 18+.

Choice B: Show How to Hold It Gently

The other children gasp. Someone drops a shell. Everyone turns to see what the teacher will do.
(Teacher name), to (his/her) credit, slowly puts down the pointing stick. How should (teacher name) respond?
Choice A: Let the Pupil Explain
Choice B: Check the Tide Together
Choice C: Let the Shore Settle It

(Teacher name) listens without interrupting. When (name) finishes, (teacher name) thanks (him/her) in front of everyone. (Name) goes pink to the ears, but sits up a little straighter for the rest of the day.
Ending A2 -- TOMORROW. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

(Name) explains it proudly to the adults, and the fishers, who had always just "felt" the tide, start using the marks to plan their trips. Ending C2 -- THE STORM. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

NEW-125. The Broken Toy Boat   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) a child: any villager 3 to 13. (adult name) a builder: any villager 18+.
EVENT TEXT
Little (name)'s favourite toy canoe was carved by (his/her) grandparent, and it has sailed in every puddle on the island. It has a name. It has a tiny sail made from a leaf. It has survived storms, younger siblings and one very curious pig.
This morning, out on the lagoon, it sank.
It had to be fished out with a long stick, and now (name) is holding it in both hands, looking at the crack running right down the hull, and trying very, very hard not to cry. (He/She) is not managing it very well. How can (adult name) help?
Choice A: Let the Child Talk About the Boat
Choice B: Mend It Side by Side
Choice C: Let the Child Test the Patches

CHOICE A: LET THE CHILD TALK ABOUT THE BOAT

Ending A1 -- A GIFT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Between sniffles, (name) explains everything: the boat is called Swift, (his/her) grandparent carved it for (his/her) fourth birthday, and it is the fastest boat on the whole island, probably the whole world. (He/She) feels better just for being taken seriously. By the end, (he/she) is smiling, and (adult name) has promised to help fix Swift tomorrow.
Ending A2 -- A SHIPWRECK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

(He/She) buries it ceremonially in the sand with a shell on top and starts telling the other children about the great storm that sank it. Ending B2 -- I'LL FIX IT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

It takes a long time and a lot of sap. The patch is enormous and lumpy. (Name) thinks it is the most beautiful patch ever made.

CHOICE C: LET THE CHILD TEST THE PATCHES

(Name) tests every mixture with great seriousness, and discovers that sap mixed with ash holds best by far. The other patches leak or crumble, but the ash one stays hard and watertight. (He/She) proudly explains it to the adults, who try it on a real canoe with a leaky seam, and it works. Soon every canoe in the village is patched with "(name)'s mix."
Ending C2 -- SUNK AGAIN. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
None of the patches hold. Swift goes into the lagoon, fills up and sinks again, with a sad little glug. (Name) fishes it out, frowns at it, and says, "Okay. Tomorrow I'm trying sap and mud. And maybe banana." (Adult name) is quietly very impressed.

NEW-126. The Child Who Feared Thunder   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) a child: any villager 3 to 13. (adult name) any villager 18+ sleeping in the same hut or nearby.
EVENT TEXT
A huge storm rolls over the island in the middle of the night. Rain hammers the thatch. The wind howls through the palms.
And every time the thunder crashes, little (name) jumps.
(He/She) refuses to lie down. (He/She) is sitting bolt upright on (his/her) mat with a blanket over (his/her) head, flinching at every boom, making small noises. Nobody else in the hut is getting any sleep either. (Adult name) rolls over for the fourth time, sighs, and sits up.
CRASH. "Eep." How can (adult name) help (name) feel safe?
Choice A: Ask What Scares Them
Choice B: Count the Thunder Together
Choice C: Let the Child Watch from the Doorway

CHOICE A: ASK WHAT SCARES THEM
First popup: (Adult name) shuffles over and sits beside the blanket-shaped lump. "Hey. What's the matter?" A small voice comes out from under the blanket...
Ending A1 -- THE ANGRY MOUNTAIN. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
"The thunder sounds like the mountain is angry," (name) whispers. "What if it's angry at us?" (Adult name) does not laugh. (He/She) explains that the mountain is very old and very big, and probably doesn't even know their little hut is there. (Name) is comforted just to be taken seriously, and falls asleep leaning against (adult name)'s arm, which (adult name) then cannot move for the rest of the night.
Ending A2 -- THE DRIP. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name) starts to explain about the thunder, then stops. "Actually... it's the drip." It turns out the real problem is a leak in the roof, dripping steadily onto the end of (his/her) mat, plip, plip, plip, which is somehow much more frightening in the dark than the thunder. Someone fetches a bowl to catch the drip. (Name) is asleep within minutes.

CHOICE B: COUNT THE THUNDER TOGETHER
First popup: (Adult name) lifts a corner of the blanket. "Want to know a secret? You can tell how far away a storm is. Watch for the next flash..."
Ending B1 -- HOW FAR. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Research (a little, +5) for (name)
At the next flash, they count together, slowly: one... two... three... four... five... BOOM. "Five. That means it's far away, out over the sea." They count every flash, and (name) learns a little about how light is faster than sound and how to tell the storm's distance. By the end, (he/she) is more interested than scared, and keeps poking (adult name) awake to count.
Ending B2 -- I'LL COUNT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
After two flashes, (name) whispers that (he/she) wants to keep counting on (his/her) own. So (adult name) sits nearby in the dark and listens to a small voice counting, very seriously, through the rest of the storm. Somewhere around "eleven," the voice turns into gentle snoring.

CHOICE C: LET THE CHILD WATCH FROM THE DOORWAY
First popup: (Adult name) wraps (name) in an extra blanket and sits with (him/her) in the doorway, where they can watch the storm out over the sea, safe and dry under the overhang...
Ending C1 -- IT'S LEAVING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
Watching the flashes over the water, (name) starts counting between flash and boom on (his/her) own, and notices the counts are getting longer and longer. "It's going away!" (he/she) announces proudly, and runs to tell the other adults it's leaving. In the morning, (he/she) tells the fishers too, and they start using the same trick to tell whether a storm is coming or going before they set out.
Ending C2 -- ASLEEP. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
They watch the lightning dance over the sea for a long time. It is actually quite beautiful. (Name) falls asleep before the storm passes, wrapped up tight in the doorway, and has to be carried back to (his/her) mat. In the morning, (he/she) asks if they can watch the next storm too.

NEW-127. The Two Best Friends   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (name1) and (name2) two children, any villagers 4 to 13. (adult name) any villager 18+.
EVENT TEXT
(Name1) and (name2) are best friends. They have been best friends since before they could walk. They do everything together.
Today they are building a bird feeder together, and it has become the most serious argument of their lives.
(Name1) insists the feeder must be ROUND, because birds are round and nests are round and the sun is round. (Name2) insists it must be SQUARE, because squares are stronger and also (name2) has already cut four straight sticks. Neither will give in. There has been stomping. There has been a declaration that they are "never speaking again," which lasted about as long as it took to say it.
(Adult name) finds them sitting back to back in the dirt, arms folded, surrounded by sticks. How can (adult name) get them talking again?
Choice A: Hear Each Friend Out
Choice B: Help Without Picking a Side
Choice C: Let the Birds Decide

CHOICE A: HEAR EACH FRIEND OUT
First popup: (Adult name) sits down between them. "All right. One at a time. Tell me about your feeder." (Name1) goes first, with diagrams drawn in the dirt...
Ending A1 -- BOTH HEARD. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Each child explains their design in enormous detail, with a great deal of pointing. (Adult name) listens to both, nodding, asking questions, and taking each one completely seriously. Somehow, by the end, the two of them feel properly heard, and are sitting side by side again, arguing more quietly about where the perch should go.
Ending A2 -- ROUND IS FINE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Halfway through (name2)'s explanation of why squares are better, (name2) stops, looks at (name1)'s drawing, and says, "Actually, round is nice." (Name1) is so surprised (he/she) says, "Actually, square is nice." They stare at each other, then burst out laughing. Nobody makes a fuss.

CHOICE B: HELP WITHOUT PICKING A SIDE
First popup: (Adult name) suggests they build both, a round one and a square one, and offers to help with the tricky parts...
Ending B1 -- HOW BIRDS LAND. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Research (a little, +5) for (name1)
While they build, (adult name) explains that birds need somewhere to land before they eat, and that their feet like to grip something thin, like a twig. (Name1) gets very excited about this and learns a little about how birds land, perch and feed. Both feeders end up with long, thin perches, and (name1) explains why to (name2) at length.
Ending B2 -- WE'LL DO IT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
After a few minutes, both children ask if they can finish it themselves now. Together. (Adult name) agrees and watches from the garden wall as they work it out between them. The finished feeder is round on one side and square on the other. It is the strangest feeder anyone has ever seen.

CHOICE C: LET THE BIRDS DECIDE
First popup: (Adult name) suggests a test. Build both, hang them side by side in the same tree, and see which one the birds choose. The two friends shake on it, very solemnly...
Ending C1 -- THE PERCH WINS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
For three days they watch, and the result is clear: the birds always go to the one with a perch, whichever shape it is, and ignore the one without. The two friends proudly explain their discovery to the adults, who are interested enough to put perches on the bird-scarers in the fields, so the birds land there instead of on the crops.
Ending C2 -- NO BIRDS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
No birds come to either feeder. Not one. Not round, not square. The two friends sit under the tree in silent disappointment. Then (name2) says, "Want to try again tomorrow?" and (name1) says, "Together?" and that seems to settle everything that mattered.

NEW-129. The Very Serious Play   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) a child: any villager 4 to 13 (the game's inventor). (referee name) the referee: any villager 4 to 7. (adult name) any villager 18+.
EVENT TEXT
The children have invented a game. It involves sticks, a coconut, three circles drawn in the sand, a lot of running, a lot of shouting, and rules so complicated that two adults tried to learn it this morning and gave up.
There is a referee. The referee is (referee name). The referee is very small.
(Name), who invented the game, is currently arguing with the referee about whether the coconut was "in the moon circle" or "in the sun circle", and the whole game has come to a halt while the players wait for a ruling. (Adult name) wanders past, curious, and makes the mistake of asking, "So how does this work?"
Every child turns to look at (adult name). How should (adult name) help?
Choice A: Ask for the Rules
Choice B: Keep Score for Them
Choice C: Let Them Fix Their Own Rules

CHOICE A: ASK FOR THE RULES
First popup: (Name) draws (himself/herself) up to (his/her) full height and begins to explain the rules...
Ending A1 -- ENORMOUS DIGNITY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name) explains the rules with enormous dignity and at great length. There are seventeen of them. Rule nine is "no biting." Rule fourteen is "the coconut is always right." (Adult name) understands almost none of it, but listens carefully all the way through, and (name) is thrilled to be taken seriously. (Adult name) is then forced to play. (He/She) loses, badly.
Ending A2 -- NEW RULES. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Halfway through explaining, (name) realizes that the rules (he/she) just described would mean (he/she) loses, so (he/she) changes them. Then changes them again. Nobody minds, least of all the players, who are already running around again. (Referee name) blows a whistle made of a leaf, for no clear reason.

CHOICE B: KEEP SCORE FOR THEM
First popup: (Adult name) offers to keep score, since there seems to be a lot of arguing about it. (Name) considers this offer very seriously...
Ending B1 -- KNOTS ON A CORD. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Research (a little, +5) for (name)
(Adult name) shows (name) how to keep score with knots tied on a cord: one knot for a point, a big knot for every five. (Name) takes over the cord almost at once and keeps score for the rest of the afternoon, learning a little about tallying and becoming very bossy about it. There are no more arguments about the score. There are a lot of arguments about everything else.
Ending B2 -- I'LL DO IT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name) decides that (he/she) will keep score alone, thank you, since it's (his/her) game. So (adult name) just watches from the sidelines, cheering for whichever side seems to be losing. At the end, (name) declares that both teams won, which everyone agrees is fair.

CHOICE C: LET THEM FIX THEIR OWN RULES
First popup: (Adult name) suggests that if the game keeps stopping for arguments, maybe the players should sit down together and fix the rules themselves...
Ending C1 -- EVEN TEAMS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
The children sit in a circle and argue for a long time, and eventually work out that the game only feels fair when the teams are even and everyone gets the same number of turns. They proudly explain this to the adults, who are a little sheepish to realize the same idea would settle some of their own arguments about sharing work. Soon the adults are using "even teams, same turns" for the fishing rota.
Ending C2 -- HAPPY CHAOS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The rules meeting collapses into happy chaos within a minute. Someone starts chasing someone else, the coconut rolls into the sea, and the referee falls asleep. The children all vow to fix the rules properly tomorrow. They will not.

NEW-130. The Young Helper   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) a child: any villager 4 to 13. (adult name) a builder: any villager 18+.
EVENT TEXT
The builders are working on a new hut, and little (name) has decided to help.
Specifically, (he/she) has decided to carry a log. One of the big logs. A log about three times (his/her) own size.

The builders have stopped working to watch. So far (name) has moved the log about the length of (his/her) own foot. It has taken all morning. How can (adult name) help without hurting (his/her) pride?

Choice B: Lift the Other End
Choice C: Let the Child Try Rollers

CHOICE A: ASK WHY IT MATTERS TO THEM

Ending A1 -- USEFUL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name) explains, between gasps, that (he/she) wants to be useful like the builders. Everybody's always too busy to let (him/her) help with anything real. (Adult name) takes this completely seriously, and talks with (name) about which jobs are real builder jobs. (Name) ends the day carrying bindings and fetching water, feeling very much part of the crew.
Ending A2 -- THE THATCH. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name) starts to explain, looks at the log, looks at the enormous pile of thatch bundles waiting by the hut, and changes (his/her) mind. "Actually, can I carry THOSE?" (He/She) can, and they're exactly what the builders need. (Name) carries bundles of thatch for the rest of the afternoon, and is far more help than the log ever was.

CHOICE B: LIFT THE OTHER END

Ending B1 -- THE ROLLER LOG. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Research (a little, +5) for (name)
As they carry it together, (adult name) shows (name) a builder's trick: lay a smaller round log underneath, and push, and the big log rolls along on top almost by itself. (Name) is astonished. (He/She) learns a little about using a roller to move heavy things, and spends the rest of the day rolling everything (he/she) can find.
Ending B2 -- ALONE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
After a few steps, (name) asks (adult name) to please put it down, because (he/she) wants to finish alone. (Adult name) does, and hovers close by, just in case. The log reaches the hut at sunset. Every builder cheers. (Name) collapses on the grass and sleeps right there.

CHOICE C: LET THE CHILD TRY ROLLERS
First popup: (Adult name) doesn't help. Instead, (he/she) leaves a row of short, round sticks lying on the ground near the log, and walks away whistling...
Ending C1 -- THE DISCOVERY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
(Name) sits down to rest, looks at the sticks, looks at the log, and frowns. Then (he/she) lays the sticks out in a row, heaves the end of the log onto them, and pushes. It rolls! (He/She) proudly runs to show the builders, who've been carrying their logs the hard way for this hut, and they use the trick for all the rest of it. It is "(name)'s trick" forever after.
Ending C2 -- NOT TODAY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name) tries the sticks, but they all roll out sideways, and the log won't budge an inch more. At last (he/she) gives up, flops down on the log, and declares, "I'm going to move it tomorrow." (He/She) says it with such confidence that the builders decide to leave the log exactly where it is.

"Somebody will eat from it," (name) says firmly, to nobody in particular, and reaches for the digging stick.
(His/Her) family exchange worried glances. (Young name) opens (his/her) mouth to say something, and then isn't sure what. Should (young name) let (name) plant it (his/her) own way, ask (him/her) to teach the old planting lore, or find a way to make the digging easier on (his/her) back?

Choice C: Bring a Stool to the Garden

NEW-132. The Forgotten Path   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) any elder. (young name) a younger villager 14 to 25.
EVENT TEXT
(Name) insists that there is a shortcut through the bamboo to the far beach. A good one. A path (he/she) ran along every day as a child, barefoot, racing (his/her) friends.
None of the younger villagers have ever seen it. They have looked. There is only bamboo, very dense, very tall bamboo, and a lot of spiders.
"It's THERE," (name) says. "You're just not looking properly." (He/She) is getting that stubborn look, the one (his/her) family know well, the one that usually ends with (name) marching off somewhere alone and everyone else chasing after (him/her). Should (young name) let (name) lead the way, ask (him/her) how to find an old path, or start clearing the bamboo for (him/her)?

Choice B: Map the Old Way
Choice C: Clear the Bamboo Ahead of Them

Ending A1 -- ON (HIS/HER) OWN TERMS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name) chooses to walk the path (himself/herself), slowly, on (his/her) own terms, poking the bamboo aside with a stick. (Young name) follows at a respectful distance. It takes all afternoon. Ending A2 -- A STRONG ARM. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

(Name) teaches (young name) how to find old paths by the lean of trees, which bend away from where people have walked for years, and by little stacks of stones the old walkers left at every turn. Ending B2 -- THE BEND. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

CHOICE C: CLEAR THE BAMBOO AHEAD OF THEM

NEW-133. The Old Fisher's Hands   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) an old fisher: any elder. (young name) a younger villager 14 to 25.
EVENT TEXT
(Name) tied half the nets on this island. (His/Her) knots are famous. Young fishers used to watch (his/her) fingers fly and try to copy them, and fail.

WHO: (Name) any elder. (young name) a younger villager 14 to 25.
EVENT TEXT
(Young name) has always wondered about the long, pale scar on (name)'s forearm. It runs from wrist almost to elbow, crooked, like a river on a map.
Tonight, by the fire, (he/she) finally asks.
Usually (name) changes the subject. Usually (he/she) makes a joke about wrestling a shark, or says "Oh, that old thing," and starts talking about the weather.

NEW-141. The Trader with No Goods   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) the villager who finds the trader: any villager 14+. The trader is a visitor (sex at random) who may become a new adult villager. (In New Believers a visitor who stays joins as a believer.)
EVENT TEXT
A canoe limps onto the beach at dawn, low in the water, its hull cracked along one side and stuffed with moss to slow the leak. The trader paddling it is soaked, sunburned and looks as if (he/she) has not slept in days.
Two nights ago, a storm caught (him/her) far out at sea. Wave after wave broke over the canoe, and one by one, the cargo went over the side: the shells, the carved bowls, the good rope, everything.
All that is left is one sack of dried fish and a single bolt of dyed cloth, so soggy it drips. The trader holds the cloth up for (name) to see, and gives a helpless, exhausted laugh. "I don't suppose," (he/she) says, "you'd like to buy a very wet blanket?" The trader has lost almost everything. How should (name) respond?
Choice A: Offer Them a Hot Meal
Choice B: Ask What the Storm Was Like
Choice C: Offer Them a Place Here
Choice D: Trade Field Work for Repairs

CHOICE A: OFFER THEM A HOT MEAL
First popup: (Name) helps the trader haul the canoe up the sand and leads (him/her) straight to the cooking fire...
Ending A1 -- HALF A DAY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The trader is given a bowl of hot stew and a dry mat in the shade, and falls asleep before (he/she) finishes the stew. (He/She) sleeps for half a day, through the noise of the whole village, with the bowl still in (his/her) lap. When (he/she) wakes, the first thing (he/she) asks is whether there's more stew. There is.
Ending A2 -- THE LAST SACK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (small)
The trader eats, then insists, absolutely insists, on sharing (his/her) last sack of dried fish with the village. "You fed me. I'm not taking it back out to sea." No amount of arguing will change (his/her) mind, and the sack goes into the storehouse. The stores gain a little food, and the village gains a story about the stubbornest guest it ever had.

CHOICE B: ASK WHAT THE STORM WAS LIKE
First popup: Once the trader has dried off, the fishers gather around, eager to hear about the storm...
Ending B1 -- READING THE SWELL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
The trader explains how (he/she) read the swell before the storm hit: the long, slow waves that come before the wind, and the way the birds stopped flying. And how (he/she) lashed the cargo so it wouldn't shift. "Not well enough," (he/she) admits ruefully. The fishers learn something genuinely useful, and start watching for the long waves before every trip.
Ending B2 -- NOT THAT NIGHT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The trader starts to talk about the storm, then goes quiet when (he/she) gets to the night the cargo went over the side. (He/She) stares into the fire for a long time. "Another day," (he/she) says at last. No one presses. Someone hands (him/her) more stew instead.

CHOICE C: OFFER THEM A PLACE HERE
First popup: (Name) asks, gently, whether the trader has anything to go back to. The trader looks down at (his/her) cracked canoe, and the dripping cloth...
Ending C1 -- STAYING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: new villager (adult): the trader
With nothing left to go back to, the trader decides to join the village for good. "I always did want to stay somewhere long enough for my clothes to dry." (He/She) moves in as a new adult villager, and the dripping cloth, once it finally dries, becomes the brightest curtain in the village.
Ending C2 -- REBUILDING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The trader thanks everyone warmly, but shakes (his/her) head. (He/She) wants to rebuild (his/her) trade, and that means going back out on the water. Once the canoe is sound, (he/she) paddles away, promising to bring the village the first and best of (his/her) new cargo. Everyone waves from the beach.

CHOICE D: TRADE FIELD WORK FOR REPAIRS
First popup: (Name) suggests a fair trade: the village will mend the canoe, and while it dries, the trader can help out in the fields...
Ending D1 -- THE TARO HARVEST. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (normal)
While the canoe's new patches dry in the sun, the trader throws (himself/herself) into the taro harvest, working from dawn to dusk and singing sea songs the whole time. The harvest comes in faster than anyone expected, adding a good load of food to the stores. The trader leaves with a mended canoe and the fields' thanks.
Ending D2 -- PATCHED AND WAVED OFF. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The villagers patch the trader's cracked hull with sap and fibre, and the trader turns out to be hopeless at farming, pulling up three taro plants by mistake. Nobody minds. They wave (him/her) off from the beach the next morning, canoe sound and spirits high.

CHOICE D: PUT THE SAILOR IN THE FIELDS

NEW-143. The Letter Across the Sea   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) the villager the letter is for: any villager 18+ (the letter is from a relative or old friend who sailed away years ago; flavour only). The courier is a visitor (sex at random) who may become a new adult villager.
EVENT TEXT
A passing boat drops off a courier, and the courier brings a roll of bark tied with braided hair.
It's a letter. For (name). From someone who sailed away from the island years ago, someone (name) had given up on ever hearing from again. (Name) holds it in shaking hands and hasn't opened it yet.
The courier who carried it all this way, from boat to boat, is still standing on the beach. (He/She) is salt-stiff, sunburned and very hopeful, mostly about the smell of dinner drifting down from the cooking fire. (Name) is desperate to read the letter, but the courier looks like (he/she) hasn't eaten in days. What should (name) do first?
Choice A: Feed the Courier
Choice B: Ask How the Letter Travelled
Choice C: Ask Whether They Would Settle
Choice D: Trade a Reply for an Afternoon's Work

CHOICE A: FEED THE COURIER
First popup: Before (he/she) can even think about opening the letter, (name) takes the courier by the arm and leads (him/her) up to the fire...
Ending A1 -- A HAMMOCK IN THE SHADE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The courier is given a hot meal and a hammock in the shade, and is snoring within minutes. (Name) sits down nearby and finally unrolls the letter. Whatever it says, (he/she) reads it three times, and then sits for a long while looking out at the sea, smiling.
Ending A2 -- DRIED FRUIT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (small)
After eating, the courier insists on sharing some of the dried fruit (he/she) carries for long trips. "Payment for the best meal I've had in a moon." It adds a small amount of food to the stores, and the children immediately try to steal it.

CHOICE B: ASK HOW THE LETTER TRAVELLED
First popup: (Name) can't stop wondering how this little roll of bark crossed so much water. (He/She) asks the courier to explain...
Ending B1 -- BOAT TO BOAT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
The courier explains how letters are passed from boat to boat across the water, each crew carrying it a little way and handing it on, with knots in the braided hair to show how many hands it has passed through. This one has eleven knots. It's a useful trick for sending news, and the village starts thinking about who else they might write to.
Ending B2 -- FOR THE LETTER TO TELL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name) asks whether the courier knows anything about the writer's life now. The courier shakes (his/her) head firmly. "That's for the letter to tell, not me." No one insists. (Name) finally unrolls it, and goes very quiet for a long time.

CHOICE C: ASK WHETHER THEY WOULD SETTLE
First popup: Over dinner, the courier mentions how tired (he/she) is of the sea. (Name) asks, half joking, whether (he/she) would ever settle down somewhere...
Ending C1 -- TIRED OF THE SEA. Chance 50%. EFFECT: new villager (adult): the courier
The courier doesn't laugh. Tired of the sea, and tired of sleeping on other people's boats, (he/she) decides to join the village permanently, and moves in as a new adult villager. "Somebody else can carry the letters for a while." (Name) is the first to help (him/her) find a sleeping mat.
Ending C2 -- MORE LETTERS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The courier smiles, but pats the bag at (his/her) side. It's full of letters, for people all over the sea. (He/She) thanks the village and sails on to the next landing in the morning, waving from the back of the next passing boat.

CHOICE D: TRADE A REPLY FOR AN AFTERNOON'S WORK
First popup: (Name) wants to send a reply. The courier agrees to carry it, and while (name) works on it, offers to help out around the village...
Ending D1 -- THE BREADFRUIT HARVEST. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (normal)
While (name) spends hours carving the perfect reply, the courier helps with the breadfruit harvest, climbing trees with alarming speed. It adds a good share of food to the stores. By evening, the reply is finished, and tucked safely into the courier's bag.
Ending D2 -- THE MENDED SATCHEL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The courier's satchel has a long tear along the bottom, and (he/she) has been losing letters through it for weeks without noticing. The villagers stitch it up with strong fibre and send (him/her) off with (name)'s reply tucked safely inside, along with a stern warning to check (his/her) bag more often.

MIXER SEED NEW-143
Premise: A courier brings a roll of bark tied with braided hair: a letter for a villager from someone who sailed away years ago. The courier is still standing on the beach, salt-stiff and very hopeful about dinner.
Roles: recipient: any villager 18+ | courier: a visitor who may become a new adult villager
Approaches: Feed the Courier | Ask How the Letter Travelled | Ask Whether They Would Settle | Trade a Reply for an Afternoon's Work
Outcome pool:
- The courier is snoring in a hammock within minutes, while the recipient reads the letter three times and looks out at the sea, smiling. [answers: Feed the Courier] [mood: warm] [EFFECT: none]
- "Payment for the best meal I've had in a moon." The courier shares their dried fruit, and the children immediately try to steal it. [answers: Feed the Courier] [mood: funny] [EFFECT: food gain (small)]
- Letters are passed boat to boat, with a knot in the braided hair for every hand. This one has eleven knots. [answers: Ask How the Letter Travelled] [mood: warm] [EFFECT: tech gain (small)]
- "That's for the letter to tell, not me." The recipient finally unrolls it, and goes very quiet for a long time. [answers: Ask How the Letter Travelled] [mood: sad] [EFFECT: none]
- Tired of the sea and of sleeping on other people's boats, the courier stays for good. "Somebody else can carry the letters for a while." [answers: Ask Whether They Would Settle] [mood: warm] [EFFECT: new villager (adult): the courier]
- The courier pats a bag full of letters for people all over the sea, and sails on in the morning. [answers: Ask Whether They Would Settle] [mood: warm] [EFFECT: none]
- While the reply is carved, the courier climbs the breadfruit trees with alarming speed. [answers: Trade a Reply for an Afternoon's Work] [mood: warm] [EFFECT: food gain (normal)]
- The villagers stitch up the courier's torn satchel, which has been losing letters for weeks, and add a stern warning to check it more often. [answers: Trade a Reply for an Afternoon's Work] [mood: funny] [EFFECT: none]
Flavour lines:
- Bark tied with braided hair.
- Salt-stiff and hopeful about the smell of dinner.
- Eleven knots, eleven hands.

NEW-144. The Farmhand from the West   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) a village farmer: any villager 18+ (prefer high Farming). The farmhand is a visitor from a western settlement (sex at random) who may become a new adult villager.
EVENT TEXT
A farmhand has come all the way from a settlement in the west to show the village their way of harvesting.
They dig taro with a curved stick instead of a straight one. And they always, always leave a piece of each plant in the ground, so it grows again. "Why dig a new hole," the farmhand says, "when the old one is already there?"
The village farmers are fascinated. They are also a little offended. (Name), who has been farming the same way for as long as (he/she) can remember, is standing with (his/her) arms folded, watching the curved stick with deep suspicion. Should (name) give these new ways a chance, or prove the village way is better?
Choice A: Welcome Them with Fresh Fruit
Choice B: Ask About Western Farming
Choice C: Offer a Plot of Their Own
Choice D: Harvest Side by Side

CHOICE A: WELCOME THEM WITH FRESH FRUIT
First popup: (Name) unfolds (his/her) arms with some effort, and offers the farmhand a ripe mango...
Ending A1 -- THE SHADIEST SPOT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The farmhand is given the mango and the shadiest spot in the village to eat it in, and the two of them end up chatting about soil for an hour. By the end, (name) has stopped looking suspicious, and has started looking curious, which is much more dangerous.
Ending A2 -- ROASTED NUTS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (small)
The farmhand is so touched that (he/she) shares a pouch of roasted nuts from home, a kind nobody here has tasted before, smoky and sweet. It adds a little food, and (name) eats far more than (his/her) share, while pretending not to.

CHOICE B: ASK ABOUT WESTERN FARMING
First popup: (Name) finally gives in to curiosity, and asks how they farm in the west...
Ending B1 -- EVERY THIRD SEASON. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
The farmhand explains how (his/her) people rest each field every third season, letting it grow wild so the soil can recover, and how the harvests are bigger afterwards. (Name) argues with every word, and then goes out and looks at (his/her) tiredest field for a long time. The village learns something useful about the harvest, and (name) rests that field the next season.
Ending B2 -- SOME SECRETS STAY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
When (name) asks about the curved stick, the farmhand smiles and taps (his/her) nose. Some of (his/her) home's farming secrets stay private, and nobody insists. (Name) spends the evening trying to carve a curved stick of (his/her) own. It breaks.

CHOICE C: OFFER A PLOT OF THEIR OWN
First popup: To everyone's surprise, it's (name) who offers. "There's a spare plot by the stream. If you want to show us properly."...
Ending C1 -- EVERY HARVEST TO COME. Chance 50%. EFFECT: new villager (adult): the farmhand
The farmhand chooses to settle in the village as a new adult villager, and help with every harvest to come. (He/She) and (name) argue about farming every single day from then on, and both of them grow the best taro on the island.
Ending C2 -- FIELDS WAITING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The farmhand thanks them warmly, but (his/her) own fields are waiting back home, and they won't harvest themselves. (He/She) heads west in the morning, leaving (name) one curved digging stick as a gift.

CHOICE D: HARVEST SIDE BY SIDE
First popup: (Name) issues a challenge: one row each, the village way and the western way, and see whose basket fills first...
Ending D1 -- A FINE HARVEST. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (normal)
Working the rows with the village farmers, competing furiously, the farmhand helps bring in a fine harvest. Nobody can agree who won. The baskets add a good amount of food to the stores, which everyone agrees is the real victory, though (name) still insists (he/she) was faster.
Ending D2 -- A NEW STICK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Halfway down the first row, the farmhand's curved stick cracks clean in two. (He/She) looks heartbroken. The villagers carve (him/her) a new curved digging stick from good hard wood, and (name) does most of the carving. The farmhand goes home with it, very pleased.

Premise: A farmhand from a settlement in the west shows the village their way of digging taro with a curved stick, always leaving a piece of each plant in the ground. The village farmers are fascinated, and a little offended.

- The farmhand explains resting each field every third season, and the farmer rests their tiredest field the next season. [answers: Ask About Western Farming] [mood: warm] [EFFECT: tech gain (small)]

NEW-145. The Returning Exile   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) a villager who remembers the old fight: any villager 30+. The returnee is a former villager who left years ago (sex at random); if they stay they rejoin as a new adult villager (their old record is gone).
EVENT TEXT
Years ago, a villager left after a bitter fight over a broken promise. There was shouting, a lot of it, and a door flap ripped right off its hut, and then they were gone, and nobody spoke their name for a long time.
Now they are standing at the edge of the village, thinner and greyer than anyone remembers, holding a small bundle. They are asking, very quietly, whether they may come back.
A few people remember what the fight was actually about. Everyone remembers the shouting. (Name) remembers both, and is standing very still, watching. Should (name) welcome them back, or does (he/she) need to hear where they have been first?
Choice A: Meet Them at the Village Edge
Choice B: Ask Where They Have Been
Choice C: Let Them Decide About Staying
Choice D: Rebuild Trust Through Work

CHOICE A: MEET THEM AT THE VILLAGE EDGE
First popup: (Name) walks out to the edge of the village alone. For a long moment the two of them just look at each other...
Ending A1 -- IN SILENCE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
"Come and eat," (name) says finally. The returnee is given a meal and a place to sleep. A few old friends come to sit with them by the fire, in silence, not saying anything about the past at all. It is more welcome than any words would have been. The returnee cries, a little, into the stew.
Ending A2 -- THE PEACE OFFERING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (small)
The returnee holds out the bundle: a basket of smoked fish wrapped carefully in leaves, a peace offering. "I didn't know what else to bring." (Name) takes it. It adds a little food to the stores, and the basket sits by the fire all evening like a promise.

CHOICE B: ASK WHERE THEY HAVE BEEN
First popup: Later, by the fire, (name) asks where they have been all these years...
Ending B1 -- THE COASTLINE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
The returnee describes the coastline they followed, mile after mile, and all the safe landings along it: which beaches have fresh water, which coves shelter from storms, which reefs to avoid. The village learns something genuinely useful about travel, and the fishers ask a hundred questions.
Ending B2 -- NOT READY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The returnee talks about the places they saw, but when the talk drifts toward the old fight, they go quiet. They are not ready to talk about it, and nobody makes them. "Another day," (name) says, and means it kindly.

CHOICE C: LET THEM DECIDE ABOUT STAYING
First popup: (Name) tells the returnee plainly that the choice is theirs, and that (he/she), at least, won't stand in the way...
Ending C1 -- HOME FOR GOOD. Chance 50%. EFFECT: new villager (adult): the returnee
The returnee decides to come home for good, and joins the village as a villager once more. It is awkward for a while. Then one evening, the person they fought with all those years ago sits down beside them at the fire, and passes them a bowl, and that is the end of it.
Ending C2 -- ONLY PEACE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The returnee shakes their head, smiling for the first time. They didn't come back to stay. They only needed to make peace, and now they have. They leave again the next morning, with a lighter step than anyone has ever seen, and (name) watches them go.

CHOICE D: REBUILD TRUST THROUGH WORK
First popup: The returnee asks to help, any way they can. (Name) hands them a digging stick and points at the fields...
Ending D1 -- DAWN TO DUSK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (normal)
The returnee throws themselves into the harvest from dawn to dusk, day after day, without being asked, without complaining. It adds a good amount of food to the stores. Slowly, the village starts nodding to them in the mornings, and then saying hello, and then saving them a seat.
Ending D2 -- SEEN OFF WARMLY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The villagers help mend the returnee's leaky canoe instead, working side by side with them for two days, and in the working, the old anger seems to wear away. When the returnee finally paddles off, they are seen off from the beach with more warmth than anyone expected, including the returnee.

MIXER SEED NEW-145
Premise: Years ago, a villager left after a bitter fight over a broken promise. Now they are standing at the edge of the village, thinner and greyer, asking very quietly whether they may come back.
Roles: rememberer: any villager 30+ | returnee: a former villager (rejoins as a new adult villager)
