NEW-178. The Hidden Diary   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) the finder: any villager 14+.
EVENT TEXT
Under the loose floorboards of an abandoned hut, (name) finds a bundle of bark pages tied up with old fishing line.
It's a diary. Whoever wrote it lived in this hut long ago, and kept careful notes, every day, for years: the weather, the wind, the tides, when the rains came.
Along with some very, very honest opinions about the neighbours.
"Third day of rain. Roof leaking. The family next door sang all night again. They cannot sing. Nobody has ever told them. I will not be the one."
(Name) reads that page three times, laughing, and then realizes that the family next door is probably somebody's great-great-grandparents. What should (name) do with the diary?
Choice A: Copy the Weather Notes
Choice B: Ask Who Lived in That Hut
Choice C: Start a Village Weather Log

CHOICE A: COPY THE WEATHER NOTES
First popup: (Name) decides the weather notes, at least, are too valuable to lose. (He/She) sits down with fresh bark and starts copying...
Ending A1 -- PRESERVED. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
(Name) copies the diary's weather notes onto fresh bark, all of them, years of them: when the first rains came each year, how long the dry seasons lasted, which winds brought storms. It's useful knowledge, carefully kept, and the farmers and fishers pore over it. (Name) leaves out the bits about the neighbours. Mostly.
Ending A2 -- CRUMBLED. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech loss (small)
The oldest pages are so brittle that they crumble at the first touch, into dust and flakes. A fragile part of the diary is lost: the first years of notes, before anyone else in the village kept any. (Name) gathers the dust into a little pot, not knowing what else to do with it.

CHOICE B: ASK WHO LIVED IN THAT HUT
First popup: (Name) takes the diary around the village, asking the oldest villagers whose it might have been...
Ending B1 -- THE FISHER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
An old woman's eyes light up. She remembers the writer from her childhood: a cranky old fisher who never missed a storm warning, not once in forty years. "He'd stand on the beach and shout at us to get the canoes in, and he was always right." That forgotten detail makes the notes far more trustworthy, and the village starts using them to plan the fishing season.
Ending B2 -- NOBODY KNOWS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Nobody agrees on who the writer was. A fisher, a healer, a lonely farmer, a spirit. Nobody pretends to know. But everyone wants to read the bits about the neighbours, and at least three families find out unflattering things about their ancestors.

CHOICE C: START A VILLAGE WEATHER LOG
First popup: Inspired by the diary, (name) proposes that the village keep its own weather log, every day, like the old writer did...
Ending C1 -- A RECORD FOR THE FUTURE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (normal)
The village begins its own careful weather log, kept in the record hut, with a new entry every single day. Different villagers take turns. Over the seasons, the patterns start to show, and the farmers and fishers use it constantly. It becomes a record for future generations. No opinions about the neighbours are allowed. Officially.
Ending C2 -- PRIVATE PAGES. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Before anything else is done with it, (name) decides the diary's personal pages should remain private. They were never meant to be read. (He/She) ties the bundle back up with its old fishing line and puts it back under the floorboards, where it was. Only the weather is copied.

NEW-179. The Old Songbook   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) a singer: any villager 14+. (elder name) an old singer: any elder.
EVENT TEXT
At the bottom of a storage basket, under some old nets and a very surprised spider, (name) finds a songbook: a bundle of damp bark pages, covered in verses nobody has sung in years.
Some of the pages are stuck together. Some are smudged beyond reading. Some have little drawings in the margins: fish, waves, a person dancing.
And one page, all by itself, has just one word written on it, very large, underlined three times: "LOUDER."
(Name) has no idea what it means. But (he/she) finds (himself/herself) grinning at it. What should (name) do with the songbook?
Choice A: Dry and Copy the Pages
Choice B: Ask the Old Singers
Choice C: Teach the Songs to the Children

CHOICE A: DRY AND COPY THE PAGES

Ending A1 -- THE NET SONG. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
As the pages dry, (name) finds a working song for hauling nets: a rhythm for pulling together, a call and a response, a verse for each heave. (He/She) copies it down and teaches it to the fishers, who find they can haul twice as smoothly when they all pull on the beat. It's useful knowledge, preserved, and the beach is a lot noisier.
Ending A2 -- TORN APART. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech loss (small)
Two of the stuck pages tear when (name) tries to peel them apart, and a fragile part of the songbook is lost, half a verse on each torn side, no longer fitting together. Ending B1 -- ROWING TIME. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
(Elder name) suddenly starts humming, then singing, in a cracked, sweet voice. (He/She) remembers this one! It was sung to keep rowing time on long canoe trips, so every paddle hit the water together. It's a forgotten detail that makes the song useful again, and the canoe crews start singing it. And "LOUDER," (elder name) explains, is what the song leader used to shout when the rowers got tired.
Ending B2 -- EVERY TUNE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The old singers disagree about every single tune. Faster. Slower. Higher. "No, it goes like THIS." Nobody pretends to be sure. They end up singing four different versions at once, very badly, and having the time of their lives.

CHOICE C: TEACH THE SONGS TO THE CHILDREN

Ending C1 -- FRESH. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (normal)
The village writes the songs out fresh, on good new bark, and (name) teaches them to the children, who learn them faster than anyone expected. Soon the old songs are being sung all over the village again, and the songbook becomes a careful record for future generations. The children's favourite part is shouting "LOUDER!"
Ending C2 -- THE SAD ONES. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
As (name) goes through the songs, (he/she) finds some very sad ones: songs about lost canoes, and lost children, and people who never came home. (He/She) decides those should stay private, sung only by those who need them. (He/She) teaches the children the happy ones, and keeps the sad ones for (himself/herself).

NEW-180. The Stone of Names   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) the carver: any villager 18+ (prefer high Building).
EVENT TEXT
At the edge of the village stands the carved stone bearing the names of the ancestors: the first villagers, and their children, and their children's children, down through the years.
It is very old. The weather has worn the oldest names down to shallow scratches. Moss fills the rest, soft and green, hiding whole lines.
Families come by often now, tracing the marks with their fingers, trying to find their own great-grandparents. Some of them find nothing, and walk away quietly. (Name) watched a child do it this morning, searching and searching, and then ask (his/her) mother, "Are we not on it?" How can (name) make sure every family is remembered?
Choice A: Trace the Last Clear Names
Choice B: Ask the Families Who Remember
Choice C: Carve a New Stone Beside It

CHOICE A: TRACE THE LAST CLEAR NAMES
First popup: (Name) brings charcoal and thin bark, and begins, very carefully, to scrub the moss away and take rubbings of the names...
Ending A1 -- THE OLD CARVERS' LINES. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
Working slowly, (name) takes rubbings of every clear name, and in the process, studies how the old carvers cut their lines: deep and angled, so the rain runs off instead of pooling. It's useful knowledge, preserved, and every carving in the village is done that way from then on. The rubbings go into the record hut, safe.
Ending A2 -- THE CRUMBLING CORNER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech loss (small)
Scrubbing off the moss in one corner, (name) feels the stone give under (his/her) brush. A crumbling corner chips away, and falls in pieces on the grass, and a fragile part of the stone is lost: four names, maybe five, gone. (Name) kneels there for a long time, holding the pieces.

CHOICE B: ASK THE FAMILIES WHO REMEMBER
First popup: (Name) invites every family to come to the stone, and share whatever they remember about the names...
Ending B1 -- ORDER OF ARRIVAL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
The families' memories, put together, reveal something nobody had noticed: the names weren't carved randomly, or by family. They were carved in order of arrival, the first ones to come to the village at the top. It's a detail that had been overlooked, and suddenly the stone makes sense. The child from this morning finds (his/her) family's name near the bottom. "We were LATE," (he/she) says, delighted.
Ending B2 -- WHOSE IS WHOSE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The families disagree about whose names are whose. Two families claim the same name. A third claims it's a spelling mistake. Nobody pretends to know. It gets heated for a while, and then everyone goes home a little sad, still unsure.

CHOICE C: CARVE A NEW STONE BESIDE IT
First popup: (Name) proposes a new stone, carved fresh, beside the old one, with every name that can still be read or remembered...
Ending C1 -- THE NEW STONE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (normal)
The village carves a new stone with every name that can still be read or remembered, and leaves room at the bottom for the names to come. It takes a whole season. When it's done, every family in the village is on it, including the child's. It's a careful record for future generations, and (name)'s carving skills grow tremendously in the making of it.
Ending C2 -- LEFT TO THE MOSS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
In the end, (name) decides that some names should be left to the moss, and to the memories of their families. Not everything needs to be carved again. (He/She) cleans the stone gently, and leaves it as it is, and plants flowers at its base.

NEW-181. The Apprentice's First Failure   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) an apprentice builder: any villager 14+ with Building under 50. (mentor name) an experienced builder: any villager 25+ (prefer the highest Building), never (name).
EVENT TEXT
It was (name)'s first solo project: a fish drying rack. Four posts, some crossbars, a lot of lashing. (He/She) worked on it all day, alone, proudly refusing help.
The first fish was hung on it at sunset.
The rack collapsed instantly. Not slowly. Instantly, all at once, into a heap of sticks, with a sound like someone dropping an armful of firewood.
The fish is fine. It's lying on top of the pile, looking unbothered.
(Name) is not fine. (He/She) has been standing there staring at the pile of sticks for an hour, not moving, while people walk past pretending not to look. How can anyone help (name) get over this?
Choice A: Look at the Fallen Rack Together
Choice B: Give Them a Smaller Job
Choice C: Call in an Old Builder

CHOICE A: LOOK AT THE FALLEN RACK TOGETHER
First popup: Someone crouches down beside the pile of sticks, picks up a crossbar, and turns it over in (his/her) hands. "Let's see what happened."...
Ending A1 -- TOO LOOSE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Building (a little, +5) for (name)
Going through the pieces one by one, (name) finds it: every lashing had slipped. (He/She) had tied them neatly, but not tightly, not nearly tight enough to hold the weight. (Name) learns, the hard way, just how tight a proper building knot has to be: so tight it creaks, and fingers hurt. The second rack, the next day, holds three dozen fish.
Ending A2 -- NOBODY SHOWED ME. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
As they look, (name) admits, very quietly, that nobody ever actually showed (him/her) how tight to pull the lashings. (He/She) just watched from a distance and guessed. It was a gap in the teaching, not laziness or carelessness, and the builders, hearing this, look at each other with some embarrassment. From then on, every apprentice gets shown properly.

CHOICE B: GIVE THEM A SMALLER JOB
First popup: The builders suggest (name) build something smaller for a while, something with less riding on it. Like stools...
Ending B1 -- STOOLS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Building small stools for a while lets (name) keep working at a pace (he/she) can manage, and practise without anyone's fish at risk. The stools get better and better. By the end of the season, half the village is sitting on (name)'s stools, and (he/she) is ready to try a rack again.
Ending B2 -- THE WOBBLY STOOL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The first stool wobbles badly. Very badly. The first person to sit on it ends up on the ground, laughing. (Name) does not laugh. The builders agree to adjust the plan tomorrow, and someone gently takes the stool away before anyone else sits on it.

CHOICE C: CALL IN AN OLD BUILDER
First popup: (Mentor name) wanders over, looks at the pile, looks at (name), and sits down on the ground beside (him/her)...
Ending C1 -- CROSS-LASHING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Building (some, +10) for (name)
(Mentor name) doesn't say anything about the rack. Instead (he/she) picks up two sticks and starts showing (name) the cross-lashing: over, under, around, pull, the knot that keeps a rack standing for years. They practise until it's dark. The next morning, they build a new rack together, and (mentor name) doesn't touch a single lashing.
Ending C2 -- ON THE CHIEF. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Mentor name) looks at the pile for a long time, then says, "My first rack fell on the chief." (Name) stares. "With the chief under it. In front of everyone. He had a fish on his head for a week." And (name), for the first time all evening, finally laughs.

WHO: (Name) any villager 18+. (mentor name) an experienced worker: any villager 25+ (prefer high Building).

(Name) finishes every job on (his/her) list by noon. Every single one. The fish are cleaned. The water is fetched. The mats are mended.

Nothing to do. For the whole afternoon. Nothing.
In the last hour, (name) has reorganized the tool shelf twice (once by size, once by colour), swept a hut that isn't (his/hers), and offered to help three different people, all of whom said no, a little nervously. Every morning, the workers cross the old log bridge over the gully to get to the fields. It saves an hour's walk.

The later start throws off the whole team's schedule. Jobs that need two people can't start until (name) arrives. The others stand around waiting. They agree to rework it tomorrow, and the comments get a little louder.

CHOICE C: ASK A BRIDGE BUILDER FOR HELP

NEW-189. The Night Shift   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) the night fire-tender: any villager 18+. (mentor name) an old night watcher: any villager 40+.
EVENT TEXT
(Name) volunteered to tend the village fires at night. Someone had to, and (name) has always liked the quiet hours, the stars, the crackle of the coals.
What (name) did not consider was sleeping during the day.
Children shriek. Pots clatter. Someone is always hammering something. And one particular bird, a small brown one with a voice like a squeaky door, sits directly outside (his/her) hut and sings, at the top of its lungs, from noon until dusk. Every day. (Name) is fairly sure it's the same bird. (He/She) is fairly sure it's doing it on purpose.
(Name) has not slept properly in a week. (He/She) has started glaring at birds. How can (name) get some sleep?
Choice A: Look at the Sleeping Hut
Choice B: Swap Every Other Night
Choice C: Ask an Old Night Watcher

CHOICE A: LOOK AT THE SLEEPING HUT
First popup: Someone suggests the problem might be the hut itself, and (name), bleary-eyed, takes a proper look at it, in the middle of the day...
Ending A1 -- GAPS IN THE WALLS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Building (a little, +5) for (name)
Lying on (his/her) mat and looking at the walls, (name) sees it: daylight streaming in through dozens of little gaps in the weave, like stars. No wonder (he/she) can't sleep. (He/She) learns how to weave a tighter wall, packing the strips close and doubling them, a practical building lesson. The hut goes dark as night. The bird is still there, but it's muffled.
Ending A2 -- NOBODY WARNED ME. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name) explains, tiredly, that nobody warned (him/her) how hard day sleeping would be. (He/She) thought it would be easy. (He/She) is struggling, not slacking, and (he/she) would really appreciate it if people stopped asking why (he/she) yawns so much. The village, a little guiltily, agrees to keep the noise down near (his/her) hut.

CHOICE B: SWAP EVERY OTHER NIGHT
First popup: Another villager offers to share the night shift, so (name) can sleep at night every other day...
Ending B1 -- MANAGEABLE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Sharing the night shift lets the work carry on at a pace both of them can manage. (Name) sleeps every other night like a normal person, and on the nights (he/she) works, (he/she) actually enjoys it again. The stars are still beautiful. The bird is still annoying, but only half the time.
Ending B2 -- WHO'S AWAKE? Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The swap confuses everyone about who is meant to be awake. On the second night, both of them fall asleep by the fire. On the third, both of them stay up. Everyone agrees to fix it tomorrow, with a marker stone by the fire to show whose turn it is.

CHOICE C: ASK AN OLD NIGHT WATCHER
First popup: (Mentor name) tended the night fires for twenty years. (Name) goes to ask how (he/she) ever managed to sleep...
Ending C1 -- THE SLEEPING SCREEN. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Building (some, +10) for (name)
(Mentor name) teaches (name) how to build a woven sleeping screen: a thick, double-layered frame that stands around the sleeping mat, blocking out light and most of the noise. They build one together. That afternoon, (name) sleeps for six hours straight, through children, pots, hammering, and the bird. (He/She) wakes up feeling like a new person.
Ending C2 -- JUST GOT USED TO IT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Mentor name) laughs. "Sleep? I never slept well in the day. Not once in twenty years. I just got used to being tired." This is not the answer (name) was hoping for. But somehow, knowing it's not just (him/her), makes it a little easier to bear.

NEW-190. The Worker Who Said No   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) a respected worker: any villager 25+. (mentor name) an experienced stone hauler: any villager 25+ (prefer high Building).
EVENT TEXT
(Name) has just finished building the new canoe shed. It took a whole season. Every post, every beam, every scrap of thatch. It's beautiful, and everyone says so.
The next morning, (name) was asked to start hauling stone for the new sea wall.
"No," said (name). "I'm spent."
Some people think (he/she) has gone soft. They've said so, at the fire, not quite quietly enough.
Those people have not hauled stone recently. Or ever, in some cases. Should the village push (name), or listen to (him/her)?
Choice A: Ask What Makes It Exhausting
Choice B: Give Them Lighter Work for Now
Choice C: Ask a Stone Hauler for Tricks

CHOICE A: ASK WHAT MAKES IT EXHAUSTING

Ending A1 -- THE DRAGGING RUNNERS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Building (a little, +5) for (name)
(Name) shows them the stone sled, and as (he/she) demonstrates, (he/she) sees the problem: its wooden runners dig deep into the sand with every pull, so it's like dragging a plough. (He/She) learns to fit it with rollers instead, logs underneath that turn as it moves. It's a practical building lesson, and the sled moves three times as easily. (Name) agrees to haul stone after all. Next week.
Ending A2 -- HOW MUCH STONE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name) explains that no one ever said how much stone was needed. Ten stones? A hundred? A whole cliff? (He/She) just finished a season of building with no rest, and was asked to start an endless job the next morning. (He/She) was worn out, not lazy. When the builders actually count, it's forty stones. That sounds much more possible.

CHOICE B: GIVE THEM LIGHTER WORK FOR NOW
First popup: The builders suggest (name) take some lighter work for a while, like thatching...
Ending B1 -- SUSTAINABLE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Moving to lighter thatching work lets (name) keep working, at a pace (he/she) can sustain, sitting in the shade, weaving. (His/Her) strength comes back slowly. A moon later, (he/she) turns up at the sea wall, unasked, and starts hauling.
Ending B2 -- ALREADY FULL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The thatching team is already full, and (name) joining makes it awkward: too many hands, not enough thatch, and the head thatcher keeps giving (him/her) things to hold. Everyone agrees to rethink it tomorrow.

CHOICE C: ASK A STONE HAULER FOR TRICKS
First popup: (Mentor name), who has hauled more stone than anyone in the village, comes over to help...
Ending C1 -- LEVER AND PIVOT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Building (some, +10) for (name)
(Mentor name) teaches (name) how to move heavy stones the clever way: a long lever and a log pivot, so one person can lift what three couldn't. "Never lift with your back," (he/she) says. "Lift with the log." (Name) tries it, and a stone (he/she) couldn't budge yesterday rolls over like a pebble. (He/She) learns a great deal about building, and agrees to haul stone after all, the clever way.
Ending C2 -- GLAD OF IT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Mentor name) listens, and then admits that (he/she) once refused the very same job, years ago, after a hard season. "Best thing I ever did. If I'd kept going, I'd have broken my back." (He/She) claps (name) on the shoulder. "You're not soft. You're sensible." (Name) feels much better.

NEW-191. The Water That Tasted Different   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) a scholar: any villager 18+ (prefer the highest Research). (novice name) a novice: any villager 14 to 25. (cook name) a cook: any villager 18+.
EVENT TEXT
Water from the old well tastes sweet and cool, the way water should.
Water from the new well tastes faintly of metal. Like licking a stone. And when it goes into the stew pot, the stew turns a funny, unappetizing grey.
The cooks have refused to touch it. "Grey stew," (cook name) announced, "is not stew." The villagers who spent a whole season digging the new well are taking this very personally. One of them has been drinking the new well's water ostentatiously in front of the cooks all morning, saying "Delicious!" with an increasingly strained smile.
(Name) has been asked to settle it. But how does anyone find out why water tastes different?
Choice A: Taste Both Wells Every Morning
Choice B: Weigh the Rock Against the Rain
Choice C: Let the Cooks Poke Holes in It
Choice D: Show a Novice How to Taste-Test

CHOICE A: TASTE BOTH WELLS EVERY MORNING
First popup: (Name) decides to taste both wells, every morning, at the same time, for a whole week, and write down exactly what (he/she) tastes...
Ending A1 -- AFTER RAIN. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
By the end of the week, there's a clear pattern: the metal taste is strongest the morning after rain, and fades as the days go dry. It's a repeatable pattern that adds to village knowledge, and the cooks agree to use the new well only on dry days. The diggers are mollified. Mostly.
Ending A2 -- CONTRADICTIONS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The tastings contradict each other from day to day: metal one day, sweet the next, metal again the day after, and "sort of fishy" the day after that. (Name) writes down the uncertainty honestly, which the diggers take as a victory and the cooks take as proof of everything.

CHOICE B: WEIGH THE ROCK AGAINST THE RAIN
First popup: (Name) has two ideas: the taste comes from the rock the well was dug through, or from rainwater seeping in. (He/She) sets up a test: a jar from each well, left to settle overnight...
Ending B1 -- RED GRIT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (normal)
In the morning, there's a thin layer of red grit at the bottom of the new well's jar, and nothing at all in the old one's. The rock, not the rain, explains it better: the new well was dug through a band of red stone. Letting the water settle overnight before using it takes most of the taste away. The cooks try it, and the stew comes out almost the right colour.
Ending B2 -- BOTH FIT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Both jars look the same in the morning, and both explanations still fit what they've seen. More tasting is needed. (Name) sighs, and fetches two more jars.

CHOICE C: LET THE COOKS POKE HOLES IN IT
First popup: (Name) invites the cooks to point out anything (he/she) might have got wrong...
Ending C1 -- THE POT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
(Cook name) narrows (his/her) eyes. "Did anyone look at the new well's water before it went in the stew pot? Or only after?" There's a pause. Nobody had. The pot they always used for the new well's water was the old iron-stained one. The grey might come from the pot! It's a hidden assumption, exposed, and the village learns to always test things in a clean bowl first.
Ending C2 -- WHOSE TONGUE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Everyone argues about whose tongue to trust. The cooks say theirs, obviously. The diggers say the cooks are biased. Someone suggests a child, because children are honest, and the child says both waters taste "like water." Eventually everyone agrees to taste from the same cup, at the same time.

CHOICE D: SHOW A NOVICE HOW TO TASTE-TEST
First popup: (Name) decides this is a good chance to teach (novice name) how a proper test is done...
Ending D1 -- FAIRLY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Research (some, +10) for (novice name)
(Name) teaches (novice name) how to repeat the tasting fairly: the same cup every time, the same hour every day, rinse the mouth between wells, and never know which water is which until afterwards. (Novice name) takes it very seriously, and learns a great deal about how to test things properly.
Ending D2 -- ALWAYS FIRST. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Watching (name) work, (novice name) notices that (he/she) always tastes the old well first. Every single time. So the new well always tastes strange by comparison. The notes are revised, and (name) is a little embarrassed, and quietly proud of (his/her) pupil.

NEW-192. The Plant That Grew Sideways   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) a gardener: any villager 18+ (prefer high Farming). (novice name) a novice: any villager 14 to 25. (child name) a child: any villager 5 to 13.
EVENT TEXT
Someone left a seedling in a pot inside the storage shelter, in the dark, and forgot about it for a week.
When (name) finds it, it has grown almost completely flat. Not up, like a plant should. Sideways. Bending hard toward a crack in the shelter wall, where one thin stripe of sunlight comes through.
Its whole stem is stretched out toward that crack, thin and pale and determined.
"It looks," says (child name), who is peering at it over (name)'s shoulder, "like it's trying to escape." Why would a plant grow sideways? (Name) wants to find out.
Choice A: Watch the Seedling for a Week
Choice B: Test Light Against Wind
Choice C: Ask Whether It Is Sick
Choice D: Teach the Turning Trick

CHOICE A: WATCH THE SEEDLING FOR A WEEK
First popup: (Name) leaves the plant where it is, but every morning, turns the pot around so the plant is facing away from the crack...
Ending A1 -- BACK TOWARD THE CRACK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
Every single day, by evening, the plant has bent itself back toward the crack. Every time. It's a repeatable pattern that adds to village knowledge: plants grow toward light, and will twist themselves around to find it. The farmers start thinking about which way their fields face.
Ending A2 -- SOME DAYS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Some days it bends back toward the crack, and some days it doesn't. (Name) can't work out why. (He/She) records the uncertainty honestly. The plant, meanwhile, keeps growing, in several directions at once.

CHOICE B: TEST LIGHT AGAINST WIND
First popup: (Name) has two ideas: the plant is chasing the light, or it's chasing the fresh air that comes through the crack. (He/She) sets up a test...
Ending B1 -- CHASES LIGHT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (normal)
One pot goes by the crack, with sun and air. One goes in a closed corner where there's a draught from under the door, but no light at all. After a few days, the first one is bending toward the crack, and the second one is just standing there, pale and confused. The plant chases light, not air. It's a useful discovery, and the gardeners start spacing seedlings so none of them are in another's shade.
Ending B2 -- BOTH POSSIBLE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Both ideas still seem possible after the test: the second plant bends a little toward the draught, but only a little. More watching is needed. (Name) sets up two more pots.

CHOICE C: ASK WHETHER IT IS SICK
First popup: (Name) asks everyone to suggest what else might be going on...
Ending C1 -- JUST SICK? Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
(Child name) raises a hand. "What if it's just sick? What if it's not clever at all, it's just droopy?" Everyone stops. They had all assumed the bending must mean something clever. It's a hidden assumption, exposed, and the gardeners learn to always check for sickness before deciding a plant is doing something on purpose.
Ending C2 -- MEASURING BENDING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The gardeners argue about how to measure "bending." By eye? By the angle? By how sad it looks? Eventually they agree to use a stick marked with notches, held up against the stem. It takes all afternoon.

CHOICE D: TEACH THE TURNING TRICK
First popup: (Name) decides to show (novice name) how to repeat the pot-turning test properly, with other seedlings...
Ending D1 -- REPEATED. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Research (some, +10) for (novice name)
(Name) teaches (novice name) how to repeat the test with other seedlings: several pots, all turned the same way at the same time, all watered the same. (Novice name) learns how to set up a test that can be trusted, and soon has a whole row of sideways plants in the shelter.
Ending D2 -- MORE WATER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Novice name) notices that one pot was always watered more than the other, because it was nearer the door. That could change everything. The group corrects its notes, and starts over with equal water.

NEW-193. The Shells with Holes   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) a child: any villager 6 to 13. (novice name) a novice: any villager 10 to 25. (adult name) any villager 18+.
EVENT TEXT
Little (name) staggers into the village with a whole basket of shells.
Every single one has a tiny hole in it. A perfectly round hole, smooth-edged, as if someone had drilled it very carefully with a very small drill.
(Name) is absolutely convinced that a very small person, with a very small drill, lives on the beach, drilling shells at night. (He/She) has a name for this person. (He/She) has a drawing of this person. (He/She) wants to leave out a very small bowl of food for this person, and has already started making one. What could really be making the holes?
Choice A: Sort the Shells by Hole
Choice B: Compare the Drill and the Snail
Choice C: Ask Whether Waves Could Do It
Choice D: Teach the Shell Count

CHOICE A: SORT THE SHELLS BY HOLE
First popup: (Adult name) suggests that if there's a tiny driller, they might learn something from the holes. (Name) tips the basket out and begins sorting, very seriously...
Ending A1 -- SAME SPOT, SAME SHELL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
Sorting them, (name) finds the holes are always in the same spot on the same kind of shell: near the hinge on the round ones, near the point on the long ones. Every time. It's a repeatable pattern that adds to village knowledge. (Name) declares that the tiny driller is "very neat."
Ending A2 -- EVERYWHERE AND NOWHERE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The holes seem to be in a different spot on every shell, with no pattern at all. (Name) writes down, in big careful letters, that (he/she) is not sure. Then (he/she) draws the tiny driller looking confused.

CHOICE B: COMPARE THE DRILL AND THE SNAIL
First popup: (Adult name) remembers something about snails, and takes (name) down to the rock pools to look...
Ending B1 -- THE CULPRIT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (normal)
In a rock pool, they catch a small snail sitting on a shell, and when they take it off, there's a tiny round hole starting, exactly like the ones in the basket. The snail drills into other shells to eat what's inside! It's a far better fit than tiny people, and a useful discovery: the fishers start checking clam beds for the drilling snails. (Name) is a little disappointed, then decides the snail IS the tiny driller, and names it.
Ending B2 -- BOTH STAY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
They don't catch any snails drilling. Both ideas stay on the table: the snail, and the tiny people. More shells are needed. (Name) leaves out the very small bowl of food that night anyway, just in case. In the morning, it's empty. (A crab.) (Probably.)

CHOICE C: ASK WHETHER WAVES COULD DO IT
First popup: (Adult name) gathers a few curious villagers and asks: what else could make holes like this?...
Ending C1 -- GRINDING SAND. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
Someone asks whether waves grinding sand against the shells could wear holes in them, over a long time. Everyone had assumed that something alive must have made them. It's a hidden assumption, exposed, and it makes everyone look at the beach differently. (Name) is horrified at the idea that the tiny driller might not exist, and refuses to believe it.
Ending C2 -- MEASURING HOLES. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The group argues about how to measure a hole. By eye? By finger? By how many grains of sand fit through? They finally agree to use a thorn, pushed in until it stops. It's very slow. (Name) gets bored and goes to play.

CHOICE D: TEACH THE SHELL COUNT
First popup: (Name) decides that (novice name) needs to learn how to properly count shells with holes, and takes on the job of teacher...
Ending D1 -- VERY SERIOUSLY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Research (some, +10) for (novice name)
(Name) teaches (novice name), very seriously, how to repeat the shell count on a different beach: walk in a straight line, pick up every shell, count the holes, don't skip the ugly ones. (Novice name) is surprised to find it's actually a good method, and learns a great deal about counting things properly. They find holes on the second beach too.
Ending D2 -- ONE POOL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Novice name) notices that half the shells in the basket came from one single rock pool, because (name) found a good spot and stayed there. That might explain everything, or nothing. The group revises its notes, and (name) is sent back to collect from somewhere else.

NEW-194. The Ant Trail Experiment   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) a scholar: any villager 18+ (prefer high Research). (novice name) a novice: any villager 14 to 25. (child name) a child: any villager 5 to 13.
EVENT TEXT
A long trail of ants runs from the edge of the jungle all the way to the honey pot in the cooking hut. It has been there for days. The cooks have tried everything.
(Name) has a different idea. (He/She) places a flat stone right across the ants' trail, sits down beside it, and waits to see what they will do.
Several villagers, walking past, sit down too. Then a few more. Soon there's a small crowd, sitting in total silence, staring intently at a stone with ants walking into it.
Nobody will admit that it's the most exciting thing they've watched all week. What will the ants do, and what can (name) learn from it?
Choice A: Count the Ants Around the Stone
Choice B: Test Scent Against Sight
Choice C: Ask Why Honey Matters
Choice D: Teach the Ant Watch

CHOICE A: COUNT THE ANTS AROUND THE STONE
First popup: (Name) starts counting the ants, and timing how long it takes them to get around the stone...
Ending A1 -- THE SHORTEST WAY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
For a whole morning, (name) moves the stone, and counts. Every time, the ants mill about in confusion, then find the shortest way around it within the hour, and the trail settles again. Every single time. It's a repeatable pattern, and the crowd cheers each time the trail reforms. The farmers start wondering what else the ants could teach them about finding the shortest path.
Ending A2 -- SOMETHING DIFFERENT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The ants do something different every time the stone moves: go left, go right, go over the top, give up and go home. (Name) records the uncertainty honestly. The crowd is still enthralled.

CHOICE B: TEST SCENT AGAINST SIGHT
First popup: (Name) wonders: are the ants following the trail with their eyes, or by smell? (He/She) sets up a test...
Ending B1 -- SCENT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (normal)
(Name) wipes a stretch of the trail clean with a damp cloth. Nothing changes that anyone can see. But the ants reach the wiped stretch and stop, completely confused, wandering in circles, as if the trail has vanished. Scent, not sight, guides them! It's a useful discovery, and the cooks immediately start wiping down the honey pot's shelf with a damp cloth every morning. The ants stop coming.
Ending B2 -- BOTH FIT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
After wiping, the ants are a little confused, but only a little, and find their way again quickly. Both explanations still fit what they saw. More ant-watching is needed, which nobody minds at all.

CHOICE C: ASK WHY HONEY MATTERS
First popup: (Name) asks the crowd if anyone has any other questions they think should be asked...
Ending C1 -- WITHOUT HONEY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
(Child name) raises a hand. "Would they still march if there wasn't any honey?" There's a long pause. Everyone had just assumed the ants march because of the honey. But nobody had checked. It's a hidden assumption, exposed. They move the honey pot, and the trail breaks up within a day. (Child name) is very pleased.
Ending C2 -- COUNTING MOVING ANTS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The watchers argue about how to count ants that won't stop moving. One by one? By the handful? By guessing? Eventually they agree to count only the ants that cross one particular leaf. It goes surprisingly well, until the leaf blows away.

CHOICE D: TEACH THE ANT WATCH
First popup: (Name) decides (novice name) should learn how to run this kind of test...
Ending D1 -- FAIRLY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Research (some, +10) for (novice name)
(Name) teaches (novice name) how to repeat the stone test fairly: the same stone, the same place, the same time of day, and always write down exactly what happens, not what anyone thinks should happen. (Novice name) learns a great deal about watching carefully, and runs the test (himself/herself) the next morning, with a crowd.
Ending D2 -- THE SHADOW. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Novice name) notices that every time (name) leans over to watch, (his/her) shadow falls across the trail, and the ants scatter. The scholar's own shadow was scaring them! The group revises its notes. (Name) watches from a respectful distance from then on.

MIXER SEED NEW-194

NEW-195. The Two Kinds of Ash   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) a cook: any villager 18+. (novice name) a novice: any villager 14 to 25. (helper name) a helper: any villager 10+.
EVENT TEXT
(Name) noticed it while washing pots.
Ash from the coconut husk fire, stirred into water, turns the water slippery. Strangely slippery, like soap. And it stings a little, in small cuts.
Ash from the driftwood fire, stirred into water, just turns the water grey.
(Name) has now washed every pot in the cooking hut twice, just to check. And then the pots from the hut next door. (He/She) cannot stop wondering why, and has started keeping the two ashes in separate jars, with labels, and talking about them at dinner. What makes the two ashes so different?
Choice A: Soak the Ash Side by Side
Choice B: Test Husk Against Driftwood
Choice C: Ask Why the Pots Got Cleaner
Choice D: Teach the Ash Test

CHOICE A: SOAK THE ASH SIDE BY SIDE
First popup: (Name) sets up two jars of water, one with husk ash, one with driftwood ash, and leaves them for a whole day...
Ending A1 -- EVERY TIME. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
(Name) soaks each ash in its own jar, day after day, and the husk ash makes the water slippery every single time, while the driftwood ash never does. It's a repeatable pattern, and the village now knows: slippery water needs husk ash. Nobody's sure yet what they want slippery water for. (Name) has ideas.
Ending A2 -- SOME BATCHES. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Some batches are slippery, and some aren't, and (name) can't work out why. (He/She) writes down the uncertainty honestly, and starts a third jar.

CHOICE B: TEST HUSK AGAINST DRIFTWOOD
First popup: (Name) has two ideas: it's the fuel itself, or it's the salt in the driftwood that makes the difference. (He/She) tests husk, driftwood, and a mix...
Ending B1 -- THE FUEL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (normal)
A simple test with husk ash, driftwood ash and a half-and-half mix shows it clearly: the more husk ash in the water, the more slippery it gets. The fuel is the cause, not the salt. And the slippery water, (name) discovers, cleans greasy pots far better than plain water ever did. The cooks start keeping a jar of husk-ash water by the washing place, and pots have never been so clean.
Ending B2 -- BOTH FIT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Both explanations, the fuel and the salt in the driftwood, still fit after the test. More tests are needed. (Name) is delighted. More tests is (his/her) favourite thing now.

CHOICE C: ASK WHY THE POTS GOT CLEANER
First popup: (Name) asks the other cooks and helpers if they've noticed anything (he/she) hasn't...
Ending C1 -- CLEANER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
(Helper name) pipes up: "Why do the husk ash pots always come out cleaner?" Everyone stops. They'd all assumed slippery meant dirty, something to rinse off. But the slippery water was cleaning the pots. It's a hidden assumption, exposed, and the village starts washing with ash water on purpose.
Ending C2 -- A HANDFUL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The group argues about how much ash counts as "a handful." Big hands? Small hands? Heaped or flat? Finally they agree on a coconut shell measure: one half shell, level. It takes all evening.

CHOICE D: TEACH THE ASH TEST
First popup: (Name) shows (novice name) how (he/she) has been running the test, so it can be done again by someone else...
Ending D1 -- SAME JAR, SAME MEASURE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Research (some, +10) for (novice name)
(Name) teaches (novice name) how to repeat the ash soak properly: the same jar, the same measure of ash, the same amount of water, the same time. (Novice name) learns a great deal about how to make a test that can be trusted, and gets the same results the very first time.
Ending D2 -- SEAWATER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Novice name) notices that one of the jars had seawater in it, not fresh water, because someone filled it at the beach. That would change everything. The group revises its notes, and (name) labels the water jars too, now.

NEW-196. The Tide Clock   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) a fisher: any villager 18+. (novice name) a novice: any villager 14 to 25. (child name) a child: any villager 5 to 13.
EVENT TEXT
(Name) has an idea. Every day, at exactly the same moment (when the sun touches the top of the big rock on the point), (he/she) will plant a marker stick in the sand at the waterline.
"If we know the tide," (he/she) explains to the other fishers, "we know the fish."
Several of the fishers think this is brilliant. Several others think it's a lot of stick-carrying. One fisher has pointed out that they already know the tide, because it's "the wet bit." (Name) is ignoring that fisher.
(Name) has already gathered a large bundle of sticks. Is it a brilliant idea, or just a lot of stick-carrying?
Choice A: Plant a Stick Every Day
Choice B: Test Moon Against Wind
Choice C: Ask Whether the Rock Moves
Choice D: Teach the Stick Line

CHOICE A: PLANT A STICK EVERY DAY
First popup: Every day for a whole moon, (name) waits for the sun to touch the rock, and plants a stick at the water's edge...
Ending A1 -- A STEADY ORDER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
After a moon of sticks, there's a long, curving line of them across the beach, and (name) can see it clearly: the waterline creeps along the beach in a steady order, day after day, and then comes back again. It's a repeatable pattern that adds to village knowledge, and the fishers start planning their trips by the stick line. Even the "wet bit" fisher.
Ending A2 -- SCATTERED. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Storms and wind scatter the line of sticks, and some get used as firewood by someone who didn't know. (Name) records honestly that (he/she) can't be sure of anything. Then (he/she) starts again, with heavier sticks.

CHOICE B: TEST MOON AGAINST WIND
First popup: (Name) wonders: is the tide following the moon, or the wind? (He/She) starts noting both, beside each stick...
Ending B1 -- THE MOON. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (normal)
Comparing the sticks with the shape of the moon each night shows it clearly: the moon fits the tide's pattern far better than the wind does. The highest sticks are at full and new moon, every time. It's a useful discovery, and the fishers start planning their biggest trips by the moon. (Name) is unbearably smug for a week.
Ending B2 -- BOTH MATTER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Both the moon and the wind still seem to matter, pulling the sticks in different directions. More sticks are needed. The other fishers groan.

CHOICE C: ASK WHETHER THE ROCK MOVES
First popup: (Name) invites everyone to poke holes in the method...
Ending C1 -- THE SUN AND THE ROCK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
(Child name) asks, innocently, "But does the sun touch the rock at the same time every day? Doesn't it go up later in the winter?" There's a long silence. Everyone had assumed the moment was always the same. It's a hidden assumption in the whole method, exposed by a child, and (name) has to rethink the whole thing. The village learns to always check the thing it's measuring with.
Ending C2 -- TOUCHING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The fishers argue about what "touching the rock" means. The bottom of the sun? The middle? When it first goes behind? They finally agree on the very top edge of the rock. The arguing takes longer than planting the sticks.

CHOICE D: TEACH THE STICK LINE
First popup: (Name) decides to teach (novice name) how to keep the stick line, so it can carry on when (name) is out fishing...
Ending D1 -- WITHOUT THE ROCK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Research (some, +10) for (novice name)
(Name) teaches (novice name) how to repeat the daily stick marking without needing the big rock at all: counting breaths from sunrise, using shadow lengths, keeping a knotted cord of days. (Novice name) learns a great deal about measuring time and tide, and keeps the line perfectly while (name) is away.
Ending D2 -- THE WRONG TIME. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Novice name) notices that two of the sticks were planted at the wrong time, on cloudy days when nobody could see the sun touch the rock. They were guesses. The group revises its notes, and marks the cloudy-day sticks with a ring of shells.

NEW-197. The Sick Plant Puzzle   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) a gardener: any villager 18+ (prefer high Farming). (novice name) a novice: any villager 14 to 25. (helper name) a young helper: any villager 8 to 17.
EVENT TEXT
In a long, healthy row of taro, every plant is tall and green and glossy. Except one.
One plant, right in the middle, has wilted. Its leaves have gone yellow and limp, drooping to the ground. The plants on either side of it are perfectly fine.
(Name) has been visiting it every hour since dawn. Crouching beside it. Looking at it. Sometimes, when (he/she) thinks nobody is watching, talking to it. As if, with enough patience, the plant might explain itself.
It hasn't, so far. What is wrong with this one plant?
Choice A: Dig Gently Around the Roots
Choice B: Test Water Against Bugs
Choice C: Ask Whether It Is Just Old
Choice D: Teach the Root Check

CHOICE A: DIG GENTLY AROUND THE ROOTS
First popup: (Name) kneels down and starts, very gently, to scoop the soil away from the wilted plant's roots, with (his/her) bare hands...
Ending A1 -- THE SOGGY HOLLOW. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
The soil around this one plant is soaking wet. It's sitting in a little hollow in the ground where water pools after rain, and its roots are drowning. (Name) checks two other weak plants elsewhere in the garden: same thing, both in hollows. It's a repeatable pattern, and the gardeners start filling in hollows before they plant.
Ending A2 -- THE SAME ROOTS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The roots look much the same as the healthy plants' roots: white, firm, normal. (Name) can't see anything wrong. (He/She) records the uncertainty honestly, packs the soil back, and apologizes to the plant.

CHOICE B: TEST WATER AGAINST BUGS
First popup: (Name) has two ideas: too much water, or bugs in the soil. (He/She) takes a cutting and sets up a test...
Ending B1 -- SOGGY SOIL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (normal)
(Name) replants one cutting in dry ground and leaves the rest of the plant where it is. Within days, the cutting in dry ground perks up, green and healthy, while the original keeps drooping. No bugs are found on either. The soggy soil explains the wilting far better than bugs do, and the gardeners learn to dig drainage channels along the wettest rows. The next harvest is the best in years.
Ending B2 -- BOTH FIT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Both explanations still fit: the cutting perks up a little, but there are some bugs, too. (Name) needs more plants to be sure. (He/She) looks at the long, healthy row, and decides not to make any more of them sick to find out.

CHOICE C: ASK WHETHER IT IS JUST OLD
First popup: (Name) asks everyone who works in the garden what they think...
Ending C1 -- PLANTED FIRST. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)

Everyone had assumed all the plants in the row were the same age. It's a hidden assumption, exposed. The plant isn't sick. It's just old, and done. The gardeners start marking when each plant goes in.
Ending C2 -- COUNTING DROOPS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The gardeners argue about how to measure "wilted." Yellow? Floppy? Sad-looking? They finally agree to count drooping leaves: anything touching the ground counts as a droop. The wilted plant has seven. It's very satisfying to have a number, though it doesn't help the plant.

CHOICE D: TEACH THE ROOT CHECK
First popup: (Name) decides to show (novice name) how to check a plant's roots without killing it...
Ending D1 -- WITHOUT HARM. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Research (some, +10) for (novice name)
(Name) teaches (novice name) how to repeat the root check without harming the plant: dig at an angle, from the side, never straight down; feel, don't pull; put everything back the way it was. (Novice name) learns a great deal about plants, and finds two more drowning taro by the end of the day.
Ending D2 -- THE SHORTCUT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Novice name) notices something nobody else did: the sick plant is also the one everyone steps on when they take the shortcut across the garden. There's a faint path of footprints right over it. The group revises its notes, and puts a fence around the taro row.

NEW-198. The Stone That Floats   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) a child: any villager 5 to 13. (novice name) a novice: any villager 10 to 25. (adult name) any villager 18+.
EVENT TEXT
Little (name) found a stone near the volcano: grey, light, full of tiny holes, like a sponge made of rock. (He/She) brought it home and dropped it in the water bucket to wash it.
It floated.
A STONE. That FLOATS.
(Name) has been standing over the bucket for an hour now, poking the stone under with a finger and watching it bob straight back up, over and over and over, with a look of total wonder. (He/She) has told everyone. Several adults have come to look and have also poked it. It bobbed back up for them too. How can a stone float? (Name) has to know.
Choice A: Float Every Volcano Stone
Choice B: Test Air Against Magic
Choice C: Ask Whether It Stays Afloat
Choice D: Teach the Bucket Test

CHOICE A: FLOAT EVERY VOLCANO STONE
First popup: (Adult name) suggests they find out if all volcano stones float. (Name) grabs a basket and drags (him/her) off toward the volcano at a run...
Ending A1 -- ONLY THE HOLEY ONES. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
They come back with a whole basket of volcano stones, and (name) tests every one. Only the light, holey ones float. Every time. The heavy, solid black ones sink straight to the bottom. It's a repeatable pattern, and the builders get very interested in stones that are light enough to carry easily.
Ending A2 -- SOME FLOAT, SOME SINK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Some holey stones float, and some sink, and some float for a while and then sink. (Name) frowns at the bucket and admits (he/she) is not sure why. It's the first time anyone has seen (him/her) stumped, and (he/she) seems to enjoy it.

CHOICE B: TEST AIR AGAINST MAGIC
First popup: Half the village thinks the stone is full of air. The other half thinks it's a little bit of volcano magic. (Adult name) suggests a test...
Ending B1 -- THE AIR. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (normal)
They grind one stone into powder, very carefully, so all the little holes are crushed. The wet powder sinks to the bottom of the bucket like sand. The trapped air in the holes explains the floating far better than magic does. It's a useful discovery, and the boat builders start wondering whether trapped air could help their canoes float higher. (Name) is sad about the ground-up stone, and keeps the rest.
Ending B2 -- STILL POSSIBLE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The ground powder sinks, but some of it floats on top for a while, which nobody can explain. Both air and a little volcano magic still seem possible, and more stones are needed. (Name) is delighted. (He/She) was rooting for magic.

CHOICE C: ASK WHETHER IT STAYS AFLOAT
First popup: (Adult name) asks everyone: "What haven't we thought of?"...
Ending C1 -- FOREVER? Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
Someone asks, "Will it still float after a whole day in the water?" Everyone had assumed floating was forever. So they leave it overnight. In the morning, the stone has sunk to the bottom: the water slowly crept into the holes. It's a hidden assumption, exposed, and the village learns that what's true for a moment isn't always true for a day.
Ending C2 -- WHAT "FLOATS" MEANS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The group argues about how to test "floats." In the bucket? In the sea? Does bobbing halfway count? They finally agree on the big water jar, filled to the brim. (Name) has already floated the stone in every container in the village anyway.

CHOICE D: TEACH THE BUCKET TEST
First popup: (Name) decides (novice name) needs to be taught the floating test, properly, by an expert. (Name) is the expert...
Ending D1 -- A NEW BASKET. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Research (some, +10) for (novice name)
(Name) teaches (novice name) how to repeat the floating test with a new basket of stones: one stone at a time, dry stones only, same bucket, write down what happens. (Novice name) is surprised to find (himself/herself) learning a great deal from a small child, and runs the test perfectly.
Ending D2 -- STILL WET. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Novice name) notices that some of the stones were still wet from the last test, so their holes were already full of water, and they sank because of that. The group revises its notes, and (name) lays all the stones out in the sun to dry, in a very neat row.

NEW-199. The Breadfruit Question   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (Name) a cook: any villager 18+. (novice name) a novice: any villager 14 to 25. (helper name) a helper: any villager 10+.
EVENT TEXT
Two breadfruit, picked on the same morning, from the same grove, sit side by side on the shelf in the cooking hut.
One has gone soft and sweet in two days, perfect for roasting.
The other is still as hard as a stone. (Name) knocked on it this morning. It went "tok."
(Name) has started talking to them. "What's different about you?" (he/she) asks the hard one, every morning. "What did you do?" (he/she) asks the soft one. The other cooks have started avoiding the shelf. How can (name) find out?
Choice A: Track Every Breadfruit Picked
Choice B: Test Sunny Tree Against Shady Tree
Choice C: Ask Whether the Basket Matters
Choice D: Teach the Breadfruit Tally

CHOICE A: TRACK EVERY BREADFRUIT PICKED
First popup: From now on, (name) decides, every breadfruit that comes into the cooking hut gets a mark: which tree, which side of the tree, and what day...
Ending A1 -- THE SUNNY SIDE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
After a few weeks of marks, the pattern shows: breadfruit from the sunny side of the tree softens first, every time, and the shady side stays hard longer. It's a repeatable pattern, and the cooks start picking from the sunny side for this week's meals and the shady side for next week's. Nothing goes to waste.
Ending A2 -- NO ORDER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The fruit soften in no clear order at all: sunny side, shady side, top, bottom, it doesn't seem to matter. (Name) writes down the uncertainty honestly, and asks the hard breadfruit, again, what it's playing at.

CHOICE B: TEST SUNNY TREE AGAINST SHADY TREE
First popup: (Name) has two ideas: it's how ripe the fruit was when it was picked, or it's how it was stored afterward. (He/She) sets up a test...
Ending B1 -- PICKED RIPE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (normal)
(Name) picks fruit from a sunny tree and a shady tree, and stores them all exactly the same way. The sunny tree's fruit softens first, the shady tree's later, even though they're stored together. How ripe the fruit was when it was picked, not how it was stored, explains it better. The pickers learn to tell ripeness on the tree by the colour of the skin, and the cooking hut's timing improves enormously.
Ending B2 -- BOTH FIT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The results are muddled, and both explanations still fit. More breadfruit are needed. The cooks don't mind; more breadfruit means more roasted breadfruit.

CHOICE C: ASK WHETHER THE BASKET MATTERS
First popup: (Name) asks the other cooks if they have any ideas, and promises not to talk to the breadfruit while they think...
Ending C1 -- THE BANANAS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
(Helper name) frowns. "Wasn't the soft one stored next to the bananas? Before it went on the shelf?" Everyone had assumed both breadfruit were kept the same way. They weren't. (Name) tests it: a hard breadfruit next to ripe bananas softens in a day. It's a hidden assumption, exposed, and a useful trick: to ripen fruit faster, store it with bananas.
Ending C2 -- "SOFT". Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The cooks argue about what counts as "soft." Squishy? Bendy? Smells sweet? Finally they agree on a thumb press: if a thumb leaves a dent, it's soft. Every breadfruit in the hut is pressed by every cook. Several are now dented.

CHOICE D: TEACH THE BREADFRUIT TALLY
First popup: (Name) decides (novice name) should learn to keep the tally, so the cooking hut can carry on the work...
Ending D1 -- ONE MARK PER FRUIT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Research (some, +10) for (novice name)
(Name) teaches (novice name) how to repeat the tally properly: one mark per fruit, one mark per day, a different mark for each tree, all on the same board. (Novice name) learns a great deal about keeping records that can be trusted, and soon the board is covered in neat marks.
Ending D2 -- SWAPPED. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Novice name) notices that two of the fruit swapped places in the basket at some point, so their marks no longer match. Someone moved them while cooking. The group revises its notes, and (name) starts carving marks directly onto the breadfruit skins.

NEW-200. The Echo in the Cave   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: (name1) and (name2) two explorers: any villagers 14+. (novice name) a novice: any villager 14 to 25.
EVENT TEXT
(Name1) and (name2) are exploring the cliffs when they find a cave mouth they've never noticed before. Naturally, (name1) leans in and shouts "HELLO!"
"HELLO!" comes back, quickly, from the left wall.
Then nothing. They wait.
Then, much later, from somewhere deep on the right: "...hello."
It's the same shout. It must be. But it came back twice, at two different times, from two different directions. And the second one sounds, (name2) insists, slightly offended. As if it was interrupted.
(Name1) and (name2) look at each other. Then at the cave. Neither of them is sure whether to shout again. What is making that second voice?
Choice A: Clap and Count Each Echo
Choice B: Test Distance Against Tunnels
Choice C: Ask Whether It Is Really an Echo
Choice D: Teach the Echo Count

CHOICE A: CLAP AND COUNT EACH ECHO
First popup: (Name1) decides to treat it scientifically. (He/She) claps once, sharply, and counts heartbeats until each echo comes back...
Ending A1 -- ALWAYS THE SAME. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
(Name1) claps and counts, over and over, and the gap is always the same: two heartbeats for the left echo, eleven for the right. Every time. It's a repeatable pattern that adds to village knowledge, and the researchers start using echoes to guess how deep caves go, without having to walk into them.
Ending A2 -- SHIFTING FEET. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The counts change every time someone shifts their feet, or turns their head, or breathes too loudly. (Name1) records the uncertainty honestly. (Name2) keeps whispering "it's offended" every time the second echo comes back.

CHOICE B: TEST DISTANCE AGAINST TUNNELS
First popup: (Name1) thinks the right wall must just be much farther away. (Name2) thinks there must be a hidden tunnel. They light a torch and go in to find out...
Ending B1 -- THE HIDDEN TUNNEL. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (normal)
Pacing the cave by torchlight, they find the right wall is no farther away than the left. But in its corner, low down, there's a narrow tunnel, curving off into the dark. The sound goes down the tunnel, bounces around somewhere deep inside, and comes back late. A hidden tunnel bending the sound explains it far better than distance. The researchers learn a great deal about how sound travels through rock, and nobody goes down the tunnel. Yet.
Ending B2 -- BOTH FIT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The cave turns out to be strangely shaped, and both explanations still fit: the right wall IS farther, and there MIGHT be a tunnel, behind some rocks. More shouting is needed. (Name1) and (name2) do a lot more shouting.

CHOICE C: ASK WHETHER IT IS REALLY AN ECHO
First popup: Back in the village, (name1) and (name2) tell the story at the fire, and ask what everyone else thinks...
Ending C1 -- PROBABLY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
Someone asks, very quietly, whether the second voice is an echo at all. Everyone goes still. They had all assumed it was. It's a hidden assumption in the whole echo investigation. So the next day, a group goes back and checks, very carefully, with claps instead of words. Claps come back. It's only an echo. Probably. The village learns to always check its assumptions, and nobody goes into that cave alone.
Ending C2 -- "VERY". Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The explorers argue about how loud to shout for a fair test. Quietly? Normally? As loud as possible? They finally agree on "very." The next day, (name1) shouts "very" loudly into the cave. "VERY," says the left wall. A long pause. "...very," says the right.

CHOICE D: TEACH THE ECHO COUNT
First popup: (Name1) decides (novice name) should learn the clap-and-count method, so the echo can be studied properly...
Ending D1 -- AT THE CAVE MOUTH. Chance 50%. EFFECT: skill + Research (some, +10) for (novice name)
(Name1) teaches (novice name) how to repeat the clap-and-count test at the cave mouth: stand on the same rock, clap the same way, count the same heartbeats, write it down. (Novice name) learns a great deal about measuring things nobody can see, and gets the same numbers as (name1), the very first time.
Ending D2 -- THE TIDE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Novice name) notices that during one count the tide was in, filling the bottom of the cave with water, and during the other it was out. Water changes how sound bounces. The group revises its notes, and starts recording the tide alongside every clap.

# MYSTERY AND MYTH MY-001 to MY-058
##############################################################################
NEW ISOLA MYSTERY AND MYTH EVENTS -- FULL ISLAND EVENTS, MY-001 TO MY-058 (draft for the owner, 2026-11-15)
Rewritten from "115 New Isola Mystery and Myth Events - Fleshed Out" as full island events in the style of the owner's handwritten events (The Aspiring Adventurer, The Cave Explorers, The Climb).
Each event is written twice: STATIC (the handwritten layout) and MIXER (a Living Event Engine seed).
The MY-### numbers are kept. Every EFFECT is the source's own PROPOSED GAMEPLAY EFFECTS line for that ending; an ending with no line in the source says "none".
Supernatural encounters stay ambiguous: every strange thing in these events could have an ordinary explanation, and none is confirmed.

How to read this:
- (Name) / (name) is the picked villager's full name; (he/she), (his/her), (him/her), (himself/herself) follow that villager's sex.
- In a sentence about a stranger, traveler or visitor, the pronouns follow that stranger's own sex, picked at random (as for the stranger in The Aspiring Adventurer).
- (name2) is a second villager when an event needs one; (name2.he/she), (name2.his/her) and (name2.him/her) follow (name2)'s sex, as (teacher.he/she) does in the owner's Child of Legend. When an ending mentions an unnamed second villager (an elder, a healer, a builder, a neighbor, a cousin), that villager is (name2) for those pronouns, picked at random from the matching villagers; such a villager only appears in the story and gets no effect. Likewise (child.his/her) follows (child).
- Mixer flavour lines may use {a|b|c}: the mixer picks one option, as in the owner's Cooking Contest.
- Unless WHO says otherwise, the picked villager is any eligible villager aged 14 or older: never a nursing mother or father, never anyone dead or away, never the game's special villagers (the Golden Child, The Lost Children's totems, The Secret City's chief, New Believers' special roles), and in New Believers believers only.
- "Ending A1" is the first outcome of the first choice in the source, "A2" the second, and so on; each ending's chance is within its choice.
- Food and tech sizes (small/normal/large) follow the REWARDS rule in the owner's events file: a random amount in the game's own island-event range, small = half, large = twice, scaled with the village.

MY-001. The Person Beyond the Torchlight   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: any eligible villager aged 14 or older.
EVENT TEXT
(Name) is walking home late after a long day's work, humming to (himself/herself) to keep the dark at bay. Just past the last torch on the path, (he/she) stops. Someone is standing there, perfectly still, at the very edge of the light. The torch spits and leans in a wind (name) cannot feel, and the figure's outline wavers like a reed in a current.
Then the figure speaks. It calls (him/her) by the silly little pet name (his/her) mother used when (name) was barely walking, a name nobody alive in the village has used in years. (Name)'s skin prickles all over. Every sensible part of (him/her) says to run. Every curious part of (him/her) wants to know how on earth this stranger knows that name. What should (name) do?

Choice A: Approach the Figure
Choice B: Call for Witnesses
Choice C: Ask How They Know
Choice D: Walk Away

CHOICE A: APPROACH THE FIGURE
First popup: (Name) swallows hard and takes one step past the torch, then another. The figure does not move. Up close, (he/she) can make out a hooded wrap, a walking stick, and a face half in shadow...
Ending A1 -- THE BURIED STONE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
"There is a storm coming," the figure says softly. "It will wash the earth from a stone that wants to be found." Before (name) can ask what that means, the figure steps behind a tree and simply isn't there anymore. (Name) circles the trunk twice, feeling foolish. Three days later a storm rolls in off the sea, and when it clears, the rain has stripped the soil from a hillside near the path, uncovering a flat stone carved with lines no one can read. The elders argue over it for a week. (Name) doesn't say much. (He/She) is still thinking about that voice.

MY-004. The Crate with No Owner   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: any eligible villager aged 14 or older.
EVENT TEXT

Choice D: Store It for Its Owner

Choice A: Open It in Calm Weather

Choice D: Give It to a Traveler

At the very height of the storm, when the wind is screaming and the huts are shaking, the box goes completely silent. Not a hum. Nothing. As if it's listening. It stays silent until the last of the wind dies down, and then, very softly, it starts humming again. (Name) doesn't sleep at all.

MY-024. The Lantern on the Empty Boat   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: any eligible villager aged 14 or older.
EVENT TEXT
Late at night, (name) is walking along the lagoon when (he/she) sees a light out on the water. A small boat is drifting in toward the shore, slow and silent, with a lantern hanging from its prow on a hook of carved bone. The flame is steady and blue in the still night.
Nobody is paddling. Nobody is sitting in it. The boat simply drifts closer and closer, as if it knows exactly where it's going, and bumps softly against the sand at (name)'s feet. The lantern keeps burning. What should (name) do?

Choice A: Bring the Boat Ashore
Choice B: Search the Coast
Choice C: Extinguish the Lantern
Choice D: Keep Watch Until Dawn

CHOICE A: BRING THE BOAT ASHORE

Ending A1 -- THE DRIED FOOD. Chance 50%. EFFECT: food gain (normal)

Ending A2 -- THE DRAWING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

CHOICE B: SEARCH THE COAST

Ending B2 -- NO ONE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

Ending C2 -- ONCE MORE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
The flame goes out. (Name) turns to walk away, and behind (him/her), the lantern quietly lights itself again, blue and steady. (Name) freezes. After a long moment, the flame flickers and finally goes dark on its own, as if it was just saying goodbye.

CHOICE D: KEEP WATCH UNTIL DAWN

Ending D1 -- THE OWNER. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

Ending D2 -- THE ROPE. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name) dozes off just before dawn. When (he/she) wakes, the boat is gone. The rope is still tied firmly to the dock post, the knot still tight, the other end neatly looped as if it had never been tied to anything at all.

MY-025. The Beggar and the Broken Cup   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: any eligible villager aged 14 or older.
EVENT TEXT
An old beggar stops (name) on the path and holds out a cup of red clay with a crack running all the way down one side. "Water, please," the beggar says. "Just a little."
(Name) freezes. That voice. (He/She) knows that voice. It sounds a great deal like someone (name) knew long ago, someone who isn't around anymore, though (he/she) can't quite place who. The beggar's face is lined and brown and entirely unfamiliar. The cracked cup trembles in (his/her) hands. What should (name) do?

Choice A: Mend the Cup
Choice B: Give a Better Cup
Choice C: Invite the Beggar to Rest
Choice D: Send the Beggar Away

CHOICE A: MEND THE CUP

Ending A1 -- THE REPAIR TRICK. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)
"No, no, not like that," the beggar chuckles, taking over. "Score the edges first. Add ash to the clay. Then bake it slow in the embers." The old one shows (name) a clay repair so strong that, when it's done, the crack is harder than the rest of the cup. (Name) passes the trick on to the potters, and the village's pots last far longer after that. Your villagers gain (award) tech points.
Ending A2 -- BROKEN AGAIN. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name) works hard on it, and the mended cup holds water beautifully. The beggar drinks, thanks (him/her) in that familiar voice, and shuffles off down the path. (Name) watches (him/her) go. Just as the beggar reaches the bend, there's a faint crack, and water splashes onto the dust. The cup has broken again, along exactly the same line. The beggar doesn't look back.

CHOICE B: GIVE A BETTER CUP

Ending B1 -- THE TURTLE CHARM. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

(Name) threads it on a string and wears it around (his/her) neck. It's only later, lying awake, that (he/she) remembers whose voice it was. Ending B2 -- THE CUP OF SOMEONE DEAR. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

So (name) fills the cracked cup instead, slowly, carefully, letting the beggar sip from it before it leaks away. They don't say much. Somehow, they don't need to.

CHOICE C: INVITE THE BEGGAR TO REST

Ending C1 -- THE OLD PLANTING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (normal)
As the afternoon goes by, a little crowd gathers around the old beggar, who tells story after story about the village as it was long ago, including one about how the farmers used to plant their yams in mounds with ash and fish bones buried underneath. Ending C2 -- NO MEMORY OF ARRIVING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

The old one has no memory of the path, or the cup, or (name). And when (he/she) speaks now, the voice is just an ordinary old voice, not the one (name) remembered. (Name) walks the old one to the edge of the village and wonders, all night, what (he/she) heard.

CHOICE D: SEND THE BEGGAR AWAY

Ending D1 -- NOTHING FOLLOWS. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

Ending D2 -- THE VOICE ON THE PATH. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

MY-026. The House That Dreamed   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]

Before long, half a dozen villagers have admitted it: the same house, the same table, the same empty seat, the same voice. Some are excited. Some are nervous. Choice B: Visit the Ruins

MY-027. The River's Returned Gift   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]

(Name)'s favourite digging tool finally snapped in half yesterday, and in a fit of temper, (he/she) flung both pieces into the river. Then (he/she) went home and sulked about it all evening.
This morning, on a flat stone just above the waterline, lies the very same tool. Only it isn't broken anymore. It's whole, and polished, and shining as if it had just been made, with a fresh new edge and a handle smoothed to a soft gleam. (Name) looks up and down the river. Nobody's there. The river is low and green and says nothing. What should (name) do?

Choice A: Use the Returned Tool

Ending A2 -- SNAP. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none

Ending B1 -- THE POLISHING METHOD. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (small)

MY-033. The Stone That Remembered   [VV1, VV2, VV3, VV4, VV5]
WHO: any eligible villager aged 14 or older. The two villagers whose argument is heard (Ending A2) are story only. (name2), in Choice B, is the oldest villager (flavour only, no effect).
EVENT TEXT
(Name) is clearing out an old fire pit when (he/she) picks up a round grey stone, smoothed by years and years of cooking pots, and still warm, though the fire has been out for days.
Then (he/she) hears it. Whispers. Coming from the stone. Fragments of conversations, voices (name) half knows, talking about things that happened years and years ago, like voices heard through a wall. "...the yams by the river..." "...don't tell your father..." "...she said yes!" What should (name) do?

Choice A: Listen Closely
Choice B: Ask an Elder
Choice C: Place It in the Sun
Choice D: Return It to the Hearth

CHOICE A: LISTEN CLOSELY
First popup: (Name) sits down, holds the warm stone to (his/her) ear, and closes (his/her) eyes, trying to catch every word...
Ending A1 -- THE OLD PLANTING. Chance 50%. EFFECT: tech gain (normal)
Among the whispers, one voice comes through clearly: an old farmer explaining, step by step, how to plant beans beside the corn so they climb it, and squash beneath so their leaves keep the soil damp. (Name) has never heard of planting that way. (He/She) tries it in a corner of the garden, and by the end of the season the three plants have outgrown everything else. The farmers are amazed. Your villagers gain (award) tech points.
Ending A2 -- THE PRIVATE ARGUMENT. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
Then the stone starts repeating something recent. An argument. A private one, between two villagers, about something they'd both rather nobody knew. (Name) yelps and drops the stone, but it's too late; a few others nearby heard it too. The two villagers are mortified, and stop speaking to each other for a whole week. Then, at last, they make up over a shared pot of stew, and everyone politely pretends it never happened.

CHOICE B: ASK AN ELDER
First popup: (Name) brings the stone to (name2), the oldest villager (he/she) can find, who takes it in two wrinkled hands and listens...
Ending B1 -- THE FORMER FAMILY. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name2)'s eyes fill with tears. "This is from the old hearth," (name2.he/she) says. "My grandmother's family lived there, before the big storm. I can hear my grandmother. I can hear her laughing." (Name2) holds the stone a long time. Then (name2.he/she) asks if (name2.he/she) may keep it, and (name) says yes, of course.
Ending B2 -- JUST THE WIND. Chance 50%. EFFECT: none
(Name2) listens patiently for a long while, then hands it back. "I hear nothing, child. Look here, though: there's a crack running right through it. When it's warm, the air inside moves, and the wind whistles through. That's all your whispers are." It's a very sensible explanation. (Name) wishes (he/she) believed it.

CHOICE C: PLACE IT IN THE SUN
